->EPICHARMUS.<-

It is my purpose in this work to give an account of the earliest ages and of the great events that happened during the infancy of the world. Consequently, I shall present to the reader what non-Jewish <note>original: "Gentile"</note> writers have said on this subject, alongside the accounts given by Moses, for as long as his writing covers the general history of mankind. By these means, I will be able to provide remarkable proof of those great occurrences which the sacred writer <note>original: "penman," referring to Moses as the traditional author of Genesis</note> recorded. 

When his history becomes more limited—focusing on a specific people and a private religious system <note>original: "dispensation"</note>—I shall proceed to show what followed his account after the migration of families and the scattering <note>original: "dispersion"</note> from the plains of Shinar <note>a region in Mesopotamia, traditionally associated with the Tower of Babel</note>. They stood their ground during the general migration of families, but were at last scattered over the face of the earth. Wherever they went, they introduced many useful arts and were looked up to as a superior order of beings; hence they were called Heroes, Daemons <note>original: "Dæmons"; in the ancient Greek sense of a benevolent, semi-divine spirit or guardian</note>, Heliadae <note>meaning "children of the Sun"</note>, and Macarians <note>meaning "the blessed ones"</note>.

They were joined in their expeditions by other nations, especially by the related branches of their family: the Mizraim, the Caphtorim, and the sons of Canaan. These were all from the line of Ham, who was held in the highest veneration by his posterity. They called him Amon, and having in the course of time raised him to a divinity, they worshipped him as the Sun. From this worship, they were called Amonians. This is a name that will continually occur in the course of this work, and I am authorized in the use of it by Plutarch. From his writing, we may infer that the name was not uncommon among the sons of Ham. He specifies particularly regarding the Egyptians that when any two members of that nation met, they used it as a term of honor in their <sup>2</sup> salutations and called one another Amonians. What I have said about Sesostris and Osiris will be repeated about Ninus and Semiramis—two personages who are just as mythical <note>original: "ideal"</note> as the former. There were never any such expeditions undertaken, nor conquests made, as those attributed to these princes; nor were any such empires ever formed as those supposed to have been established by them. I place just as little value on the histories of Saturn, Janus, Pelops, Atlas, Dardanus, Minos of Crete, and Zoroaster of Bactria. Regarding Greece, I can give credit to very few events that occurred before the Olympiads <note>the four-year periods used by the Greeks for dating, beginning in 776 BC</note>. I cannot give the slightest belief to the story of Phryxus and the golden fleece. After having cleared my path, I shall proceed to the sources from which the Greeks drew. I shall provide an account of the Titans and the Titanic War, along with the history of the Cuthites <note>the descendants of Cush, whom the author believes were a primary ancient civilization</note> and the ancient Babylonians. This will be accompanied by the pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note> history of the Great Flood <note>original: "Deluge"</note>, the migration of mankind from Shinar, and the dispersion from Babel. The whole work will be crowned with an account of ancient Egypt, in which many circumstances of great importance to chronology will be stated. In the execution of this entire project, many surprising proofs will be brought forward to confirm the Mosaic account <note>the biblical history written by Moses</note>. <header># PREFACE.</header>

Since my research covers very distant subjects and draws on various histories, and because the truth must often be reached through logical deduction, I have found it necessary to present my sources directly to the reader. This allows the reader to judge the accuracy <note>original: "propriety"</note> of my citations and see that my conclusions are valid. 

This approach, however, will make my quotations quite numerous, which might be discouraging to some, especially since they are mostly from Greek authors. I have tried to fix this inconvenience in most important cases, either by summarizing the content before the quote or by providing a translation afterward. Perhaps better days will come when the Greek language is held in higher regard and its beauty is more appreciated. 

Because I am primarily indebted to the Greeks for my information <note>original: "intelligence"</note>, I have followed their spelling <note>original: "orthography"</note> in some respects and have recorded ancient terms as they were written by them. In fact, I see no reason why we should not present all names of Greek origin as they were written by those people, instead of following the Roman style of pronunciation. I know of almost nothing that has harmed ancient history more than the tendency of writers to inconsistently record foreign terms rather than using the original native versions. 

I will admit, however, that I have not followed my own principles consistently, as I have only used Greek spelling in certain instances. I have only dared to use it for specific terms where I felt the word's origin <term>etymology</term> <note>the study of the history and origins of words</note> was at stake. Even though this method is justified and valid, I feared it would seem too strange <note>original: "novel"</note> to be used everywhere.

<page-num>xvii</page-num>

<header>PREFACE</header>

My purpose throughout has been to give a new direction to ancient history and to place it on a more secure foundation. The mythology of Greece is a vast collection of obscure traditions that have been passed down from the earliest times. They were described in hieroglyphics <note>original: "hieroglpyhics"</note> and have been hidden in allegory; the same history is often repeated under a different system and arrangement. Much of this information <note>original: "intelligence"</note> has come down to us through the poets, which has made it even more extravagant and strange.

We find the whole subject to be like a grotesque picture—vividly colored, glaring, and filled with groups of fantastic imagery, like what one might see on an Indian screen. Such things amuse the eye in a tiring way <note>original: "painfully amused"</note>, but they offer little that is satisfactory or useful. We must, however, make this distinction: in the allegorical stories of Greece, there was always a hidden meaning, even if it has escaped our notice.

In short, we must view ancient mythology as still being in a chaotic state, where the human mind has grown weary from wandering through its disorganized form <note>original: "crude consistence"</note> without ever finding a single spot where it could rest safely. This is why the request "Where can I stand?" <note>original: "πῶς στῶ" (pōs stō). This is a reference to the famous quote attributed to Archimedes regarding the use of a lever: "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth."</note> has been repeated for ages. It is my hope and my belief <note>original: "presumption"</note> that such a landing place <term>appulse</term> <note>a point of arrival or contact</note> may be found—a place where we may take our stand. From there, we may have a full view of the mighty expanse before us, and we may also discover the original design and order of all those subjects that time and distance have made so confused and uncertain.

# RADICALS

->Persuasion’s path it is, for it attends upon Truth.<-
<note>original Greek: Πειθες δ’ εσι κελευθος, αληθειη γαρ οπηδει (Peithes d' esti keleuthos, alētheiē gar opēdei)</note>

->PARMENIDES<-

The materials of which I propose to make use in the following inquiries are comparatively few and will be contained within a small compass. They are such as are found in the composition of most names occurring in ancient mythology, whether they relate to deities then revered or to the places where their worship was introduced. But they appear nowhere so clearly as in the names of those places situated in Babylonia and Egypt. From these regions, they were over time transferred to far remote countries—beyond the Ganges to the east and to the furthest reaches of the Mediterranean to the west—wherever the sons of Ham <note>The "sons of Ham" refers to the descendants of the biblical Ham, whom the author identifies as the primary spreaders of ancient civilization, architecture, and religion.</note>, under their various names, either settled or traded. For as I have mentioned, these people were great adventurers and began an extensive commerce in very early times. They gained a foothold in many regions where they founded cities that were famous in their day.

# RADICALS

They likewise built towers and temples; and upon headlands and promontories, they raised pillars for sea-marks <note>Markers or beacons used to guide navigation at sea.</note> to direct them in their dangerous expeditions. All these were named based on circumstances that had some reference to the religion which these people practiced, and to the ancestors from whom they descended. The deity which they originally worshipped was the Sun. However, they soon gave his titles to some of their ancestors, from which a mixed form of worship arose. They particularly deified the great Patriarch <note>The "great Patriarch" refers to a foundational ancestor, likely Noah or Ham, whom the author believes was later worshipped as a god.</note>, who was the head of their lineage, and worshipped him as the source of light—making the Sun only a symbol of his influence and power. They called him Bal and Baal, and there were others among their ancestors joined with him, whom they called the Baalim. Chus <note>original: "Chus"; the biblical Cush, son of Ham and father of Nimrod.</note> was one of these, and this idolatry began among his sons. 

Regarding the names which these people, over time, gave either to the deities they worshipped or to the cities they founded, we shall find them generally composed of certain original terms as a foundation—such as Ham, Cham, and Chus—or else from the titles with which those figures were honored in later times. These were Thoth, Men or Menes, Ab, El, Aur, Ait, Ees or Ish, On, Bel, Cohen, Keren, Ad, Adon, Ob, Oph, Apha, Uch, Melech, Anac, Sar, Sama, and Samaïm. We must also take notice of those common names by which places are distinguished, such as Kir, Caer, Kiriath, Carta, Air, Col, Cala, Beth, Ai, Ain, Caph, and Cephas. Finally, we should include the particles Al and Pi, which were used among the ancient Egyptians.

I shall first discuss these terms, which I consider to be so

# RADICALS

...many elements from which most names in ancient mythology have been composed, and into which they may be easily broken down. ### HAM or CHAM.

It must be admitted that the author derives the name from *Sydic* <note>meaning justice</note>. To be honest, he has mixed so many fictional characters with real historical figures using ancient terms that it is difficult to uncover the actual truth.

The term *Nebros* <note>original: Νεϐρος</note>, which was substituted by the Greeks for Nimrod, signifying a fawn, gave occasion to many allusions about a fawn and a fawn-skin in the Dionysian <note>original: Dionuſiaca; rites dedicated to Dionysus/Bacchus</note> and other mysteries. There was a town, Nebrissa, near the mouth of the Baetis <note>the modern Guadalquivir River</note> in Spain, called by Pliny "Veneria." <gloss>28 Among the estuaries of the Baetis is the town Nebrissa, surnamed Veneria. <note>original: Inter æſtuaria Bætis oppidum Nebriſſa, cognomine Veneria.</note></gloss> I should think this was a mistake for *Venaria* <note>a name related to hunting (venari), rather than Venus</note>, for there were other places of that name. Here, the same rites and memorials were preserved as those mentioned above, in which there was no allusion to Venus, but rather to Nimrod and Bacchus. The island and its rites are mentioned by Silius Italicus:

> <margin>29</margin> *And Nebrissa, witness to the Dionysian wands, which nimble Satyrs inhabited, crowned with the sacred fawn-skin.* <note>original: Ac Nebriſſa Dionuſæis conſcia thyrſis, Quam Satyri coluere leves, redimitaque ſacra Nebride.</note>

The priests at the Bacchanalia, as well as the worshippers, were dressed in this manner:

> <margin>30</margin> *Among the mothers, the impious Maenad comes as a companion to the ancient Dionysus, her side girded with the sacred fawn-skin.* <note>original: Inter matres impia Mænas Comes Ogygio venit Iaccho, Nebride ſacra præcincta latus. 'Ogygian' refers to something of immense age.</note>

Statius describes them in the same attire:

> <margin>31</margin> *One strikes the lyre, another the yellow fawn-skin with its spotted back, another the wands, another the musical quill.* <note>original: Hic chelyn, hic flavam maculoſo Nebrida tergo, Hic thyrſos, hic plectra ferit.</note>

# RADICALS 11

The history of Nimrod was largely lost due to the greater reverence shown to Chus, or Bacchus; yet there is reason to think that divine honors were paid to him in ancient times. The family of the Nebridæ <note>original: Nebridæ; a name derived from *nebris*, the Greek word for a fawn-skin worn during religious rites</note> at Athens, and another of the same name on the island of Cos, were—as we may infer from their history—the descendants of people who had been priests to Nimrod. He seems to have been worshipped in Sicily under the names of Elorus, Pelorus, and Orion. He was likewise styled Belus; but as this was merely a title bestowed upon other persons as well, it makes his specific history very difficult to distinguish.

->TITLES of the DEITY.<-

Theuth, Thoth, Taut, and Taautes are all variations of the same title, belonging to the chief god of Egypt. Eusebius <note>a 4th-century Roman historian and Christian scholar</note> speaks of him as being the same as Hermes. "The Egyptians called him Thoyth, the people of Alexandria called him Thoth, and the Greeks translated the name as Hermes." <note>original Greek: ’Ον Αιγυπτιοι μεν εκαλεσαν Θωυθ, Αλεξανδρεις δε Θωθ, ’Ερμην δε ’Ελληνες μετεφρασαν.</note> From "Theuth," the Greeks derived the word *Theos* <note>original: ΘΕΟΣ; the Greek word for God</note>, which was the most general name for the Deity among that nation. Plato, in his treatise titled *Philebus*, mentions him by the name of—

<sup>35</sup> Theuth <note>also known as Thoth</note> was looked upon as a great benefactor and the first person to cultivate the vine.

He was also supposed to have invented letters; an invention that is likewise attributed to Hermes. <sup>37</sup> "From Misor came Taautus, who discovered the writing of the first alphabet—whom the Greeks called Hermes." <note>original Greek: Απο Μισωρ Τααυτος, ὁς εὑρε την των πρωτων στοιχειων γραφην. — Ἑλληνες δε Ἑρμην εκαλεσαν. Eusebius is quoting Sanchoniathon, a legendary Phoenician author.</note> Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine Greek historian and lexicographer</note> calls him Theus and says that he was the same as Arez <note>the Greek god of war, Ares/Mars</note>, styled by the Arabians "Theus Arez," and worshipped in this way at Petra. "Theusares, which is to say the God Ares, in Petra of Arabia." <note>original Greek: Θευσαρης, τετ' εστι Θεος Αρης, εν Πετρᾳ της Αραβιας.</note> Instead of a statue, there was "a black stone, square and uncarved" <note>original Greek: λιθος μελας, τετραγωνος, ατυπωτος</note>—a pillar of stone without any figure or representation. He was the same deity whom the Germans and Celts worshipped under the name of Theut-Ait, or Theutates, whose sacrifices were very cruel, as we learn from the Roman poet Lucan:

> <sup>38</sup> "And those by whom cruel Theutates is appeased with dreadful blood." <note>original Latin: Et quibus immitis placatur sanguine diro Theutates.</note>

### A B.

## AUR, OUR, OR.

Aur—sometimes expressed as Or, Ur, and Our—signifies both light and fire. From this came the *Orus* <note>the Greek name for the Egyptian god Horus</note> of the Egyptians, a title given to the Sun. <sup>39</sup> "What we translate as the Sun is, in Hebrew, אור (*Ur*); which denotes light, fire, and even the Sun itself." <note>original Latin: Quod solem vertimus, id in Hebræo eſt אור, Ur; quod lucem, et ignem, etiam et Solem denotat.</note> It is often compounded with the term mentioned above <note>the root 'Ab', meaning father</note> and rendered as Abor, Aborus, and Aborras; it is also varied in other ways. This title was often given to Chus <note>Cush, the son of Ham</note> by his descendants, whom they styled Chuſorus. From *Aur*, used to refer to a physical element, came the Latin words *Uro* <note>to burn</note> and *Ardeo* <note>to be on fire</note>. When used to refer to a deity, it gave rise to *oro* <note>to pray</note>, *hora* <note>hour</note>, and the Greek words *hōra* (ὥρα), *hieron* (Ιερον) <note>a sacred place or temple</note>, and *hiereus* (Ιερευς) <note>a priest</note>. Zeus was styled Cham-Ur, which the Greeks rendered as *Komuros* (Κωμυρος); he was worshipped under this title at Halicarnassus. He is called by this name by the poet Lycophron: <sup>40</sup> "When the burning Lion performs sacrifices to Komuros." <note>original Greek: Ἡμος καταιθων θυσθλα Κωμυρῳ Λεων.</note> Regarding this, the Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator</note> observes: "Komuros is the name under which Zeus is honored at Halicarnassus." <note>original Greek: (Κωμυρος) ὁ Ζευς εν Ἁλικαρνασῳ τιμαται.</note>

Not only the deity, but also the minister and attendant shared the same name; for the priests of antiquity were almost universally named after the god they served or after his temple. The name appears to have been once very general. <gloss>47</gloss> "The ministers of all sacred matters were called *Camilli*." <note>original Latin: Rerum omnium sacrarum administri Camilli dicebantur</note> But Plutarch seems to limit the term to one particular office and person. <gloss>48</gloss> "The young boy with both parents living <note>term: amphithalês; a child whose father and mother are both alive, often required for specific religious rituals</note> who served in the Temple of Zeus was called *Camillus*, as was Hermes; thus some of the Greeks called Hermes '*Camillus*' because of his service." <note>original Greek: Τον ὑπηρετοῦντα τῳ Ἱερῳ τȣ Διος αμφιθαλη παιδα λεγεσθαι Καμιλλον, ὡς και τον Ἑρμην· οὕτως ενιοι των Ἑλληνων Καμιλλον απο της διακονιας προσηγορευον</note> He suggests the name was given to Hermes because of the service and duty required of him. 

But there is nothing of this nature to be inferred from the terms. The Hermes of Egypt had nothing similar to his counterpart in Greece. *Camillus* was the name of the chief god, *Cham-El*, the same as *Elion*, the Most High <note>original Greek: ὁ ὑψιστος</note>. He was sometimes written as *Casmillus*, but still referred to Hermes. <gloss>49</gloss> "Casmillus is Hermes, as Dionysiodorus records." <note>original Greek: Κασμιλλος ὁ Ἑρμης εςιν, ὡς ἱσορει Διονυσιοδωρος</note> The deity *El* was especially invoked by Eastern nations when they launched a battle charge; at such times, they used to cry out "*El-El*" and "*Al-Al*." ### O N and E O N.

On, Eon, or Aon, was another title of the Sun among the Amonians <note>term: Amonians; the descendants of Ham, whom the author argues established the first great solar-worshiping civilizations</note>. We find this explained by Cyril in his commentary on Hosea: "On is the Sun" <note>original Greek: Ων δε εστιν ὁ Ηλιος</note>. Speaking of the Egyptians in the same commentary, he says, "Among them, On is the Sun" <note>original Greek: Ων δε εστι παρα αυτοις ὁ Ηλιος</note>.

The "Seventy" <note>term: The Septuagint; the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> likewise, wherever the word occurs in Scripture, interpret it as the Sun and call the city of On, "Heliopolis" <note>the Greek name for the Egyptian city, meaning "City of the Sun"</note>.

It is said of Solomon, that he *had a vineyard at* <gloss>53</gloss> *Baal-Hamon*; a name probably given to the place by his Egyptian wife, the daughter of Pharaoh. The term *El* <note>a common ancient Semitic word for "God"</note> was combined in the same manner; and many places sacred to the Sun were styled *El-on*, as well as *El-our*. It was sometimes rendered *Eleon*; from which came the Greek words *Helios* <note>original Greek: ήλιος</note> and *Helion* <note>original Greek: ήλιον</note>, both meaning the Sun. The Syrians, Cretans, and Canaanites went farther, and made a combination of the terms *Ab-El-Eon*, meaning "Father Supreme Sun" <note>original Latin: Pater Summus Sol</note> or "Father God Sun" <note>original Latin: Pater Deus Sol</note>; hence they formed *Abellon* and *Abelion*, which were mentioned before. Hesychius <note>an ancient Greek grammarian</note> interprets *Abelion* as the "Sun" <note>original Greek: Αϐελιον, Ηλιον</note> and as "Solar" <note>original Greek: Αϐελιον, Ηλιακον</note>.

Vossius thinks, and with good reason, that the Apollo of Greece and Rome was the same as the Abelion of the East. <gloss>54</gloss> "Perhaps Apollo comes from the Cretan *Abelios*; for the ancient Romans said *Apello* instead of *Apollo*, just as they said *hemo* for *homo* [man], *benus* for *bonus* [good], and other similar examples" <note>original Latin: Fortasse Apollo ex Cretico Αϐελιος· nam veteres Romani pro Apollo dixere Apello: ut pro homo, hemo; pro bonus, benus; ac similia</note>. The Sun was also worshiped under the title *Abaddon*; which, as we are informed by the Evangelist <note>referring to John in the Book of Revelation</note>, was the same as Apollo; or, as he terms him, *Apollyon*— <note>original Greek: Απολλυων; the catchword "λυων" at the bottom of the page completes this word</note>

The term *El* was combined in the same manner, and many places sacred to the Sun were styled *El-on*, as well as *El-our*. It was sometimes rendered *Eleon*, from which came *Helios* <note>original Greek: ηλιος</note> and *Helion* <note>original Greek: ηλιον</note>. The Syrians, Cretans, and Canaanites went further and created a combination of the terms *Ab-El-Eon*, meaning "Supreme Father Sun" <note>original Latin: Pater Summus Sol</note> or "Father God Sun" <note>original Latin: Pater Deus Sol</note>. ## A I T.

Another title of Ham or the Sun was *Ait*, and *Aith*: a term of which little notice has been taken, yet it is of great consequence in respect to etymology. It occurs continually in Egyptian names of places, as well as in the composition of names belonging to deities and men. It relates to fire, light, and heat, and to the consequences of heat. We may, to some degree, learn its various and opposite meanings when compounded from ancient words in the Greek language that were derived from it. Several of these are listed in the lexicon of Hesychius <note>a 5th-century Greek grammarian</note>:

*   *Aithai*: black or dark <note>original Greek: Αιθαι, μελαιναι</note>.
*   *Aithein*: to burn <note>original Greek: Αιθειν, καιειν</note>.
*   *Aithaloen*: (a compound of *Aith-El*) scorched or burnt <note>original Greek: Αιθαλοεν, κεκαυμενον</note>.
*   *Aithinos*: smoke <note>original Greek: Αιθινος, καπνος</note>.
*   *Aithon*: bright or flashing <note>original Greek: Αιθον, λαμπρον</note>.
*   *Aithona*: (of the same etymology, from *Aith-On*) black or fiery <note>original Greek: Αιθωνα, μελανα, πυρωδη</note> <gloss>56</gloss>.
*   *Aithos*: heat or burning <note>original Greek: Αιθος, καυμα</note>.

The Egyptians, when they consecrated anything to their deity or made it a symbol of a supposed attribute, called it by the name of that attribute or emanation <gloss>57</gloss>. As there was scarcely anything that they did not hold sacred, almost everything was appropriately—

"The fiery-eyed child Dionysus" <note>original Greek: Αιθιοπαιδα Διονυσον</note>. Anacreon. Others use this for wine; others for Artemis. Hesychius. Altered to "fiery child" <note>original Greek: Αιθοπα παιδα</note> by Albertus.

<header>R A D I C A L S.</header>

...priated; it necessarily happened that several objects often had the same reference and were named alike. For not only did men take these sacred titles for themselves, but birds, beasts, fish, reptiles, as well as trees, plants, stones, drugs, and minerals, were also supposed to be under some particular influence, and received their names from it. And if they were not exactly the same, they were nevertheless composed of very similar elements. Ham, as the Sun, was titled <gloss>58</gloss> *Ait*; and Egypt, the land of Ham, consequently had the name *Ait*, which the Greeks rendered as *Aetia*: "Egypt was called Aeria, Potamia, Ethiopia, and <gloss>59</gloss> *Aetia*" <note>original Greek: Εκληθη (ἡ Αιγυπτος) και Αερια, και Ποταμια, και Αιθιοπια, και ΑΕΤΙΑ</note>.

One of the most ancient names of the Nile was *Ait*, or *Aetos* <note>original Greek: Αετος, meaning "Eagle"</note>. It was also a name given to the eagle, as the bird particularly sacred to the Sun. Homer alludes to the original meaning of the word when he calls the eagle <gloss>60</gloss> "the fiery eagle" <note>original Greek: Αιετος αιθων</note>. Among the parts of the human body, the term was applied to the <gloss>61</gloss> heart; for the heart in the body may be regarded as what the Sun is in his system: the source of heat and life, providing the same animating principle. Because this word had these two meanings, the Egyptians used a heart over a vase of burning incense as an emblem of their country <gloss>62</gloss>.

*Ath* was sometimes joined to the ancient title *Herm*, which the Greeks, by adding a suffix, rendered <term>Hermes</term> <note>original Greek: Ἑρμης</note>. From *Ath-Herm* came the words <term>Thermae</term> <note>original Greek: Θερμαί; meaning hot springs</note>, <term>Thermos</term> <note>original Greek: Θερμος; meaning warm</note>, and <term>Thermaino</term> <note>original Greek: Θερμαίνω; meaning to heat or warm</note>. These terms were sometimes reversed and expressed as *Herm-athena*.

# AD.

*Ad* is a title that occurs very often in compound words, such as in *Ad-Or* and *Ad-On*, from which were formed Adorus, Adon, and Adonis. It is sometimes found compounded with itself and was used in this way as a supreme title with which both deities and kings were honored. We read of Hadad, king of <gloss>78</gloss> Edom; and there was another of the same name at Damascus, whose son and successor was styled <gloss>79</gloss> Ben-hadad. According to <gloss>80</gloss> Nicolaus of Damascus, the kings of Syria for nine generations had the name of Adad. There was also a prince named Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of <gloss>81</gloss> Zobah;

...and Hadoram, son of the king of <gloss>82</gloss> Hamath. The god Rimmon was styled Adad; and the Prophet mentions the mourning of Adad Rimmon in the valley of <gloss>83</gloss> Megiddo. The feminine form of it was Ada, a title mentioned by Plutarch when speaking of a <gloss>84</gloss> queen of Caria. It was a sacred title and was assigned by the Babylonians to their chief <gloss>85</gloss> goddess. Among all the eastern nations, *Ad* was a distinct title and was originally bestowed upon the Sun. If we can trust Macrobius, it meant *One*, and was interpreted as such by the Assyrians: <note>original Latin: "Deo, quem summum maximumque venerantur, Adad nomen dederunt. Ejus nominis interpretatio significat unus. Hunc ergo ut potissimum adorant Deum.—Simulacrum Adad insigne cernitur radiis inclinatis."</note> "To the god whom they worship as highest and greatest, they have given the name Adad. The interpretation of this name signifies *one*. Therefore, they worship him as the most powerful god. The notable statue of Adad is seen with rays inclining downward."

I suspect that Macrobius, in his account, has mistaken the cardinal number for the ordinal; what he translates as *one* should actually be *first* or *chief*. We find that it was a sacred title; when used alone, it was given to a Babylonian deity, but when repeated, it must indicate greater excellence. This is because the Amonians <note>A term the author uses for the descendants of Ham, who he argues shared a common solar-based religion.</note> generally formed their superlative by doubling the positive: for example, *Rab* was great, while *Rabrab* meant very great. It is indeed clear from the account that it must have been a superlative; for

he says it was designed to represent what was esteemed the "highest and greatest" <note>original Latin: *summum maximumque*</note>. I should therefore think that *Adad*, in its primitive sense, signified "first" <note>original Greek: *πρωτος* (*protos*)</note> and "pre-eminent" <note>original Greek: *πρωτευων* (*proteuon*)</note>; and in a secondary meaning, it denoted a chief or prince. By these means, we may rectify a mistake in Philo <note>Philo of Byblos, a grammarian who claimed to translate the Phoenician history of Sanchoniathon.</note>, who makes Sanchoniathon say that *Adodus* of Phoenicia was king of the country. He renders the name as *Adodus*, but we know for certain that it was expressed as *Adad* or *Adadus* in Edom, Syria, and Canaan. Moreover, he makes him "King of the Gods" <note>original Greek: *βασιλευς Θεων* (*basileus theon*)</note>; but it is plain that the word *Adad* is a compound. As the two terms of which it is made up are precisely the same, there should be a reciprocal resemblance in the translation. 

If *Ad* is a chief or king, *Adad* should be superlatively so and signify a "King of Kings." I should therefore suspect that in the original text of Sanchoniathon, the true reading was not "King of the Gods," but "King of Kings" <note>original Greek: *βασιλευς βασιλεων* (*basileus basileon*)</note>. In short, *Ad* and *Ada* signified "first" <note>original Greek: *πρωτος* (*protos*)</note>, and in a more general sense, a prince or ruler. *Adad*, therefore, which is a repetition of this title, means "first of the first" <note>original Greek: *πρωτος των πρωτων* (*protos ton proton*)</note> or "of the most pre-eminent" <note>original Greek: *πρωτευοντων* (*proteuonton*)</note>; it corresponds to the "Most High" or "Most Eminent."

->EES and IS.<-

*Ees*, rendered as *As* and *Is*, like the Hebrew word *Esh* <note>original Hebrew: אש, meaning fire</note>, related to light and fire; it was one of the titles of the Sun. It is sometimes compounded as *Ad-Ees* and *Ad-Is*, from which came the *Hades* of the Greeks and *Atis* and *Attis* of the Asians; these were different names for the same deity, the Sun. Many places were named after it, particularly a city in Africa mentioned by ⁸⁸ Polybius. There was also a river, ⁸⁹ Adesa, which flowed past the city of Choma in Asia Minor.

It was undoubtedly the work of some of his kindred, the sons of Cush <note>original: "Chus"</note>, who introduced the rites of fire and the worship of the Sun there. For this reason, it was called *Adesa*, which the Greeks rendered as *Edessa*. Even today, one of the names for fire among those in the East who worship it is ⁹⁰ *Atesh*. # RADICALS.

[This] word⁹⁵ is often found combined with *Or*; as in *Asorus* and *Esorus*, under which titles the Deity was worshiped in Syria, Sicily, and Carthage; he was even supposed to have been the founder of Carthage. It is often compounded with *El* and *Il*; and many places were named from these combinations, such as *Alesia*, *Elysa*, *Eleusa*, *Halesus*, *Elysus*, and *Eleusis*. Through apocope <note>original: "apocope," a linguistic term for the loss of one or more sounds from the end of a word</note>, these were shortened to *Las*, *Lasa*, *Laesa*, and *Lasaia*; as well as *Lissa*, *Lissus*, and *Lissia*. 

Sometimes we find these terms reversed; instead of *El Ees*, they are rendered as *Ees El*. From this, we have places named *Azilis*, *Azila*, and *Asyla*, which were contracted into *Zelis*, *Zela*, *Zeleia*, and *Zelitis*; also *Sele*, *Sela*, *Sala*, *Salis*, *Sillas*, *Silis*, and *Soli*. 

All these places were founded or named by people of the Amonian worship <note>The author's term for an ancient sun-worshiping religion he believes originated with the descendants of Ham (Amun)</note>. Upon inquiry, we may always perceive something very peculiar in their history and situation. They were particularly devoted to the worship of the Sun, and they were generally situated near hot springs, or else upon foul and foul-smelling <note>original: "fetid"</note> lakes and pools of bitumen. It is also not uncommon to find mines of salt and nitre near them, along with caverns that emit pestilential vapors <note>original: "exhalations"</note>.

hollows in Italy, says that the exhalations were insupportable. $^3$ "They call them breathing holes, and others call them *Charonian* ditches, as they exhale a death-bringing spirit" <note>original Latin: "Spiracula vocant, alii Charoneas scrobes, mortiferum spiritum exhalantes."</note>. It may seem remarkable; but the Amonians <note>The author's term for descendants of Ham, whom he identifies as sun-worshipers</note> chose the locations for both their cities and temples based on these strange phenomena. They considered no places so sacred as those where there were fiery eruptions, unusual vapors, and sulfurous exhalations. In Armenia, near $^4$ Comana and Camisena, stood the temple of $^5$ Anait, or the "fountain of the Sun." This was a Persian and Babylonian deity, as well as an Armenian one, who was honored with *Puratheia* <term>fire-temples or open-air altars dedicated to the sacred fire</term>, where the rituals of fire were specifically maintained. The city itself was named Zela, and right behind it lay a large nitrous <note>likely referring to saltpeter or alkaline mineral deposits common in volcanic regions</note> lake. In short, from the Amonian terms *Al-As* <note>meaning "God of Fire"</note> came the Greek words for salt (*halos*, *halas*, *hals*); just as from the same terms reversed (*As-El*), the Latin words for salt (*Sal*), the sun (*Sol*), and the sea (*Salum*) were formed. Wherever the Amonians found places with these natural or supernatural properties, they held them sacred and founded their temples near them.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the etymology of "Al-As" and "As-El," connecting these terms for fire and the sun to the names of sacred sites, specifically those involving salt or water with unusual properties.</meta>

# RADICALS.

$^6$ Selenousia in Ionia was situated on a salt lake, which was sacred to Artemis. In Epirus, there was a city called Alesa, Elissa, and Lesa; nearby were the Alesian plains, similar to the Elysian plains in Egypt. In these plains, a great quantity of "fossil salt" <note>rock salt or mineral salt deposits</note> was produced. $^7$ There was also an Alesia in Arcadia, and a mountain named Alesium with a temple upon it. Here, an ancient figure named Aepytus was said to have been suffocated with salt water. In this legend, there is a clear allusion to the etymology of the name. 

It is true that the historian Pausanias $^8$ supposes the place was called Alesia because the goddess Rhea had wandered there—"it was called Rhea’s because of her wandering, as they say" <note>original Greek: δια την αλην, ὡς φασι, καλουμενον την Ῥεας</note>. However, the name did not derive from *ale* (wandering), but from *halas* and *halos* (salt); it was named after the deity to whom that substance was sacred. This is confirmed by another tradition that prevailed there: it is said that in ancient times, there was an eruption of sea water within the temple. $^9$ "There is an ancient story that a wave of the sea appeared in this temple" <note>original Greek: Θαλασσης δε αναφαινεσθαι κυμα εν τῳ Ἱερῳ τοτῳ λογος εσιν αρχαιος</note>. 

Nor was this name restricted to one particular type of fountain or water. All waters that possessed any uncommon property were similarly sacred to *Elees* or *Ees-El*. This was an ancient title of Mithras and Osiris in the East, the same as $^{10}$ *Sol*, the Sun. From this root comes the word—

### RADICALS.

The priests of the Sun were called Soli and Solimi in Cilicia, Selli in Epirus, and Salii at Rome; all were originally priests of fire. As such, they are described by Virgil:

->Then the Salii went around the burning altars to their songs. <note>original Latin: "Tum Salii ad cantus incensa altaria circum"</note><-

In like manner, the Silaceni of the Babylonians were worshipers of the same deity and were devoted to the fire rites that accompanied the worship of the Sun.

The chief city of Silacena was Sile or Sele, names derived from eruptions of fire. Sele is the place or city of the Sun. Therefore, whenever *Sal*, or *Sel*, or the same letters reversed <note>forming "Las"</note> occur in the composition of any place’s name, we may be fairly certain that the place is remarkable either for its religious rites or its geographical situation, and is attended by some of the circumstances ^11 mentioned above. Many instances may be produced of places named for the quality of their waters. In the river ^12 Silarus of Italy, everything became petrified. The river ^13 Silias in India would allow nothing to swim <note>meaning everything would sink in its waters</note>. The waters of the ^14 Salassi in the Alps were of great use in refining gold.

***

^11 Many instances might be produced of those places called Lasa. The fountain at Gortyna in Crete was very sacred and called Lasa and Lysa. There was a tradition that Jupiter, when a child, was washed in its waters; the name was therefore changed to *Lousa* <note>original Greek: Λουσα, from the word for "washing"</note>. Pausanias says, "It provides the coldest water of any river" <note>original Greek: ὑδωρ ψυχροτατον παρεχεται ποταμων</note>. Book 8, p. 658.

In Judea, there were some medicinal waters and warm springs of great reputation at a place called of old Lasa. "Lasa itself is that which is now called Callirrhoë, where warm waters flow into the Dead Sea" <note>original Latin: "Lasa ipsa est, quæ nunc Callirrhoë dicitur, ubi aquæ calidæ in Mare Mortuum defluunt." Jerome (Hieron.) on Isaiah, chapters 17 and 19</note>.

"Herod used the warm springs at Callirrhoë" <note>original Greek: ‘Ηρωδης τοις κατα Καλλιῤῥοην θερμοις εκεχρητο</note>. Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 1, chapter 33.

"Alesa, a city and fountain of Sicily" <note>original Latin: "Alesa, urbs et fons Siciliæ"</note>. Solinus, chapter 11. The fountain was of a wonderful nature.

### RADICALS.

The fountain at Selinus in Sicily had a bitter, salty taste. I have already mentioned the salt lake near Selinousia in Ionia. The fountain of Siloam <note>original: Silöe</note> at Jerusalem was also somewhat salty. Ovid mentions Sulmo, his birthplace, as being famous for its cool waters. This is notable because cold streams were just as sacred to the Sun as those of an opposite nature <note>meaning hot or volcanic springs</note>. The excellent waters at Ænon, where John the Baptist baptized, were called Salim. The River Ales near Colophon ran through the grove of Apollo and was considered the coldest stream in Ionia. "The river Ales is the coldest of those in Ionia" <note>original Greek: Αλης ποταμος ψυχροτατος των εν Ιωνια</note>. In the land of the Alazonians, there was a bitter fountain that flowed into the Hypanis River. These terms were sometimes combined with the name of Ham, resulting in "Hameles" and "Hamelas," which were eventually shortened to Meles and Melas. A river by this name flowed through the region of Pamphylia and was famous for its exceptionally cold and pure water. The Meles near Smyrna was equally admired: "The people of Smyrna have the river Meles; its water is most beautiful, and there is a cave at its springs..." <note>original Greek: Σμυρναιοις δε ποταμος Μελης· υδωρ εϛι καλλιϛον, και σπηλαιον επι ταις πηγαις</note>

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of "radicals"—the fundamental roots of ancient names—specifically how variations of "Melas" and "Sal" (salt) appear in sacred geographical locations. # RADICALS.

The river Melas in Cappadocia <note>A region in modern-day Turkey</note> was of a contrary quality to the one previously mentioned. It ran through a hot, inflammable country and formed many fiery pools. "And these marshes are everywhere susceptible to fire." <note>original Greek: Και ταυτα δ' εςι τα ελη πανταχου πυριληπτα. Strabo, Book 12, p. 812.</note> In the region of Pontus were Amasus, Amasia, and Amasene, where the area abounded with hot springs: "Above the city of the Amasians lie the hot waters of the Phazemonites, which are exceptionally healthy." <note>original Greek: Ὑπερκειται δε της των Αμασεων τα τε θερμα ὑδατα των Φαζημονειτων, ὑγιεινα σφοδρα. Strabo, Book 12, p. 839.</note>

It is wonderful how far the Amonian <note>Referring to the "Amonians," descendants of Ham, whom the author believes spread a specific system of sun worship</note> religion and customs were carried in the earliest ages. The ancient Germans and Scandinavians were led by the same principles; they founded their temples in the same types of locations as those described above. Above all others, they chose places where there were nitrous or saline waters. "They were firmly persuaded that groves (or lakes) fertile in producing salt are closest to Heaven, and that the prayers of mortals are heard nowhere more closely; as Tacitus, a witness beyond all exception, teaches by the example of the Hermunduri <note>An ancient Germanic tribe</note>." <note>original Latin: Maxime autem lucos (or lacus) sale gignendo fæcundos Cœlo propinquare, precesque mortalium nusquam propius audiri firmiter erant persuasi...</note>

The Ionians expressed it as *Zen* <note>original Greek: Ζην</note> and *Zena* <note>original Greek: Ζηνα</note>. Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> tells us that the Sun was called *Saos* <note>original Greek: Σαως</note> by the Babylonians. It should be noted that the Greeks, when adopting foreign words, continually omitted the final *Nu* <note>The Greek letter 'n'</note> and substituted a *Sigma* <note>The Greek letter 's'</note>. The true Babylonian name for the Sun was undoubtedly *Saon*, often expressed as *Soan*. 

This was the same as *Zauan* of the Sidonians <note>People of Sidon, a major Phoenician city</note>, under which name they worshiped Adonis, or the Sun. Hesychius says, "*Zaunas*, a certain god in Sidon" <note>original Greek: Ζαυνας, θεος τις εν Σιδωνι</note>. It is plain to see who this deity was. The same writer mentions that the Indian Hercules—by which is always meant the chief deity—was styled *Dorsanes*: "Dorsanes, the Hercules among the Indians" <note>original Greek: Δορσανης, ὁ Ηρακλης παρ’ Ινδοις</note>. 

The name *Dorsanes* is an abridgment of *Ador San*, or *Ador-Sanes*, which means *Ador-Sol*, or "the Lord of Light" <note>Bryant is connecting "Ador" to a title of lordship and "San" to "Sol," the Latin word for Sun</note>. This was a title conferred upon Ham <note>The biblical son of Noah, whom Bryant identifies as the progenitor of the "Amonian" sun-worshiping peoples</note>, and also upon others of his family, whom I have previously mentioned were collectively called the *Baalim* <note>Plural of Baal, a common title for "Lord" or "God" among ancient Near Eastern peoples</note>. Similarly, they were also called the *Zaanim* and *Zaannanim*; a temple was erected to them by the ancient Canaanites, which was named after them: ²⁹ *Beth-Zaananim* <note>Literally, "House of the Zaananim"</note>. # RADICALS.

The name was rendered Sonam <note>original Greek: Σωναμ</note> by Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Roman historian and Christian polemicist</note>, which was undoubtedly named in honor of the same persons. Their posterity looked up to them as the *Heliadae* <term>Heliadae</term><note>descendants of the Sun, from the Greek 'Helios'</note>, and named them after that luminary. According to Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian</note>, it was a title not unknown in ancient Greece, where princes and rulers were styled *Zanides* <note>original Greek: Ζανιδες, Ἡγεμονες; literally "Zan-descendants" or "Leaders"</note>. 

In the works of Diodorus Siculus <note>A 1st-century BC Greek historian</note>, mention is made of an ancient king of Armenia called Barsanes, a name which signifies the "offspring of the Sun." We also find temples erected to the same deity with the same meaning, styled in the singular *Beth-San*, which means the "Temple of the Sun." Two places of this name occur in Scripture: one in the tribe of Manasseh and the other in the land of the Philistines. The latter seems to have been a city and also a temple, where the body of King Saul was exposed after his defeat upon Mount Gilboa. For it is said that the Philistines <sup>32</sup> *“cut off his head and stripped off his armor—and they put his armor in the house of Ashtoreth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-San.”* 

They seem to have sometimes used this term with a reduplication <note>The repetition of a root word or syllable</note>, for we read of a city in Canaan called <sup>33</sup> Sansanah, which signifies a place sacred to the most illustrious "Orb of Day" <note>the Sun</note>. Some ancient statues near Mount Cronius in Elis were called *Zanes* by the natives, as we are told...

Semon (Sem-On) signifies the *Heavenly Sun* <note>original Latin: Cœlestis Sol</note>.

Some of the ancients thought that the soul of man was a divine emanation—a portion of light from the Sun. For this reason, it was probably called *Zoan* after that luminary; for we find it named this way in the writings of Macrobius <note>A Roman provincial of the early 5th century AD, known for his work on Saturnalia</note>. <sup>39</sup>

> The ancients permitted no sacred animal to remain within their own territories, but drove them away to the borders of the Gods to whom they were sacred. However, they believed that the souls of consecrated men, whom the Greeks call *Zoanas*, were owed to the Gods. <note>original Latin: Veteres nullum animal sacrum in finibus suis esse patiebantur; sed abigebant ad fines Deorum, quibus sacrum esset: animas vero sacratorum hominum, quos Græci ZΩANAΣ vocant, Diis debitas æstimabant.</note>

## DI, DIO, DIS, DUS.

Another common name for the Deity was *Dis*, *Dus*, and similar variations, which are analogous to *Deus* and *Theos* <note>The Latin and Greek words for God, respectively</note> in other nations. The Sun was called *Arez* in the East, and was compounded into *Dis-arez* and *Dus-arez*, which signifies the "God Sun" <note>original Latin: Deus Sol</note>. This name is mentioned by Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, c. 155–220 AD</note>. <sup>40</sup>

> Every province and city even has its own God—as Astarte is to Syria, and Dysares to Arabia. <note>original Latin: Unicuique etiam provinciæ et civitati suus Deus est, ut Syriæ Astarte, Arabiæ Dysares.</note>

I previously noted that Hercules, the chief Deity among the Indians, was called Dorsanes. He also had the names Sandis and Sandes, which signifies "God the Sun" <note>original Latin: Sol Deus</note>. <sup>43</sup> "They called Belus 'Zeus,' Sandes 'Heracles,' and Anaitis 'Aphrodite,' and so on for others." <note>original Greek: Βηλον μεν τον Δια τυχον, Σανδην τε τον Ἡρακλεα, και Αναϊτιδα την Αφροδιτην, και αλλως αλλυς εκαλεν.</note> This is according to Agathias <note>A 6th-century Byzantine historian</note> writing about the peoples of the East. 

Probably the Deity Bendis, whose rites were so celebrated in Phrygia and Thrace, was a compound of *Ben-Dis*, "the offspring of God." The natives of this country represented Bendis as a female and supposed her to be the same as <sup>44</sup> Selene, or the moon. The same Deity was also both masculine and feminine: what was the "Moon Goddess" <note>original Latin: Dea Luna</note> in one country was the "Moon God" <note>original Latin: Deus Lunus</note> in another.

<margin><sup>43</sup> Agathias, Book 2, page 62.
<sup>44</sup> "This name Bendis is Thracian; thus the Thracian theologian [Orpheus] gives many names to the Moon, and refers Bendis to the Goddess... Plethone, and Euphrosyne, and mighty Bendis." <note>original Greek: Το ονομα τουτο Θρακον ἡ Βενδις... Πλετωνη τε, και Ευφροσυνη, Βενδις τε κραταια.</note> — From Proclus. See *Poesis Philosophica*, edited by H. Stephanus, page 91.</margin>

<margin>

From this perhaps came the Greek words <term>zoein</term> <note>ζωειν</note> and <term>zēn</term> <note>ζην</note>, "to live"; and <term>zoon</term> <note>ζωον</note>, "an animal"; and hence the title of Apollo, <term>Zenodotēr</term> <note>Ζηνοδοτηρ</note>, "the giver of life."

Some of the ancients thought that the soul of man was a divine emanation—a portion of light from the Sun. For this reason, it was probably called *Zoan* after that celestial body, for we find it named so in Macrobius: <gloss>39</gloss> "The ancients allowed no sacred animal to remain within their own borders, but drove them to the borders of the Gods to whom they were sacred. Indeed, they considered the souls of consecrated men—whom the Greeks call *Zoanas*—to be owed to the Gods." <note>original Latin: Veteres nullum animal sacrum in finibus suis esse patiebantur; sed abigebant ad fines Deorum, quibus sacrum esset: animas vero sacratorum hominum, quos Græci ΖΩΑΝΑΣ vocant, Diis debitas æstimabant.</note>

### DI, DIO, DIS, DUS.

Another common name for the Deity was *Dis*, *Dus*, and similar terms, which are analogous to *Deus* [God] and *Theos* [God] of other nations. In the East, the Sun was called *Arez*, and when combined, it became *Dis-arez* and *Dus-arez*, which signifies "God Sun" <note>original Latin: Deus Sol</note>. This name is mentioned by Tertullian <gloss>40</gloss>: "To every province and city there is also its own God; for example, Syria has Astarte, and Arabia has Dysares." <note>original Latin: Unicuique etiam provinciæ et civitati suus Deus est, ut Syriæ Astarte, Arabiæ Dysares.</note>

<margin>

## PETAH

I have previously noted this Amonian <note>The author uses "Amonian" to refer to descendants of the biblical Ham, whom he believed established a widespread solar religion.</note> term of honor in a former treatise. I have shown that it could be found in many Egyptian <gloss>58</gloss> names, such as *Petiphra*, *Petiphera*, *Petifonius*, *Petofiris*, *Petarbemis*, *Petubastus* the Tanite, and *Petefuccus*, the builder of the Labyrinth. *Petes*—called *Peteos* in Homer—the father of Mnestheus the Athenian, shares the same origin: <gloss>59</gloss> "For Petes, the father of Mnestheus, who campaigned against Troy, was clearly an Egyptian, etc." <note>original Greek: Τον γαρ Πετην, τον πατερα Μενεσθεως, του στρατευσαντος εις Τροιαν, φανερως Αιγυπτιον υπαρξαντα κτλ.</note> All the great officials of the Babylonians and Persians took their names from some sacred title of the Sun. Herodotus mentions <gloss>60</gloss> *Petazithes* the Magus <note>a member of the priestly caste in ancient Persia</note>, and <gloss>61</gloss> *Patiramphes*. The latter was the charioteer for Xerxes during his expedition to Greece, but he was named after a different office; for he was the brother of Smerdis and a *Magus*, which was a title for a priest of the Sun. This term is sometimes added at the end of a word, as in *Atropatia*, a province in <gloss>62</gloss> Media. This region was so named, as we learn from Strabo, <gloss>63</gloss> after Atro— <note>original Greek: απο του Ατρο-</note>

This etymology is based on the idea that the Amazons were a community of women who killed every man they had any interaction with, yet they survived as a people for centuries. The title mentioned above was given to them because of their worship. *Oiorpata*—or, as some manuscripts have it, *Aorpata*—is the same as <margin>65</margin> *Petah Or*, meaning "the priest of Orus" <note>Horus, the Egyptian sky god</note>; or, in a broader sense, "the worshippers of that God." They were "man-slayers" <note>original Greek: Ανδροκτονοι</note> in the sense that they sacrificed all strangers whom fortune brought to their coast. Consequently, the entire Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note> where they lived became infamous for their cruelty, but they did not actually derive their name from that circumstance.

### BEL and BAAL

*Bel*, *Bal*, or *Baal* is a Babylonian title attributed to the Sun. It was used by the Amonians <note>A term the author uses for the descendants of Ham, whom he associates with sun-worshiping civilizations.</note> in other countries, particularly in Syria and Canaan. It meant *Lord* <note>original Greek: Κυριος</note> and is often found combined with other terms, such as in *Bel-Adon*, *Belorus*, *Bal-hamon*, *Belochus*, and *Bel-on*. From this last name came the Roman goddess *Bellona*. It also appears in *Baal-shamaim*, meaning "the great Lord of the Heavens." 

This was a title given by the Syrians to the Sun: <margin>67</margin> "They call the Sun *Beelsamen*, which among the Phoenicians means Lord of Heaven, and among the Greeks, Zeus" <note>original Greek: Τον Ἡλιον Βεελσαμην καλεσιν, ὁ εστι παρα Φοινιξι Κυριος Ουρανε, Ζευς δε παρ' Ἑλλησι.</note>. From this, we can decode the name of the Sun mentioned earlier by Damascius, who calls that deity *Bolathes*: <margin>68</margin> "The Phoenicians and Syrians name Saturn *El*, *Bel*, and *Bolathen*" <note>original Greek: Φοινικες και Συροι τον Κρονον Ηλ, και Βηλ, και Βολαθην επονομαζεσι. Kronos/Saturn was frequently identified with the Sun in ancient solar theology.</note>. What he terms *Bolathes* is a compound of *Bal-Ath*, or *Bal*—

Philo Biblius <note>original: Philo Biblius; a Phoenician historian of the Roman period.</note> interprets it as Zeus; Damascius <note>original: Damascius; a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> supposed it to mean Cronus <note>The Greek Titan associated with time and harvest, often equated with the Roman Saturn.</note>, as did Theophilus likewise: <note>original Greek: Ενιοι μεν σέβονται τον Κρονον, και τουτον αυτον ονομαζουσι Βηλ, και Βαλ, μαλιστα οι οικουντες τα ανατολικα κλιματα. ### KEREN

*Keren* signifies in its original sense **a horn**; but it was always esteemed as an emblem of power and used as a title of sovereignty and might <note>original: "puissance"</note>. For this reason, it is common for the sacred writers to say, <margin>70</margin> *“My horn shall you exalt”*— <margin>71</margin> *“his horn shall be exalted with honor”*— <margin>72</margin> *“the horn of Moab is cut off”*; and the Evangelist <margin>73</margin> <note>Referring to the author of the Gospel of Luke.</note> speaks of Christ as a *horn of salvation* for the world. 

The Greeks often changed the final *nu* <note>The Greek letter 'n' (ν).</note> into *sigma* <note>The Greek letter 's' (σ/ς).</note>. Therefore, from *keren* they formed *keras* and *keratos* <note>original Greek: κερας, κερατος; meaning "horn".</note>. From those, they derived the words *kratos* <note>strength or power</note> and *krateros* <note>strong or mighty</note>, as well as *koiranos* <note>ruler/lord</note>, *kreon* <note>ruler</note>, and *karenon* <note>head or peak</note>—all of which relate to strength and eminence. *Gerenius* <note>original Greek: Γερηνιος</note>, a title applied to Nestor <note>A legendary king in Greek mythology known for his wisdom and age.</note>, is an Amonian term <note>The author's term for the ancient cultures he believes descended from Ham, the son of Noah.</note> and signifies a princely and venerable person.

# RADICALS

The Egyptian Crane, because of its great services, was held in high honor, being sacred to the God of light, Abis <note>original Hebrew: אב אש, "Ab Ash," meaning "Father of Fire"</note> or, as the Greeks expressed it, Ibis; from which the name was given. It was also called *Keren* and *Kerenus*; and by the Greeks *Geranos* <note>original: Γερανος</note>, the noble bird, being the most honored of all. It was a title of the Sun himself: for Apollo was named *Craneus* and *Carneüs* <margin>74</margin>; which was none other than *Cereneüs*, the supreme deity, the Lord of light. His festival, styled *Carnea* <note>original: Καρνεια</note>, was an abbreviation of *Cerenea* <note>original: Κερενεια</note>. The priest of Cybele in Phrygia was styled *Carnas*, which was a title of the deity he served and had the same meaning as *Carneus* mentioned above.

## O P H

*Oph* signifies a serpent and was at times pronounced and written as *Ope*, <margin>75</margin> *Oupis* <note>original: Ουπις</note>, *Opis*, and *Ops*; and by Cicero <margin>76</margin>, *Upis*. As the same Cicero <margin>77</margin> testifies, "Vulcan was called Opas by the Egyptians" <note>original Latin: "Vulcanus Ægyptiis Opas dictus est, eodem Cicerone teste"</note>. # RADICALS

It may possibly be only a variation of the term mentioned above <note>The term "Ob" or "Aub," meaning serpent, from the bottom of the previous page.</note>. We are told by Horapollo <note>original: "Orus Apollo," an author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> that the basilisk, or royal serpent, was named *Oubaios*: "Oubaios, which in Greek means Basilisk" <note>original Greek: Ουβαιος, ὁ εστιν Ἑλληνισι Βασιλισκος</note>. It should have been rendered *Oubos* <note>original: Ουβος</note>; for *Oubaios* is a possessive form and not a proper name. The deity named in this way was considered prophetic, and his temples were consulted for oracles. 

This idolatry is alluded to by Moses <margin>79</margin>, who, in the name of God, forbids the Israelites from ever inquiring of those demons, *Ob* and *Ideone* <note>In modern Bibles, these are often translated as "mediums" and "spiritists" or "familiar spirits" and "wizards"</note>; this shows that the practice was of great antiquity. The symbolic worship of the serpent was very extensive in the earliest ages and was introduced into all the religious mysteries, wherever they were celebrated <margin>80</margin>. As an ancient text states: "Among all those whom you consider gods, the serpent is recorded as a great symbol and mystery" <note>original Greek: Παρα παντι των νομιζομενων παρ’ ὑμιν Θεων ΟΦΙΣ συμβολον μεγα και μυστηριον αναγραφεται</note>. 

It is remarkable that wherever the Amonians <note>A term used by the author for the descendants of Ham, whom he believes spread sun and serpent worship</note> founded any places of worship and introduced their rites, there was generally some story of a serpent. There were legends about a serpent at Colchis, at Thebes, and at Delphi, as well as in other places. The Greeks even called Apollo himself *Python*, which is the same as *Opis*, *Oupis*, and *Oub*.

### A I N.

**Ain**, **An**, or **En**—as it is sometimes written—signifies a fountain. This term was prefixed to the names of many places situated near springs, which were named after them. In Canaan, near the crossing points of the Jordan River, there were several famous waters which, based on their names, appear to have been sacred to the Sun in ancient times. The name of the place was **Ænon** <gloss>88</gloss>, or the "fountain of the Sun." This was the same location where people traveled to be baptized by John the Baptist. This was not because they believed there was any inherent holiness in the waters—that idea had been forgotten for ages, and the name had originally been given by the Canaanites—but rather, as the Gospel of Saint John records <gloss>89</gloss>, "*John also was baptizing in Ænon near Salim, because there was much water there; and they came and were baptized.*"

Many places were named **An-ait**, **An-abor**, **Anabouria**, **Anathon**, **Anopus**, and **Anorus**. Some of these were named for their geographical situation, while others were named for the religious worship established there. The Egyptians had many subordinate deities which they considered to be "emanations" <note>original Greek: απορ̇ῥοιαι (aporrhoiai)</note> from their chief God, as we learn from the writings of Iamblichus, Psellus, and Porphyry. They called these derivative powers **fountains** <gloss>90</gloss>, and...

***

<gloss>88</gloss> *Ænon near Salim.* <note>original Greek: Αινων εγγυς του Σαλειμ</note> (Eusebius, *On the Place Names in Holy Scripture*). **Ain On** means "fountain of the sun" <note>original Latin: fons solis</note>. **Salim** does not come from *Salem* (meaning "peace"), but from *Sal*, the Sun—the same as the Latin *Sol*. Thus, **Salim** means "Waters of the Sun" <note>original Latin: Aquæ solis</note>; it also refers to "salty waters" <note>original Latin: Aquæ falsæ</note>.

The nymph **Oenone** was actually a fountain, **Ain-On** <note>Ain-On: Fountain of the Sun</note>, in **Phrygia**, and was sacred to the same deity. Fittingly, she is said to have been the daughter of the river **Cebrenus** <gloss>93</gloss>. The island of **Aegina** was also named **Oenone** and **Oenopia**, likely because of the worship practiced there <gloss>94</gloss>. I have mentioned that all springs and baths were sacred to the Sun; for this reason, they were called **Bal-ain**, meaning "the fountains of the great Lord of Heaven." From this term, the Greeks formed *Balaneia* <note>original Greek: Βαλανεια; public baths</note> and the Romans formed *Balnea* <note>Latin: baths</note>. The southern seas were once full of large whales, and it is well known that they have openings near their nostrils through which they spout water in a great stream to a high elevation. Because of this, they were also named **Bal-ain**, or *Balaenae* <note>Latin: whales</note>. The **Amonians** <note>followers of the ancient religious system centered on Ham or Amon-Ra</note> consecrated everything unusual to their deity and named these things after his titles. This practice is very evident among the animals of Egypt.

The term **Ouranus** <note>original Greek: Ουρανος; Uranus or the Heavens</note> originally referred specifically to the orb of the Sun, but in later times, it was used to describe the entire expanse of the heavens. It is a compound of **Our-ain**, meaning "the fountain of **Orus**" <note>the Egyptian solar deity</note>, and its etymology reveals its true origin. Many places were named **Ees-ain** (the reverse of **Ain-ees** or **Hanes**), and others were further compounded as **Am-ees-ain** and **Cam-ees-ain**, which became **Amisene** and **Camisene**. The natural history of these places usually confirms this etymology. The Amonians settled along the Tiber River, and the ancient town of **Janiculum** was originally named **Camese** <note>Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 7, page 151</note>, with the surrounding region called **Camesene**. <meta>This page continues the author's investigation into the radical term "Ain" (fountain) and its variations in ancient place names, specifically addressing the transition from the term "Camesene" to "Anna Perenna" and the linguistic structure of these compound words.</meta>

<header># RADICALS.</header>

...undoubtedly from the fountain *Camesene*, called afterward *Anna Perenna* <note>an ancient Roman deity of the new year</note>, whose waters ran into the sacred pool of *Numicius* $^{97}$: and whose priests were the *Camœnæ* <note>Roman fountain goddesses often identified with the Greek Muses</note>.

I am aware that some very learned men do not quite approve of terms being reversed in the way I have presented them—such as in *Ath-ain*, *Bal-ain*, *Our-ain*, *Cam-ain*, and other examples. This is considered a deviation from the common usage of the Hebrew language, where the "governing word" (as it is called) always comes first. There are many instances of this, such as *Ain-Shemesh* <note>fountain of the sun</note>, *Ain-Gaddi* <note>fountain of the kid</note>, *Ain-Mishpat* <note>fountain of judgment</note>, and *Ain-Rogel* <note>fountain of the fuller</note>; also *Beth-El* <note>house of God</note>, *Beth-Dagon* <note>house of Dagon</note>, *Beth-Aven* <note>house of vanity</note>, and *Beth-Oron* <note>house of Horon</note>. 

But, with all due respect, this does not affect the etymologies <note>the study of word origins</note> I have presented to the reader, for I do not derive them from Hebrew. And although there may have been a great similarity in ancient times between Hebrew and the languages of *Egypt*, *Cutha* <note>ancient Ethiopia or Babylonia</note>, and *Canaan*, they were nonetheless all different tongues. There was once only one language among the sons of men $^{98}$. Upon the dispersion <note>scattering</note> of mankind, this branched out into dialects, and those were subdivided again. All of these varied in every age—not only in relation to one another, but each language also diverged from its original form more and more over time. It is, therefore, impossible to force all of these into the style and standard of any single language.

# RADICALS.

Furthermore, the terms from which I believe these names are formed are not strictly in the *construct state* <note>original: "in regimine"; a grammatical term referring to a word being governed by another, common in Hebrew to show possession, like "House of God"</note>; rather, they are used as adjectives, which is common in almost every language. We encounter in Greek writings phrases like "the Hellenic army" <note>original: Ἕλληνα στρατον</note>, "the Greek dialect" <note>original: Ἑλλαδα διαλεκτον</note>, and "stifled the Greek voice" <note>original: εσβεσεν Ἑλλαδα φωνην</note>. We also find "the Sicilian island" <note>original: νασον Σικελαν</note>, "a woman’s breast" <note>original: γυναικα μαζον</note>, "the Persian army" <note>original: Περσην στρατον</note>, "the sailor’s course" <note>original: ναυτην δρομον</note>, and "the Scythian path" <note>original: Σκυθην οιμον</note>. Why should we not assume that the same practice existed in Cutha <note>ancient Ethiopia or Babylonia</note> and Egypt? 

This practice was not entirely foreign to the Hebrews either. We do indeed read of *Beer-sheba* <note>Well of the Oath</note> and *Beer-lahoiroi* <note>Well of the Living One who sees me</note>, and so on; but we also read of *Baalath-Beer* $^{100}$, which is exactly similar to the instances I have produced. We encounter *Beth-El* <note>House of God</note> and *Beth-Dagon* <note>House of Dagon</note> in the sacred writings, but we sometimes find the governing word placed afterward, as in *Elizabeth*—or the "temple of Eliza." This was a Canaanite name <note>original: "Canaanitish"</note>, identical to *Elissa*, *Eleusa*, and *Elasa* found in Greece and other countries. See Stephanus of Byzantium <note>original: Stephanus Byzant.</note> regarding Manakarta, Dadokarta <note>original: Δαδοκαρτα</note>, and Zadrakarta <note>original: Ζαδρακαρta</note>. See Bochart’s notes on Stephanus of Byzantium, page 823. Also Vologesakerta <note>original: Vologefakerta</note>, mentioned in Pliny, Book 6, page 332.

There was *No-Amon* in Egypt, as well as *Amon-No*. See also *Guebr-abad* in Hyde, page 363, and *Ghavrabad*, page 364. Also *Atesh-khana*, meaning "house of fire" <note>original: domus ignis</note>, page 359. *An-Ath*, whose temple in Canaan was called *Beth-Anath*, is often found reversed as *Ath-An*. From this came *Athana* and the Greek *Athena* <note>original: Αθηνα</note>. *Anath* signified "the fountain of light" and was abbreviated to *Nath* and *Neith* by the Egyptians. They worshiped a divine emanation under this title, whom they believed to be the Goddess of Wisdom. The Athenians, who originated from Sais in Egypt, were named after this deity, whom they called *Ath-An* or *Athene* <note>original: Αθηνη</note> in the Ionian style. "The founding deity of the city (Sais) is, in Egyptian, named Neith, and in Greek, according to their account, Athena" <note>original: Της πολεως (Σαϊτων) Θεος αρχηγος εστιν, Αιγυπτιςι μεν τ’ουνομα Νηϊθ, Ελληνιςι δε, ως ο εκεινων λογος, Αθηνα (Tēs poleōs Saitōn Theos archēgos estin, Aigyptisti men t'onoma Nēith, Hellēnisti de, hōs ho ekeinōn logos, Athēna)</note>. See Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 21.

### RADICALS.

Regarding Azania in Arcadia, the reader may judge my interpretation by the account given of the excellence of its waters: "Azania is a part of Arcadia—there is a fountain in Azania which makes those who have tasted its water unable to endure even the smell of wine." <note>original: Αζανια, μερος της Αρκαδιας—εϛι κρηνη της Αζανιας, ἡ τȣς γευσαμενȣς τȣ ὑδατος ποιει μηδε την οσμην τȣ οινȣ ανεχεσθαι.</note> <margin>Stephanus Byzantinus <note>A 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary of place names.</note></margin> Hanes in Egypt <margin>Isaiah, chapter 30, verse 4</margin> was the reverse of Azan; it was formed, however, of the same terms and with precisely the same meaning. <note>I shall treat Hanes more fully hereafter.</note>

Regarding this city, it may be objected that if it had signified what I suppose, we should have found it expressed in the sacred text as *Ain-Ash* <note>Hebrew: עין אש, potentially meaning "fountain of fire/sun"</note> instead of *Hanes* <note>Hebrew: חנס</note>. If this were true, we would be forced to assume that whenever the sacred writers found a foreign name composed of terms similar to those in their own language, they reshaped them according to their own mode of expression and reduced them to Hebrew orthography <term>orthography</term><note>The conventional spelling system of a language.</note>. 

In short, we would have to assume that if the etymology of an Egyptian or Syriac name could possibly be obtained in their own language, they always kept such an etymology in mind and rendered the word precisely according to the Hebrew manner of writing and pronunciation. But this cannot be allowed. We cannot suppose the sacred writers to have been so unnecessarily scrupulous. As far as I can judge, they appear to have acted in a manner quite the reverse. They seem to have established an excellent rule, which would have been very useful had it been universally followed: this was to present every name as it was expressed at the time they wrote, and by the people to whom they addressed themselves. <meta>This page continues the argument that biblical writers did not strictly adhere to ancient etymologies but rather used the names and pronunciations current in their own times to ensure they were understood by their readers.</meta>

# RADICALS.

If, over the length of time, the original etymology was no longer reflected in the pronunciation, it was unnecessary for the sacred writers <note>original: "Penmen"</note> to maintain it in their works. They wrote to be understood; however, they would have defeated their own purpose if they had called things by names that no longer existed. If the passage of time had introduced any variations, those changes were respected: for example, what was called *Shechem* by Moses is termed *Sicham* <note>original: Σιχαμ</note> or *Sychar* <note>original: Συχαρ</note> by the Apostle <note>Refers to the writers of the New Testament.</note>.

# RADICALS.

It was not only Vulcan who was so named, but Diana was also called $^{16}$ Apha and Aphaea; and in Crete, the goddess Dictynna had the same name. The ancient lexicographer Hesychius observes: "Aphaea is Dictynna" <note>original Greek: Αφαια, ἡ Δικτυννα</note>. The twin gods Castor and Pollux were styled $^{17}$ *Apheterioi* <note>original Greek: Αφετηριοι; likely meaning "those who preside over the start," often associated with races</note>, and Mars *Aphaeus* was worshiped in Arcadia $^{18}$. Apollo was likewise called $^{19}$ *Aphetor* <note>original Greek: Αφητωρ; typically interpreted as "the Archer" or "the Prophet"</note>, but this was properly the name of the place of worship, though Hesychius explains it otherwise.

*Aphetor* was what the ancient Dorians expressed as *Apha-Tor*, a $^{20}$ fire tower or *Prytaneum* <note>A public building in ancient Greek cities containing the holy fire of Hestia</note>. This is the same structure which the Latins of old called *Pur-tor*, having a similar meaning <note>from "Pur," meaning fire, and "Tor," meaning tower</note>. In later times, this term was rendered as *Praetorium*, and the chief officials who presided there were called *Praetores*. They were originally priests of fire, and for that reason were called $^{21}$ *Aphetae*. Every *Praetor* <note>a high-ranking Roman official</note> had a brazier of glowing coals carried before him as a symbol of his office.

In early times, every district was divided according to the number of sacred hearths, each of which constituted a community or parish. In different places, these were called *Puratheia*, *Empureia*, *Prutaneia*, and *Praetoria*; also $^{23}$ *Phratriai* and *Apaturia*. However, the most common name was *Asta*. These were all places of general gathering for people of the same community. Perpetual fires were kept burning here, and such places were used as courts of law, where the laws of the country, *Themistai* <note>original Greek: Θέμισται; divine laws or decrees</note>, were explained and enforced. Therefore, when Homer speaks of a person unworthy of the rights of society, he calls him $^{24}$ "without family, without law, and without a hearth" <note>original Greek: Αφρητωρ, αθεμιστος, ανεστιος (Aphretor, athemistos, anestios)</note>.

The names of these buildings were given to them based on the rituals practiced there, all of which related to fire. In later times, the Greeks expressed the term *Asta* as *Astu* <note>original Greek: Αστυ</note> and applied it specifically to a city. The name of Athens was at first $^{25}$ *Astu*, and then *Athenae*, which has the same meaning. This is because *Athenae* is a compound of *Ath-En*, "the fountain of fire" <note>original Latin: Ignis fons</note>; in which

In different regions, these were styled *Puratheia*, *Empureia*, *Prutaneia*, and *Praetoria*; also $^{23}$ *Phratriai* and *Apaturia*, but the most common name was *Asta*. These were all places of general rendezvous for people of the same community. Here, perpetual fires were kept burning, and places of this sort were used for courts of justice where the laws of the country—*themistai* <note>original Greek: θεμισται; customs or divine decrees</note>—were explained and enforced. Hence Homer, speaking of a person unworthy of the rights of society, calls him $^{24}$ "one without a clan, without law, and without a hearth" <note>original Greek: Ἀφήτωρ, ἀθέμιστος, ἀνέστιος; here the author identifies "Aphetor" with those excluded from the sacred fire</note>.

The names of these buildings were given to them based on the rites practiced there, all of which related to fire. In later times, the term *Asta* was expressed by the Greeks as *Astu* <note>original Greek: Ἄστυ</note> and was used to refer specifically to a city. The name of Athens was at first $^{25}$ *Astu*, and then *Athenae*, which had the same meaning; for *Athenae* is a compound of *Ath-En*, meaning "fountain of fire" <note>original Latin: Ignis fons</note>, in which

->And do not think of Vesta as anything other than a living flame.<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of linguistic radicals related to fire worship, specifically focusing on the etymology of names derived from "Asta" and "Esta" (fire or hearth). # RADICALS.

The name refers to both the guardian Goddess of the city and the perpetual fire kept within its boundaries. The God of fire, Hephaestus <note>original: Hephaistus</note>, was an Egyptian compound of *Apha-Astus*, which the Ionian Greeks rendered as Hephaestus.

The $^{26}$ Camoenae <note>original: Camœnæ</note> of Latium, who were believed to have shown the sacred fountain to the Vestals, were probably the original priestesses whose duty it was to fetch water from that stream for ritual washings <term>lustrations: ceremonial purifications using water</term>. For *Cam-Ain* means "the fountain of the Sun," and the Camoenae were named for their service to that Deity. The hymns in the temples of this God were sung by these women; consequently, the Camoenae were established as the goddesses of music.

Many regions where fire rituals were maintained will be found to have been named *Asta*, *Hestia*, *Hestiaea*, or *Hephaestia*, or to have had cities so $^{27}$ named. This is evident from the histories of Thessaly, Lycia, Egypt, and Lemnos, as well as other countries.

From *Asta* and *Esta* come the terms *Aestas* <note>original Latin: summer</note>, *Aestus* <note>original Latin: heat or tide</note>, *Aestuo* <note>original Latin: to burn or seethe</note>, *Azu* <note>original Greek: Αζυ; to dry up</note>, *Hestia* <note>original Greek: Ἑστια; hearth or the goddess Vesta</note>, and *Hestiazein* <note>original Greek: Ἑστιαζειν; to entertain at a hearth</note>.

# RADICALS.

### SHEM, SHAMEN, SHEMESH.

Shem and Shamesh are terms that relate to the heavens and to the Sun, similar to the Hebrew words *Shem* <note>original: שם</note>, *Shamaim* <note>original: שמים; heavens</note>, and *Shemesh* <note>original: שמש; sun</note>. Many places of reputed holiness, such as Same, Samos, Samothrace, and Samorna, were named after these terms. Philo of Byblos <note>original: Philo Biblius</note> informs us that the Syrians and Canaanites lifted up their hands to Baal-Samen, the Lord of Heaven, under which title they honored the Sun: $^{28}$ "To lift their hands to the heavens toward the Sun; for this, he says, they considered the only god, calling him Baal-Samen, the Lord of Heaven." <note>original Greek: Τὰς χεῖρας ὀρέγειν εἰς οὐρανοὺς πρὸς τὸν Ἥλιον· τοῦτον γὰρ, φησὶ, θεὸν ἐνόμιζον μόνον, ΟΥΡΑΝΟΥ ΚΥΡΙΟΝ ΒΑΑΛΣΑΜΗΝ καλοῦντες.</note> 

Ephesus was a place of great sanctity, and its original name was $^{29}$ Samorna, which seems to be a compound of *Sam-Oran*: "Celestial Sun, fountain of Light." <note>original Latin: Cæleſtis Sol, fons Lucis.</note> We read of Samicon in Elis, $^{30}$ "the place Samikon," <note>original Greek: χωριον Σαμικον</note> which featured a sacred cavern, and of a town called $^{31}$ Samia that lay above it. The word *Semnos* <note>original Greek: Σεμνος</note> was a contraction of *Semanos*, derived from *Sema-on*, and properly signified "divine" and "celestial." From this come the terms "holy goddesses" <note>original Greek: σεμναὶ θεαί; often referring to the Eumenides or Furies</note> and "holy maiden." <note>original Greek: σεμνὴ κόρα; often referring to Persephone</note> 

Ancient Syria was particularly devoted to the worship of the Sun and of the Heavens, and it was called Shems and Shams by the natives. This undoubtedly means "the land of Shemesh," named after the worship practiced there. It retains the <meta>catchword: name</meta>

# MACAR.

This was a sacred title given by the Amonians <note>worshipers of Amon or Ham</note> to their gods. It often appears in the Orphic hymns whenever any deity is invoked.
