# RADICALS.

The term "Macar" was so significant that many places and people were named after it. Macar, as a person, was esteemed by some to be the offspring of $^{46}$ Lycaon; by others, he was considered the son of $^{47}$ Aeolus. Diodorus Siculus calls him $^{48}$ Macareus and speaks of him as the son of Jupiter. This term is often found as a compound word, Macar-On <note>The author implies a connection between "Macar" and "On," the Egyptian name for the Sun</note>. From this, certain people were named *Macarones* <note>original Greek: Μακαρωνες</note> and $^{49}$ *Macrones* <note>original Greek: Μακρωνες</note>, and various places were called *Macron* <note>original Greek: Μακρων</note>. This was likely the origin of the name given to the islands famously known as the *Islands of the Blessed* <note>original Greek: Μακαρων νησοι (Makaron nesoi)</note>. These islands were found in the *Pontus Euxinus* <note>The Black Sea</note> as well as in the Atlantic.

The Acropolis of Thebes in Boeotia was likewise called the $^{50}$ *Island of the Blessed*. It was certainly an Amonian <note>A term the author uses for ancient Egyptian or North African cultures, derived from Ham or Amun</note> sacred term. The inland city of Oasis stood in an Egyptian province that had the $^{51}$ same name; therefore, the true meaning of the word must not be sought in Greece. This term was sometimes expressed in the feminine form, *Macris* and *Macra*. The Greeks interpreted this as "long" <note>original Latin: *longa*</note>, as if it related to the ex- <note>The text continues on the next page; the catchword suggests "extent."</note>

I believe we can be certain that it had nothing to do with length. Euboea was called *Macris* in ancient times and might be seen as relatively long; however, Icarus, Rhodes, and Chios were also given this name, yet they do not extend in length any more than the islands in their neighborhood. > <gloss>54</gloss> "And the place there is called Macrai" <note>original Greek: Μακραι δε χωρος εσ' εκει κεκλημενος</note>.

All these places were so named for religious reasons after Macar, a title of the Deity.

## ANAC.

Anac was a title of great antiquity and seems to have been originally assigned to persons of great strength and stature. In the plural, such people were called Anakim; and one family of them was found at <gloss>63</gloss> Kirjath-Arba. Some of them were also among the Caphtorim, who settled in Palestine. *Sar* means a "rock," and was used to signify a promontory <note>a high point of land or rock overlooking a body of water</note>. ### RADICALS.

The name of Sarah was given to the wife of Abraham as a title of eminence; it signifies a <gloss>68</gloss> lady, or princess. This root is continually found in the composition of names relating to places or persons esteemed sacred by the Amonians <note>Followers of an ancient religious system, identified by the author as descendants of Ham/Ammon</note>. We read of Serapis, Serapion, and Serapammon; also of Sarchon and Sardon, which is a contraction for *Sar-Adon* <note>Meaning "Lord-Lord" or "Prince-Lord"</note>. In the Book of Tobit, mention is made of <gloss>69</gloss> Sarchedonus; this is the same name as the former, but with the Eastern aspirate <note>A "breathy" pronunciation common in Near Eastern languages</note>.

The *Sarim* in the Book of Esther are noted as persons of high <gloss>70</gloss> honor. The same dignity seems to have been known among the Philistines, by whom it was rendered <gloss>71</gloss> *Sarna*, or *Sarana*. From this came the <gloss>72</gloss> Tyrian word *Sarranus* <note>original Latin: "Ostrum Sarranum," referring to the famous Tyrian purple dye</note> for anything noble and splendid. 

In the prophet Jeremiah, the titles of the chief princes who attended Nebuchadnezzar in his expedition against Judea are enumerated. Among others, he mentions the <gloss>73</gloss> *Sar-sechim*. This is a plural term, compounded of *Sar* and *Sech* (also rendered as *Shec*), which means a prince or governor. *Sar-Sechim* signifies the "chief of the princes and rulers." *Rab-shekah* has nearly the same meaning; it signifies the "great prince," just as *Rab-sares* means the chief <gloss>74</gloss> eunuch, and *Rabmag* means the chief of the Magi <note>A class of priests or wise men in ancient Persia</note>. Many places in Syria and Canaan have the term *Sar* in their composition, such as Sarabetha, Sariphæa, and Sareptha.

### RADICALS.

Sardis, the capital city of Croesus, was the city of *Sar-Ades*, which is the same as Atis, the deity of that country.

High <gloss>75</gloss> groves—or rather hills covered with woods of ancient oaks—were named *Saron* because they were sacred to the deity of that name. Pliny mentions the Saronian bay near Corinth and the oaks that grew near it: <margin>Pliny, Book 4, chapter 8.</margin> "The Harbor of Coenitis and the Saronian Gulf were once wreathed with an oak grove, which gave them their name" <note>original Latin: Portus Coenitis, Sinus Saronicus olim querno nemore redimitus; unde nomen</note>. ### RADICALS.

The same name was often varied in different ages and by different writers. Since priests adopted the titles of the deities they served, the Roman poet Lucan correctly introduced a priest of Egypt under the name of Achoreus:

-> Among whom was Achoreus, <-
-> now peaceful in his old age, and more humble as his years declined. <note>original Latin: quos inter Achoreus, Jam placidus senio, fractusque modestior annis</note> <-

The name of Osiris seems originally to have been *Uc-Sehor* and *Uc-Sehoris*. According to the historian Hellanicus, if a person in Egypt had asked about the term "Osiris," they would not have been understood, for the true name was *Usiris* <note>original Greek: Υσιριν</note>. Philo of Byblos, drawing from the works of Sanchoniathon, calls the same deity *Isiris* <note>original Greek: Ισιρις</note>. He adds that Isiris was the brother of Cna—also known as Canaan—and the inventor of three letters: "Isiris, the inventor of three letters, brother of Cna the Phoenician" <note>original Greek: Isiris, tōn triōn grammatōn heuretēs, adelphos Chna tou Phoinikos</note>. I believe *Isiris*, *Usiris*, and *Osiris* are all versions of the name *Uc-Sehoris*, softened and adapted to suit the ears of the Greeks.

The Sun was also styled *El-Uc*, which the Greeks changed to *Lucos* <note>original Greek: Λυκος; likely a play on the Greek words for "wolf" and "light"</note>, as we learn from Macrobius. He was also called *El-Uc-Or*, which was changed to *Lycoreus* <note>original Greek: Λυκωρευς</note>; and *El-Uc-Aon*, rendered as *Lycaon* <note>original Greek: Λυκαων</note>. # RADICALS.

...was the same as *El-Uc*, or *Lycos* <note>original Greek: Λυκος</note>; it was fabled of him that he was turned into a wolf. The cause of this absurd notion arose from this fact: every sacred animal in Egypt was distinguished by some title of the Deity. But the Greeks never considered whether the term was to be taken in its primary or in its secondary meaning. Consequently, they applied the history to an animal when it actually related to the God after whom the animal was named.

*Lycos* <note>original Greek: Λυκος</note> was, as I have shown, the name of the Sun. Therefore, wherever this term appears in a compound word, there will commonly be found some reference to that Deity or to his substitute, Apollo. We read of the ^96^ Temple of Lycian Apollo <note>original Greek: Λυκιου Απολλωνος ἱερον</note>; of ^97^ Lycorus, a supposed son of Apollo; of ^98^ Lycomedes, another son; and of ^99^ Lycosura, the first city which the Sun beheld. <meta>This page continues the exploration of the solar title "Lucos" (often translated as wolf), arguing that its true root refers to light and the Sun. The author demonstrates how this root appears in Latin and Greek words for light, as well as in the names of sacred places dedicated to Apollo.</meta>

# RADICALS.

Both names were sacred to the God of light. From *Lucos* <note>original: "Lucos"</note> in this sense came the Latin words *lux* (light), *luceo* (to shine), *lucidus* (bright or clear), and the title *Jupiter Lucetius* (Jupiter the Light-bringer). From the same root, the Greeks derived *lychnos* (a lamp), *lychnia* (a lampstand), and *lychneuo* (to give light) <note>original Greek: λυχνος, λυχνια, λυχνευω</note>. It also produced the terms *Lykabas* (a year, or "path of light") and *amphilykos* (twilight, or "between lights") <note>original Greek: Λυκαβας, αμφιλυκος</note>, though they are expressed differently. For this reason, many places sacred to Apollo were named *Leuce*, *Leuca*, *Lycia*, *Leucas*, and *Leucate* <note>original Greek: Λυκια</note>.

> Soon the cloudy peaks of Mount Leucata appear,
> And Apollo, dreaded by sailors, is revealed. ³

This is also the source of the inscriptions ⁴ TO THE GOD OF LEUCANIA <note>original Latin: DEO LEUCANIÆ</note>, a term that seems to mean *Sol-Fons*, the "fountain of day." The name *Lycophron* <note>original Greek: Λυκοφρων</note>, which some would derive from *Lykos* (a wolf), actually signifies a person of an enlightened mind. Groves were also held very sacred; therefore, the Latin word *lucus* (a grove), which some would absurdly derive "from not shining" <note>original Latin: a non lucendo; this refers to a famous ancient etymological joke that a dark grove is called a "light-place" (lucus) because there is no light (non lucere) there</note>, was actually named after the Deity worshipped there. The word *Alsos* <note>original Greek: 'Αλσος</note> served the same purpose among the Greeks.

These people, who received their theology from Egypt and Syria, often dropped the leading vowel and tried to make up for it by adding a new ending. To tell the truth, this method of abbreviation is often seen in the original languages from which these terms are derived. *Kyros* <note>original Greek: Κυρος</note>, the name of Cyrus, seems to have undergone an abridgment—

It was probably a compound of *Uch-Ur* <note>In the author's system, "Uch" often signifies a king or lord, and "Ur" signifies fire or the Sun.</note>, the same as *Achor*, and *Achorus* of Egypt—the great luminary, the Sun. In ancient times, all kings, priests, and people of consequence took sacred titles for themselves. But just as *Aneith* was shortened to *Neith*, and *Acherez* to *Cherez*, so *Achorus* was rendered *Chorus* or *Curus*. It is clear, then, that *Curus* signified the Sun.

Plutarch notes: "Now Cyrus took his name from Cyrus the ancient; and they say he took it from the Sun; for the Persians call the Sun 'Cyrus'." ⁵ <note>original Greek: Ὁ μεν ουν Κυρος απο Κυρου του παλαιου ονομα εσχεν· εκεινῳ δε απο του Ἡλιου γενεσθαι φασι· Κυρον γαρ καλειν Περσας τον Ἡλιον</note>

Ctesias likewise informs us that the name of Cyrus had this meaning: "And his name was given to him from the Sun." ⁶ <note>original Greek: Και τιθεται το ονομα αυτου απο του Ἡλιου</note> It was the same as *Orus* (Horus); and according to Strabo, it is sometimes expressed that way, as we may infer from a river of this name, of which he says: "It was previously called Koros." ⁷ <note>original Greek: Εκαλειτο δε προτερον Κορος</note> We find it sometimes rendered *Curis*, but still with a reference to the Sun, the Adonis of the East. Hesychius explains *Curis* as "Adonis" <note>original Greek: ὁ Αδωνις</note>. In Phocis was *Currha*, where *Apollo Cyrrhaeus* was honored; these names were more commonly expressed as *Kirrha* and *Kirrhaeus*. The people of Cyrene are said by Pausanias...

# RADICALS.

...Palaephatus <note>The OCR reads "læphatus," but this is a reference to Palaephatus, an ancient Greek author who specialized in explaining myths.</note> believed them to have been originally Ethiopians or Cuthites <note>Cuthites: In the author's system, these are the descendants of Ham, often identified with the builders of early civilizations.</note>. They, as well as the Egyptians, worshiped the Sun under the title of *Achur* and *Achor*; and like them, they esteemed him as the god who drives away flies <note>original Greek: Θεος απομυιος (Theos apomyios). This was a title given to deities believed to protect people from pests.</note>. From the God *Achur*, we may infer that their country was at first called *Acurana*, which is a compound of *Achur-Ain* and signifies "the great fountain of light." *Acurana* was abbreviated to *Curane* and *Cyrene*, but it was always supposed to relate to the Sun and Heaven. Hence the Greeks, who formed mythological characters out of every obsolete term, supposed Cyrene to have been the daughter of the supreme deity. *The city of Cyrene in Libya was named after Cyrene, the daughter of Hypsius (the Most High).* <note>original Greek: Κυρηνη, πολις Λιβυης, απο Κυρηνης της Υψεως</note> ¹⁰ There was a fountain here of great sanctity, which was similarly named after the Sun. It was called the fountain of Cyra <note>original Greek: Κυρη πηγη (Kyre pege)</note>, which—

***

⁹ "The people of Cyrene call upon the god Achor when a multitude of flies brings a pestilence; the flies perish immediately after a sacrifice is made to that god." <note>original Latin: Cyrenäici Achorem Deum (invocant) muscarum multitudine pestilentiam adferente; quæ protinus intereunt, postquam litatum est illi Deo.</note> Pliny, Book 10, chapter 28. See also Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Heathen*, page 33.

Some late editors, and particularly Harduin <note>Jean Hardouin (1646–1729), a French scholar known for his skeptical and controversial editions of ancient texts.</note>, not knowing that Achor was worshiped at Cyrene as the "god who drives away flies," have omitted his name and transferred this history to the region of Elis. But all the ancient editions mention Achor of Cyrene; "The people of Cyrene [call upon] the god Achor, etc." I have examined those printed at Rome (1470, 1473), those of Venice (1472, 1476, 1487, 1507, 1510), those of Parma (1476, 1479, 1481), and one at Brescia (1496). I have also checked the editions from Paris (1516, 1524, 1532) and the Basel edition by Froben (1523), and they all contain this reading. The edition by Johannes Spira (1469) also has "Acorem," though with some variation. The false reading, "the people of Elis [worship] the fly-catching god" <note>original Latin: Elei myagrum Deum</note>, was, I imagine, first admitted into the text by Sigismund Gelenius, who was misled by the similarity of the two histories. Harduin has followed him blindly, without taking any notice of the older and more accurate reading.

Orus and Arez. His descendants considered themselves of the Solar race by way of eminence. The great founder of the Persian Monarchy was called Achamin, translated by the Greeks as Achæmenes <note>original Greek: Αχαιμενης</note>. All of his family later held the title of Achæmenians <note>original Greek: Αχαιμενιοι and Αχαιμενιδαι</note> based on these same claims. This serves to support my etymology and shows that the term is derived from Cham, the Sun. However, its meaning was generally more specific, and the title was restricted to the royal line of the Persians, who were seen as the offspring of the Sun. The Cuthites <note>Cuthites: In this context, descendants of Cush, the son of Ham</note> of African Ethiopia <note>original Latin: Ethiopia Africana</note> held the same high opinion of themselves. For this reason, Calasiris, in the writings of Heliodorus, invokes the Sun as his great ancestor: "Let the Sun, the founder of our race, be called as witness" <note>original Greek: Επικεκλησθω μαρτυς ο Γεναρχης ημων ‘Ηλιος</note>. Chariclea, in another passage, uses a similar invocation: "O Sun, the great source of my ancestry" <note>original Greek: ‘Ηλιε, Γεναρχα προγονων ημων</note>.

Those who settled by the River Po <note>original Latin: Padus</note> did the same. <meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient titles derived from the name of the Sun, specifically focusing on the radical term "Uc." It follows the previous page's point about how various families and nations claimed descent from the "Solar race."</meta>

# RADICALS.

The meaning of the word is "Solar ones" <note>original: Solares</note>; it carries the same meaning as the *Shemsi* and *Shamsi* of the Arabians.

The term <term>Uc</term> <note>original Greek: Υκ</note>, which I have been discussing, was obsolete and scarcely known during the times when Greece most flourished. Yet some traces of it may be found, though they are strangely distorted from their original meaning. Because the writers of that nation did not know the significance of the words they found in their ancient hymns, they changed them to something similar in sound. In this way, they retained them with a degree of religious, yet blind, reverence. I have shown that from *El-Uc* they formed <term>Lykos</term> <note>original Greek: Λυκος</note> and *Lucus*, which was recognized as a name for the Sun. From *El-Uc-Aon*, they formed <term>Lycaon</term>; and from *El-Uc-Or*, they formed <term>Lycorus</term> and <term>Lycoreus</term>:

> ²⁵ "Either the lyre, or the bows, the weapons of Lycorean Phoebus <note>original Greek: Η κιθαριν, η τοξα Λυκωρεος εντεα Φοιβε; Phoebus is a common title for Apollo</note>."

Similarly, from *Uc-Ait*, another title of the God, they formed <term>Hecatus</term> and a feminine version, <term>Hecate</term>. For this reason, Nicander speaks of Apollo by this title:

> ²⁶ "Sitting upon the tripods of the Clarian Hecatus <note>original Greek: Ἑζομενος τριποδεσσι παρα Κλαριοις Ἑκατοιο; the "Clarian" refers to Apollo's oracle at Claros</note>."

And Herophile the Sibyl says of the same Deity:

> ²⁷ "Having a portion of the dominion then belonging to Hecatus <note>original Greek: Μοιραν εχουσ’ Ἑκατῳ της τοτ’ Ανακτοριης</note>."

Homer. <note>original: "...mer."</note> He had been in Egypt and was an admirer of that nation's theology. <meta>This page continues the etymological analysis of the term "och" (derived from ancient solar titles), focusing on its usage with "aristos" (best) in the works of Homer and the Orphic poets. # RADICALS.

In these and in all other instances of this term occurring in Homer, it is observable that it is always used in the same sense, and uniformly precedes the same word, <term>aristos</term> <note>original: αριϛος; the Greek word for "best"</note>. It is indeed found in the poetry ascribed to ³⁵ Orpheus; but as those verses are clearly imitations of Homer, we must not look upon it as a common term of the times when that poetry was composed. Nor was it ever, I believe, in common use—not even in the age of Homer. It was an Amonian <note>A term used by the author to describe the ancient descendants of Ham, particularly in Egypt and Chaldea, whom he associates with solar worship</note> term, joined inseparably with another word borrowed from the same people. For <term>aristos</term> was derived from Egypt and Chaldea. Indeed, most of the irregular degrees of comparison in Greek come from that region, being derived from the Sun—the great deity of the pagan world—and from his various titles and properties. Both <term>areōn</term> <note>original: αρεων; "better"</note> and <term>aristos</term> were derived from <term>Ares</term> <note>original: αρης</note>, the *Arez* of the East. From the deities Bel and Baaltis came <term>beltiōn</term> <note>original: βελτιων; "better"</note> and <term>beltistos</term> <note>original: βελτιϛος; "best"</note>; <term>ameinōn</term> <note>original: αμεινων; "better"</note> is an inflection from the god Amon. From the god Aloeus came <term>lōios</term>, <term>lōiteros</term>, and <term>lōistos</term> <note>original: λῳϊος, λῳϊτερος, and λῳϊϛος; "more desirable" or "better"</note>. From <term>keren</term> <note>a Chaldean or Hebrew term for "horn," symbolizing power</note>, which changed to <term>keras</term> <note>original: κερας</note> and <term>keratos</term> <note>original: κερατος</note>, were formed <term>kressōn</term>, <term>kreissōn</term>, <term>krateros</term>, and <term>kratistos</term> <note>original: κρεσσων, κρεισσων, κρατερος, and κρατιϛος; terms relating to strength and superiority</note>.

# RADICALS.

## P H I.

<margin>
³⁶ Genesis 45:21.
³⁷ Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 8, Chapter 6.
</margin>

*Phi* signifies a mouth; it also means language and speech. It was used by the Amonians <note>The author's term for the ancient descendants of Ham, particularly the Egyptians and Chaldeans, whom he identifies as solar worshippers.</note> specifically for the voice and oracle of any God, and was attached to the end of the name of that deity. The primary oracle in the earliest ages was that of Ham, who was worshipped as the Sun and styled *El* and *Or*. Consequently, these oracles were called *Ampi*, *Omphi*, *Alphi*, *Elphi*, *Urphi*, and *Orphi*. In the Book of ³⁶ Genesis, the term is used to signify the voice or command of Pharaoh. From *Phi* in this sense came the Greek and Latin words for speaking and reputation: *phēmi* <note>original: φημι; "I say"</note>, *phēmē* <note>original: φημη; "report" or "reputation"</note>, *phēmys* <note>original: φημυς; "speech"</note>, *phaskō* <note>original: φασκω; "to say"</note>, *phatis* <note>original: φατις; "an oracle" or "rumor"</note>, *fama* <note>Latin: "reputation" or "fame"</note>, and *fari* <note>Latin: "to speak"</note>—as in the phrase "so he began to speak" <note>original: *ita farier infit*</note>. I imagine that the title Pharaoh itself is a compound of *Phi-Ourah*, meaning "the voice of the Mouth, or of God" <note>original: *Vox Ori, sive Dei*</note>. It was common among the ancients to call the words of their prince the voice of God. Josephus informs us that the name signified a king: ³⁷ "Pharaoh among the Egyptians signifies a king" <note>original: Ὁ Φαραων παρ' Αιγυπτιοις βασιλεα σημαινει</note>. Similarly, in the Copto-Arabic *Onomasticon* <note>A dictionary or list of names</note>, the word *Ouro* is said to mean the same thing; however, I believe this was only a secondary meaning of the original term.

*Phi* is also used for any opening or cavity. Because of this, we often find the head of a fountain named after it—or at least the place where the fountain emerges or disappears into the earth. Since all streams were considered sacred, and all cavities in the earth were viewed with religious awe <note>original: "horrour"</note>, the Amonians called them *Phi-El*, *Phi-Ainon*, and *Phi-Anes*. These were translated by the Greeks as *Phiale*, *Phaenon*, *Phanes*, *Phaneas*, and *Paneas*. The chief

The source of the river Jordan disappeared underground and emerged again several miles away. It sank at Phiale and rose again at ^38 Paneas. Pliny speaks of a place of this sort at ^39 Memphis, called Phiala; and, as he imagines, the name comes from its shape. However, it was undoubtedly a covered aqueduct by which some branch of the river was carried. The Nile itself is said to be lost underground near its sources, and that place was also called Phiala. ^40 "Its source is called Phiala, and the river itself is swallowed into underground channels" <note>original: *Phialam appellari fontem ejus, mergique in cuniculos ipſum amnem*</note>. There was also a fountain of this name at ^41 Constantinople. Sometimes the name occurs without the aspirate <note>The "h" sound</note>, as in Pella, a city of Palestine, named undoubtedly from its fountains; for Pliny calls it ^42 "Pella, rich in waters" <note>original: *Pellam aquis divitem*</note>.

Mines were held sacred; and like fountains, they were named after Ænon and Hanes, which were titles of the Sun. In Arabia near Petra was a mine worked by condemned persons, which was named ^43 Phinon and Phænon. Epiphanius mentions the ^44 Phanesian mines <note>original: Φανησια μεταλλα</note>, or the mines of Hanes, to which Meletius, a bishop of the Thebaïs, was condemned.

island. In other regions, it had much the same meaning as the Greek word *aia* <note>original: αια</note> and signified any ^45 region or country. This is why the Greeks represented so many place names as plurals ending in *-ai*, such as Athenai (Athens), Thebai (Thebes), Pherai, Patrai, Amyclai, Therapnai, Clazomenai, and Celaenai. Others end in *-eia*, such as Chaeroneia, Coroneia, and Eleia. In other names, the sound was shortened, as in Oropia, Ellopia, Ortygia, Olympia, Ethiopia, Scythia, Caenia, and Icaria.

It is also found expressed by a single letter added to the end of a proper name: hence we see Etna, Arbela, Larissa, Roma (Rome), Himera, Hemera, Nusa, Nyssa, Patara, Arena, ^46 Cabasa, and similar examples. From these and countless other instances, we can prove that among Eastern peoples, as well as other nations, the word <term>in regimine: a grammatical term referring to a word in a specific relationship with another, here used as a suffix</term> was often placed at the end. Thus, the land of Ion was called Ionia; the land of Babylon, Babylonia; from Assur came Assyria; from Ind came India; and from Lud came Ludia <note>original: Ludia (Lydia)</note>. In all these cases, the region is specified by the suffix. Therefore, to say *Lydia tellus* (the land of Lydia) or *Assyria tellus* (the land of Assyria) is actually ^47 redundant.

In the name for Egypt, however, this term came first: the country was called *Ai-Gupt* <note>original: Αιγυπτος (Aigyptos)</note>, meaning "the land of the Gupti," who were later called Cupti or Copts.

# RADICALS.

## COMMON NAMES RELATING TO PLACES.

Regarding the common names found combined with additional terms to describe the nature and location of places: they are for the most part similar to those in ancient Chaldean <note>original: Chaldaic</note> and show little variation.

**Air** means a city; it is often expressed as **Ar** and **Ara**. From this root come Arachosia, Arachotus, Aracynthus, Arambis, Aramatha (from *Ar-Ham-aith*), Archile, Arzilla, and Arthedon. All of these were either cities or regions named after them.

**Kir**, **Caer**, and **Kiriath** are words with the same meaning. In the Scriptures, we read of Kiriath Sepher, Kiriath Arba, and Kiriath Jearim. In some parts, it was pronounced **Kirtha** and **Cartha**. Melicartus, the Hercules of the Phoenicians <note>original: Phenicians</note> and Cretans, was properly **Melech-Carta**, meaning "the King of the City" <note>from the roots Melech (King) and Carta (City)</note>. The city built by Tigranes the Great in Armenia was called Tigranocerta.

One name for Carthage was Karkhedon <note>original: Καρχηδων</note>, derived from **Car-Chadon**, which is the same as *Adon* <note>meaning Lord or Master</note>. It was also called **Carthada** from *Cartha-Ada*, meaning "the city of the queen or Goddess." The Romans identified this goddess as Juno, but she was actually the <term>Amonian: a term the author uses to refer to a specific ancient lineage associated with the god Amon</term> Elisa <note>also known as Dido, the legendary founder of Carthage</note>.

Among many ancient nations, **Caer** signified a city or fortress. We can see this in place names like Carteia, Carnaim, Caronium, Caroura, and Carambis. Among the ancient Britons, there were exactly analogous place names, such as Carlisle <note>original: Caerlisle</note>, Cardiff <note>original: Caerdiff</note>, Caerphilly, Caernarvon, and Caeruriah in Cornwall.

**Kir** and **Caer** are the same term expressed differently. In Scripture, we encounter Kir Haresh and Kir-Hareseth (Isaiah 16:7 and 11), Kir Moab (Isaiah 15:1), and Kir Heres, which has the same meaning as Kir Haresh and is mentioned

# RADICALS.

Mentioned by *Jeremiah*, chapter 48, verse 31. Upon the *Euphrates* river were the cities of *Cercusium* and *Carchemish*. In *Cyprus* was *Kironia*, which was translated as *Keronia* <note>original: Κερωνια</note> by <gloss>48</gloss> *Ptolemy*; its true name was *Kir-On*, the City of the Sun <note>from "Kir" (city) and "On" (a name for the Sun god)</note>. There, a temple stood dedicated to *Our-Ain* <note>the "Fountain of Light"</note>, who was called *Urania*. *Kir-On* was often translated as *Cironis* or *Coronis*; and the deity was called *Coronus* and <gloss>49</gloss> *Cronus* <note>the Greek titan often associated with time or Saturn</note>. By these means, the name of the place was substituted for the name of the deity, and the place itself became an object of worship. I shall speak of this abuse of language often. *Artemis* <note>the Greek goddess Diana</note> was properly the name of a city, *Ar-Themis*, which was the same as the Egyptian god *Thamuz*. What was called *Artemis* and *Artemisium* was in some places reversed, with the word *Kir* <note>city</note> added to the end; hence we find *Themiscir* and *Themiscura* in the region of *Pontus*.

This root was sometimes expressed as *Tar*; from this came Tarquinia, Taracena, Tarragona in Spain, and Tarne (*Tar-ain*), which gave its name to a fountain in Lydia. ### GAU, expressed as CAU, CA, and CO.

*Gau* is likewise a term that signifies a house, as we learn from Plutarch. The great and decisive battle between Alexander and Darius is generally said to have been fought at Arbela. But we are assured by this writer that it was decided at Gaugamela <gloss>65</gloss> <note>original: "Eratosthenes has recorded these things; but it happened that the great battle against Darius took place not at Arbela—but at Gaugamela; and they say that in that language the name signifies the House of a Camel." Plutarch, *Life of Alexander*, Vol. 1, p. 683. Strabo says the same: "This is a notable place, and the name, when translated, means the House of a Camel." Book 16, p. 1072.</note>. He says that *Gau* signified a house in the language of that country, and that the meaning of the word *Gaugamela* was "the house of a camel." This name, it seems, was given to the town because of a tax collected for the upkeep of a camel that had saved the life of a certain king when he fled from battle. The reason why Alexander’s victory was attributed to Arbela was that it was more famous than the other location; Gaugamela was not well-known enough. Therefore, the honor of this victory was given to Arbela, even though it was five hundred or, according to others, six hundred *stadia* <gloss>66</gloss> <note>original: "Those who have written the most say that it is six hundred stadia away, while those who say the least put it at five hundred. But Ptolemy and Aristobulus say the battle against Darius took place at Gaugamela near the River Bumodus; Gaugamela was not a city, but a large village, and the place was neither famous nor was its name pleasant to the ear."</note> <term>stadia</term> <note>A Greek unit of distance; 600 stadia is roughly 70 miles.</note> away.

I will only mention that, in my opinion, Arbela and Gaugamela were the same place. The king alluded to is said by <gloss>67</gloss> Strabo to have been Darius, the son of Hystaspes. 

But is it believable that so great a prince—who possessed horses of the famous breed of Nysa, as well as those of Persia and Arabia, the fastest of their kind—should be in such a situation in battle that he was forced to mount a camel that could scarcely move six miles an hour? This would be especially unlikely at a time when the greatest speed <note>original: "dispatch"</note> was necessary. 

This author [Strabo] gives a different reason for why the place was named this way. He says that the area was set aside for the maintenance of a camel that used to bring the king's provisions from Scythia, but which grew tired and broke down <note>original: "failed"</note> on the road. I do not know which of the two details in this short account is more questionable: a king of Persia's supplies being brought to Babylon or Susa <note>original: "Sushan"</note> from Scythia, or a tired camel receiving such a pension. 

The truth is this: the Greeks <note>original: "Grecians"</note> misinterpreted the name and then invented these legendary stories to support their <gloss>68</gloss> mistake. Had they understood the term, they would have been consistent in their history. **Gau**—and as it was sometimes expressed, **Cau**—certainly signifies a house or temple. It also refers to a cave or hollow, near which the temple of the deity was founded. For the Amonians <note>The author uses this term for the "descendants of Ham," whom he believes established the first great civilizations and religious systems.</note> built most of their sacred buildings near

...then well imagine that there existed in the time of *Plutarch* many mistakes, both regarding the geography of remote countries and the ⁷¹ language of nations with whom the *Romans* were little acquainted. The great battle we have been speaking of was admittedly fought at *Gaugamela*. *Ptolemy Ceraunus*, who was present, asserted this, as did *Aristobulus*; and it has been recorded by *Plutarch* and others. It is also attributed to *Arbela* by persons of equal credibility, and it must certainly have actually taken place there. For, despite the excuses made by *Plutarch*, it is utterly unbelievable regarding such a great victory that the scene of action would be identified by this place if it were sixty or, as some say, seventy miles out of the way. 

But in reality, it was not at such a distance. *Diodorus Siculus* says that immediately after the victory, *Alexander* attacked *Arbela* and took it; he found in it many evidences of it being a place of consequence. ⁷² <note>original: "Θαψας τες τετελευτηκοτας επεβαλε τοις Αρβηλοις, και πολλην μεν ευρεν αφθονιαν της τροφης, ουκ ολιγον δε κοσμον, και γαζαν βαρβαρικην, αργυριε δε ταλαντα δισχιλια."</note> "After burying the dead, he advanced against Arbela and found there a great abundance of food, a significant amount of furnishings, barbarian treasure, and two thousand talents of silver." The Chaldeans and Egyptians, from whom these titles were borrowed, considered Hermes to be the chief deity—the same as Zeus, Bel, and Adon. They knew nothing of "Mercury the Attendant" <note>original Latin: *Mercurius pedissequus*</note> or "Hermes the Lackey." They called their chief god Cam-Il, or Camillus, and his priests were given the same title. The god did not borrow the name from the priests; rather, they received it from him. The name is sometimes written as Camulus. The Amonians <note>A term the author uses for the descendants of Ham, who he believes spread solar worship.</note>, who traveled westward, brought his rituals and worship into Western Europe. Consequently, inscriptions can be found addressed ⁷⁷ "To Camulus, Most Holy and Most Strong" <note>original Latin: *Camulo Sancto Fortissimo*</note>. He was sometimes identified as Mars, as we learn from an inscription recorded by Gruter:

->⁷⁸ TO MARS CAMULUS.<-
->For the health of Tiberius Claudius Caesar, the citizens of Rheims erected this. <note>original Latin: *Ob Salutem Tiberi Claud. Cæs. Cives Remi posuerunt.*</note><-

This is the history of this deity, whose worship was better known in the earliest ages. His temple was called "Gau-Camel," which the Greeks rendered as "Gaugamela." I have no doubt that Arbela was the same place, for locations often had as many names as the deity worshiped there had titles. Arbela was likely the name of the city, and Gaugamela the temple ⁷⁹; both were sacred to the same deity under different names.

And here it is proper to take notice of a circumstance which I must continually remind the reader of, as it is of great consequence toward deciphering the mythology of ancient times: the Greeks often mistook the place of worship for the deity worshipped. Consequently, the names of many Gods are in reality the names of temples where they were adored. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the etymology of "Coel" (Heaven) and how its original meaning of "sacred" or "heavenly" was misinterpreted by the Greeks.</meta>

# RADICALS.

Many places and regions that were held sacred and called *Coel* by the Amonians <note>Followers of the Egyptian god Amon, whom the author believes spread ancient wisdom and religion</note> were translated by the Greeks as *koila* <note>original: κοῖλα</note>, meaning "hollows" <note>original: cava</note>. Consequently, we read of "Hollow Lacedaemon" <note>original: Κοίλη Λακεδαίμων (Koile Lakedaimon)</note>, "Hollow Elis" <note>original: Κοίλη Ἦλις (Koile Elis)</note>, and similar names. Syria was styled *Koile* <note>original: Κοίλη</note>, "the hollow," by them, but its true name was *Coëla*, meaning the "heavenly" or "sacred." It was named this by the Cuthites <note>A group the author identifies as ancient travelers and descendants of Ham, often associated with building civilizations</note> who settled there, because of the religion they established. Therefore, it was also named *Shem* and *Shama*, which are terms with the same meaning, signifying "divine" or "heavenly." It is a name it still retains today, as we are informed by Abulfeda <margin>6</margin> and others. 

"Hollow" Elis <note>Elis Coela</note> was the most sacred part of Greece, especially the regions of Olympia, Cauconia, and Azania. It was named *Elis* from *El* <note>original: Ἠλ</note>, meaning the Sun; and what the Greeks translated as "hollow" <note>original: Koile</note> originally meant "heavenly" <margin>7</margin>. For this reason, Homer specifically calls it "Sacred Elis" <margin>8</margin> <note>original: Ἤλιδα δῖαν (Elida dian)</note>. Just as "Hollow Syria" <note>Coele Syria</note> was called *Sham* and *Sama*, we find places in Elis that refer to this same term. A town of great antiquity was named *Samicon* <margin>9</margin>, which signifies "Lord of Heaven" <note>original: Coeli Dominus</note>. Here there was also a temple of Poseidon Samius, surrounded by a grove of olives, where festivals called *Samia* were observed. Likewise, in ancient times, there was a city named *Sama* or *Samos*. Strabo suggests this might have been named for its high elevation, noting that "high places were called—"

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the etymology of "Coel" and "Sama," arguing that these terms signify "heavenly" or "sacred" rather than physical characteristics like "hollow" or "high."</meta>

# RADICALS.

$^{10}$ *Samia*. The term certainly implies height to some degree; however, the true meaning of *Sama* was "heavenly," similar to the terms *Sam*, *Sham*, and *Shamem* used by Eastern nations <note>These are Semitic roots for the sun and the heavens</note>. For this reason, places like Same, Samos, Samothrace, and Samacon were so named because of their sanctity. The historian Strabo <margin>10</margin> notes that the city of Samos in Elis was situated in the Samian plain; therefore, it could not have received its name from being in a high location. Furthermore, it is inconsistent to suppose that regions described as *hollows* <note>original: κοῖλα (koila)</note> or *cavities* <note>original: cava</note> were named after *Sama*, meaning "high." 

In short, both terms have been misunderstood. In its original usage, *Coilus* certainly signified "heavenly." This is why we read in the lexicons of Hesychius and Suidas the term *Coioles, the Priest* <note>original: Κοιόλης, ὁ Ἱερεύς (Koioles, ho Hiereus)</note>. From this, we learn that a *Coioles* was a sacred or heavenly person—in other words, a priest of *Cœlus* <note>The Roman personification of the sky or heavens</note>. In the word *Coioles*, there is only a slight variation from the original term, which was a compound of *Coi-El* or *Co-El*, the *Cœlus* of the Romans.

Regarding the term *Cœl* used by the poet Ennius, $^{11}$ the scholar Janus Gulielmus <margin>11</margin> notes that this poet followed the Dorians in using abbreviations, writing *Cœl* instead of *Cœlus* or *Cœlum*. But in this, the learned gentleman is mistaken. The Dorians were not as much to blame for their "abbreviating" as the other Greeks were for their unnecessary word endings and grammatical changes. For the most part, we may consider terms to be more ancient and genuine the simpler they are. In the language of the Dorians, we can perceive more terms related to the true mythology of the country—and find them rendered in a way more similar to the ancient style of expression—than are elsewhere to be...

found. We must therefore, in all etymological inquiries, have recourse to the Doric manner of pronunciation to obtain the truth. They came into Greece, or Hellotia <note>An ancient name associated with Crete or early Greece</note>, under the name of Adorians; and from their simplicity of manners, and from the little intercourse they maintained with foreigners, they preserved much of their ancient tongue. Houses in the infancy of the world are supposed to have been caves or grottos <note>original: $^{14}$ "Then first they entered houses; houses were caves." Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 1, line 121.</note>. They expressed this as *Cai*, *Caia*, or *Caias*, which is similar to the words *cava* [hollow], *cavus* [hollow/cave], and *cavea* [cavity or enclosure] used by the Romans. When these places were of a great depth or extent, they were looked upon with a kind of religious horror. 

A cavern of this sort was located at Lacedaemon <note>The region of ancient Greece containing Sparta</note>, with a building over it; in later times, they used this place to confine criminals. It was called *Kaiades* <note>original: Καιαδης</note>, or as the Spartans expressed it, *Kaiadas* <note>original: Καιαδας</note>, meaning the "house of death" <note>original: $^{15}$ *Kaiadas desmōtērion — to para Lakedaimoniois*; translation: Kaiadas, a prison — that of the Lacedaemonians. By the Ionians, he was called *Ades* or *Hades*, and by other nations *Ait* and *Atis*. Hence, these caverns were also called *Kaietes* <note>original: Καιετες</note> and *Kaietoi* <note>original: Καιετοι</note>.

The rites of fire were practiced there <note>referring to the caverns discussed on the previous page</note>. The name **Cacus** is the same as **Cuscha** <note>Cuscha or Cush is often associated with the biblical grandson of Noah and the region of Ethiopia</note> in Ethiopia, only with the syllables reversed. The history of this name was obsolete by the time of **Virgil** <note>The famous Roman poet (70–19 BC)</note>; yet some traces of it still remained.

The poet, speaking of **Theseus**, **Dryas**, **Polyphemus**, and other heroes of the Mythic age, mentions their encounter with the mountaineers of Thessaly, whom he styles *phēres oreskōoi* <note>original: *φηρες ορεσχωοι*; mountain-dwelling beasts</note>:

> "Those were indeed the strongest of men bred upon the earth; they were the strongest, and they fought with the strongest: the mountain-dwelling beasts." <note>original: $^{19}$ *Kartistoi dē keinoi epichthoniōn traphen andrōn, Kartistoi men esan, kai kartistois emachonto Phērsin oreskōoisi*. *Oreskōos* signified a person who lived in a mountain habitation, whose retreat was a house in a mountain. *Co* and *Coa* were the names of such a house. Strabo says that this term is alluded to by Homer when he styles **Lacedæmon** <note>The region of ancient Greece containing Sparta</note> "cavernous Lacedæmon" <note>original: $^{20}$ *Lakedaimona kētōessan*</note>, for many thought it was called that because of its caverns. From this we may fairly conclude that *kētōessa* <note>cavernous</note> was a mistake, or at least a variation, for *kaietaessa* <note>original: *καιεταεσσα*</note>, derived from **Cai-Atis**; and that *Co*, *Coa*, and *Caia* all shared the same meaning.

# RADICALS.

But this term does not relate merely to a cavern; but to temples founded near such places: oftentimes the cave itself was a temple. **Caieta** in Italy near **Cumae** <note>An ancient Greek colony near modern Naples</note>, called *Kaiētē* <term>original: Καιητη</term> by **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a first-century BC Greek historian</note>, was so named on this account. It was a cave in the rock, abounding with a variety of subterranean passages, cut out into various apartments. These were inhabited in ancient times by **Amonian priests** <note>Priests of the sun god Amon or Ammon, central to Egyptian and later Libyan mythology</note>; for they settled in these parts very early. It seems to have been a wonderful work.

> "From there, massive openings in the earth appear, revealing caverns of a great extent; which afforded very ample and superb apartments." <note>original: $^{23}$ *Aneōge t’ enteuthen spēlaia hypermegethē, katoikias megalas, kai polytelcis dedegmena*. Strabo, Book 5, p. 357.</note>

Diodorus informs us that what was in his time called **Caieta** had sometimes been styled **Aiete** <note>original: $^{24}$ *Aiētēn*</note>. From this, we may see that it was a compound word; and consisted of two or more terms, but these terms were not precisely applicable to the same object. **Ai-Ete**, or **Ai-Ata**, was the region of **Ait**, the Deity to whom it was sacred. **Colchis** <note>An ancient region on the eastern coast of the Black Sea</note> had the same name; which is why its king was called **Aietes**. Egypt had the same name as well, expressed by the Greeks as **Aetia** <term>original: Αετια</term>. **Aiete** was the district; **Caieta** was the cave and temple in that district where the Deity was worshiped.

The river <note>Referencing the river Cephissus discussed on previous pages</note> descended and was lost. It afterwards emerged from this gulf and passed freely to the sea. The place of eruption was called **An-choa**, which signifies "Opening of the Fountain" <note>original Latin: *Fontis apertura*</note>. The later Greeks expressed it as **Anchoe** <note>original Greek: $^{26}$ *Anchoē*</note>: "The place is called **Anchoe**; and there is a harbor of the same name" <note>original Greek: *Kaleitai d’ ho topos Anchōē; esti de limēn homōnymos*</note>. I am confident that the etymology is plain and authenticated by the history of the place.

From **Cho** and **Choa** was probably derived the word ***Choikos*** <term>earthy or made of dust</term>, used by the Apostle Paul <note>original: $^{27}$ 1 Corinthians 15:47–48</note>: "The first man was of the earth, **earthy**; the second man is the Lord from heaven. As was the **earthy** man, such also are those who are **earthy**" <note>original Greek: *Ho prōtos anthrōpos ek gēs Choikos; ho deuteros anthrōpos ho Kyrios ex ouranou. Hoios ho Choikos, kai toioutoi hoi Choikoi*</note>. **Hesychius** <note>A 5th-century Alexandrian grammarian</note> observes that ***Choikos*** means "made of clay" or "of the earth" <note>original Greek: *Choikos pēlinos, gēinos*</note>. From this, we may perceive that by **Cho** was originally meant a house or temple in the earth. It was, as I have shown, often expressed as ***Gau*** and ***Go***, and made to signify any house. Some nations used it in a still more extended sense; and by it denoted a town, or village, and any habitation at large. It is found with this meaning among the ancient **Celts** and **Germans**, as we learn from **Cluverius** <note>Philipp Clüver (1580–1622), a founding father of historical geography</note>.

> "Among the Germans themselves, the native word for such districts was ***Gaw***; and in varying dialects, ***gǎw***, ***gew***, ***gǒw***, ***gow***. From this come: **Brisgaw**, **Wormesgaw**, **Zurichgow**, **Turgow**, **Nordgaw**, **Andegaw**, **Rhingaw**, **Hennegow**, and **Westergow**." <note>original Latin: $^{28}$ *Apud ipsos Germanos ejusmodi pagorum vernaculum vocabulum fuit Gaw; et variantibus dialectis...* Cluverius, *Germaniae Antiqua*, Book 1, ch. 13, p. 91.</note>

Together with the words mentioned above, the particles ***Al*** and ***Pi*** are often found in combination. ***Al*** or ***El***—for it is expressed differently in our alphabet—is still an Arabic prefix, though it is not absolutely confined to that country, even if it is found there most frequently. # RADICALS.

The king whom Alexander the Great fought at the Indus River was named after the primary object of his worship, **Or** <note>original Hebrew: אור; meaning light or fire</note>, combined as **Pi-Or** and **P’Or**. This was written by the Greeks as **Porus** <note>original Greek: Πωρος</note>. **Pacorus** the Parthian has the same linguistic origin, being a compound of **P’Achorus**, referring to the Egyptian deity **Achor**. This is also the case for the city of <gloss>30</gloss> **Pacoria** in Mesopotamia, mentioned by the geographer **Ptolemy**. Even the Greek word for fire, ***pur*** <note>original Greek: πυρ</note>, was of Egyptian or Chaldean origin and has the same structure (**P’Ur**) as the words mentioned above. For <gloss>31</gloss> **Plato** informs us that the words for fire, water, and dogs—***pur***, ***hydor***, and ***kynes*** <note>original Greek: πυρ, υδωρ, κυνες</note>—were considered to be of foreign origin.

After the line of Egyptian kings ended and the country fell under the rule of the Greeks, the local people continued to use this prefix, as did other <gloss>32</gloss> nations that were merged with them. They applied it not only to words in their own language but also to those of other countries they discussed. Consequently, their writings often contain terms like <gloss>33</gloss> **Pizous** <note>original Greek: Πιζευς; likely "the Zeus"</note>, **Pimartyr** <note>original Greek: Πιμαρτυρ; "the martyr"</note>, **Pimathetes** <note>original Greek: Πιμαθητης; "the disciple"</note>, **Pisoma** <note>original Greek: πισωμα; "the body"</note>, **Pilaos** <note>original Greek: πιλαος; "the people"</note>, **Pidux** <note>a hybrid of "Pi" and the Latin *dux*, meaning "the leader"</note>, **Picurator** <note>a hybrid meaning "the administrator"</note>, and **Pitribunus** <note>meaning "the tribune"</note>. Personal names also appear with this prefix, such as **Piterus**, **Piturio**, **Pionius** the martyr, as well as **Pior**, **Piammon**, and **Piambo**. These figures are all mentioned by ecclesiastical <gloss>34</gloss> writers as being natives of that country <note>Egypt</note>.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that many ancient titles for "boys" (pueri) were actually misinterpretations of titles for "priests of fire" (P'ur). He focuses on the etymology of the Latin word "puer" and the festival of Purim.</meta>

### RADICALS.

That this word *Puer* <term>Puer: Latin for "boy"</term> was originally *Pur* may be proved from a well-known passage in Lucretius:

> "Boys often, near a water-basin or curved jars, when overcome by sleep, believe they are lifting their clothes." <note>original Latin: *Puri sæpe lacum propter ac dolia curva / Somno devincti credunt se attollere vestem.* Lucretius, Book 4, verse 1020. The author uses "Puri" here to support his etymological link between "puer" and "pur" (fire).</note>

Many instances, were it necessary, might be brought to support this point. It was a name originally given to the priests of the Deity who were named from the Chaldean *Ur* <note>original Chaldaic: אור</note> (meaning fire); and by the ancient Latins they were called *P’uri*. At Præneste, the name was particularly preserved on account of this divination by lots <margin>58</margin>. These were styled *Purim* by the Ammonians <note>original: Amonians. Bryant's term for the descendants of Ham, whom he believes established a global solar religion.</note>, being accompanied by ceremonies involving fire, and were supposed to be carried out through the influence of the Deity. Præneste seems to be a compound of *Puren Esta*, meaning "the lots of Esta," the deity of fire.

These are terms which seem to occur continually in ancient Ammonian history. Most names are compounded from these, and they are easily broken down into these roots. There are a few more which might perhaps be very properly introduced, but I am unwilling to impose too much on the reader, especially as they may be easily noticed in the course of this work. I could wish that my learned readers would grant me enough credit to defer passing a general judgment until they have read the whole; for much more clarity will emerge.

What in the book of Esther <note>original: Hester</note> is called *Purim*, the Septuagint <note>original: "the Seventy"</note> translates in chapter 9, verse 29 as *phrourai* <note>original Greek: φρουραι, meaning "guards" or "watches"</note>. The days of Purim were called *phrourai*. "In their dialect they are called *phrourai*" <note>original Greek: Τη διαλεκτω αυτων καλονται φρουραι</note>; so also in chapter 10. The Greek additions to Esther mention "the existing letter regarding the *phrourai*" <note>original Greek: την προκειμενην επιστολην των φρουραι</note>, instead of *phourai* and *Pyrai* <note>original Greek: φουραι and Πυραι</note>: from *P'Ur* and *Ph'Ur*, meaning fire <note>original Latin: ignis</note>.

<note>Empedocles (c. 494–434 BC) was a Greek pre-Socratic philosopher. This prayer asks for divine guidance to speak clearly and truthfully, avoiding the "madness" or confusion of others.</note>

It may appear offensive <note>original: "invidious"</note> to call to account men of learning who have preceded me in investigations of this nature, and to point out the defects in their writings. However, it is a task which I must, to some extent, undertake, as the best writers have, in my opinion, failed fundamentally in these researches. Many, in the extravagance of their imagination, have yielded to the most groundless guesses; they have done so with a lack of restraint <note>original: "licentiousness"</note> for which no amount of learning or ingenuity can compensate.

# ETYMOLOGY.

It is, therefore, so far from being harmful <note>original: "injurious"</note> that it appears absolutely necessary to point out the path they took and the nature of their failure. This is done so that their authority does not give a seal of approval to their mistakes. On the contrary, if my method should appear more plausible or more certain, its superiority may be seen upon comparison and be proved by the contrast.

The Greeks <note>original: "Grecians"</note> were so convinced by a notion of their own excellence and antiquity that they supposed every ancient tradition had originated with themselves. Consequently, their mythology is founded upon the gravest mistakes, as they assumed all external history and every foreign term to be of Greek origin. Many of their learned writers had traveled abroad and knew how baseless <note>original: "idle"</note> the pretensions of their countrymen were. Plato, in particular, saw the falsehood of their claim and admitted it more than once; yet, on this subject, no one was more obsessed <note>original: "infatuated"</note>. His *Cratylus* <note>A dialogue by Plato regarding the origin of names and whether language is natural or conventional.</note> consists of a most absurd system of etymology. <margin>59</margin> Herodotus explicitly says that the gods of Greece came largely from Egypt. Yet, in this treatise, Plato has Socrates derive *Artemis* from "the sound and unharmed" <note>original Greek: *to artemes*; Latin: *integritas*</note>; *Poseidon* from "fetters to the feet" <note>original Greek: *posi desmon*</note>; *Hestia* from "substance and essence" <note>original Greek: *ousia*</note>; *Demeter* from "giving as a mother" <note>original Greek: *didousa hōs mētēr*</note>; *Pallas* from "to vibrate or dance" <note>original Greek: *pallein*</note>; *Ares* (Mars) from "male and manly" <note>original Greek: *arren*; Latin: *masculum et virile*</note>; and the word *Theos* (God)—undoubtedly the *Theuth* <note>Thoth, the Egyptian god of wisdom and writing.</note> of Egypt—from

# ETYMOLOGY. 133

...person inhabited. But is it believable, or indeed possible, for these cities to have been named from terms so vague, casual, and indefinite? These names seem to have very little relation to the places to which they are assigned, or to any places at all. The history of the Chaldeans is of great importance, and one would be eager to know their origins. They are properly called Chasdim and are rightly considered to have been the first established nation on earth. It is said of the patriarch Abraham that he came from the city *Ur* of the Chasdim. Where did they get their name? The learned Hyde <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703), an English orientalist and author of the cited work.</note> answers <sup>67</sup> that it was from Chesed, their ancestor. 

Who was Chesed? He was the fourth son of Nahor, who lived in *Aram*, the upper region of Mesopotamia. Does history record that he was the father of this people? There is no mention made of it. Is it ever stated that he was in *Chaldea*? No. Is there the slightest reason to think that he had any acquaintance with that country? We have no grounds to assume so. Is there any reason to believe that this people—who are mentioned repeatedly as existing ages before him—were in reality established after his time? None. 

What, then, has led writers to suppose that he was the father of this people? It is because "Chesed" and "Chasdim" have a remote similarity in sound. And is that all? That is absolutely everything that is or can be alleged <note>original: "alledged"</note> in support of this notion. Furthermore, since the Chasdim are mentioned several ages before the birth of Chesed, some scholars argue that the passage was introduced proleptically <term>proleptically: describing something as existing before it actually did, or using a name before it was officially given</term>; others suppose it to be an interpolation <term>interpolation: a passage or remark inserted into a text, often by a later editor, that was not in the original</term> and would delete it from the sacred text. To such an extent does whim triumph over judgment, that even...

<meta>This page continues the argument that the origins of the god Vulcan have been misunderstood by previous scholars like Bochart and Gale. # ETYMOLOGY.

...name from *Chores Ur* <note>Hebrew original: כורש אור</note>, meaning a craftsman in fire.^94 These learned men do not consider that although the name they refer to is ancient and Middle Eastern <note>original: "oriental"</note>, the character and attributes are relatively modern, having been introduced from a different source. 

**Vulcan the blacksmith**, the master of the Cyclopes who forged iron in Mount Etna, was a character familiar to the Greeks and Romans. However, among the Egyptians and Babylonians, this deity had nothing similar to this description. They esteemed Vulcan as the chief of the gods—the same as the Sun. His name is a sacred title, compounded from *Baal-Cahen*, meaning "The holy Belus, or the Prince" <note>original: "Belus sanctus, vel Princeps"</note>, and is equivalent to Horus <note>original: "Orus"</note> or Osiris. 

Even if the name had a different origin, it would be pointless to seek an etymology based on later ideas and derived from qualities that were not originally part of the personage. According to Hermapion,^95 he was viewed as the source of all divinity; consequently, the inscription upon the entrance of the temple at Heliopolis was:

->**To Vulcan, the Father of the Gods.** <note>Greek original: Ἡφαιστῳ τῳ Θεων Πατρι</note><-

In short, those who first gave the name of Vulcan to their deity had no concept of him being a craftsman in brass or iron, or a craftsman of any kind. Therefore, we must be cautious when forming ideas about the ancient theology of nations based on the current notions of the Greeks and Romans, and especially from the descriptions of their poets. **Polytheism**, which was originally corrupt and unjustifiable, was rendered

# ETYMOLOGY.

...ten times more base by coming through their hands. To give an instance in one particular: among all the demon herd, what figure is as odious and contemptible as Priapus? He was an obscure, ill-formed deity who was ridiculed and dishonored even by his own devotees. His hideous figure was used only as a bugbear <note>a source of dread or a scarecrow used to frighten children</note> to scare children and to drive the birds away from fruit trees, with whose filth he was generally smeared. 

Yet this contemptible god, this scarecrow in a garden, was held in high repute at Lampsacus <note>an ancient Greek city in Asia Minor</note> and was esteemed as the same as **Dionysus** <gloss>96</gloss>. He was likewise reverenced by the Egyptians as the principal god—none other than the Chaldean **Aur**, the same as Orus <note>Horus</note> and Apis, whose rites were particularly solemn. It was from this source that he received his name; for the Priapus of Greece is only a compound of *Peor-Apis* among the Egyptians. He was sometimes styled *Peor* alone, and also *Baal-Peor*, the same deity whose rites were so often rebuked <gloss>98</gloss> among the Israelites. His temples are also mentioned, being styled *Beth-Peor*. In short, this miserable divinity of the Romans was looked upon by others as the soul of the world—the first principle that brought all things into light and being. "Priapus is the world, or the Word <note>original: Logos</note> that presides over it" <gloss>99</gloss> <note>original: Πριαπος ὁ κοσμος, ἡ ὁ προεστως αυτου Λογος</note>. It is appropriate to first take notice of the writers we will specifically rely on, and whose evidence is most dependable in investigations <term>disquisitions</term> of this kind. However, we must approach the Helladians <note>original: "Helladians." Apollonius was a native of Egypt, and the other two also lived there and frequently refer to the ancient history <term>antiquities</term> of that country. # HELLADIAN *and other* GREEK WRITERS.

These are writers of high rank; particularly *Diodorus*, *Strabo*, and *Pausanias* among the non-Christian <note>original: "Gentile"</note> authors. Among the Church Fathers, there are *Theophilus*, *Tatian*, *Athenagoras*, *Clement*, *Origen*, *Eusebius*, *Theodoret*, and *Syncellus*; as well as the compiler of the *Sicilian Chronicles* <note>original: "Fasti Siculi"</note>, otherwise called the *Paschal Chronicle* <note>original: "Chronicon Paschale"</note>. Most of these writers were from either *Egypt* or *Asia*. They had a genuine interest in antiquity and lived at a time when some real insight could be obtained. Until the *Roman* empire was fully established and every province was in a state of peace <term>tranquillity</term>, very little information could be gathered from those countries where the mythology of *Greece* actually originated. 

The native Greeks <term>Helladians</term> were very limited in their knowledge. They had accepted, without question <note>original: "in the gross"</note>, whatever was handed down by tradition, and they claimed as their own every history that was imported from abroad. Moreover, they viewed every nation but their own as "barbarous"; consequently, their overwhelming pride <note>original: "insuperable vanity"</note> made it impossible for them to make any great progress in historical knowledge. 

But the writers I just mentioned either did not have these prejudices, or lived at a time when such biases had greatly subsided. They were willing <note>original: "condescended"</note> to quote countless authors—some of great antiquity—to whom the pride of *Greece* would never have appealed <term>resorted</term>. 

I once had many discussions on this subject with a learned friend, now deceased <note>original: "since lost to the world"</note>, who could hardly tolerate that *Herodotus*, *Thucydides*, and *Xenophon* should be set aside for *Clement*, *Origen*, or *Eusebius*; or that the orators *Lysias* and *Demosthenes* should give way to *Libanius* and *Aristides*. He could not even bear the names of *Tzetzes* or *Eustathius* <note>Tzetzes and Eustathius were 12th-century Byzantine scholars known for their extensive commentaries on classical works.</note>. To all of this, I repeatedly answered that it was by no means my intention to set aside any of the [writers,]

But I must, at the same time, take it upon myself to weigh those merits—to see what they consisted of and to what degree they were to be trusted. The native Greeks <term>Helladians</term> were much to be admired for the smoothness of their sentence structures <term>periods</term> and the skillful arrangement <term>collocation</term> of their words. They showed great correctness in their choice of vocabulary <term>diction</term> and a beautiful organization of their ideas; the whole work was accompanied by a rhythm and harmony found nowhere else. 

But they were, at the same time, under the influence of intense prejudices. The subject matter they treated was generally so brief and limited that very little could be obtained from it regarding the history of other countries or a knowledge of ancient times. Even in respect to their own affairs, whatever light had been passed down to them was so distorted, and came through such a flawed perspective <term>dim a medium</term>, that it is difficult to make use of it for any specific or useful purpose. Yet the beauty of their writing style <note>original: "composition"</note> has been accompanied by a wonderful influence. Many have been so captivated by this "magic" that they have blindly believed everything that has been passed down, sacrificing their judgment for the pleasures of the imagination <note>original: "fancy"</note>.

Those who add color and embellishment often have the least regard for the truth. Yet all the rites of the Helladians <term>Helladians: An archaic term for the people of Hellas, or ancient Greeks.</term>, as well as their gods and heroes, were imported from the East <note>See Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 10, ch. 4, p. 469 and ch. 5, p. 473; also Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book 1, p. 361; Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, pp. 62–63 and 86–87.</note>—and chiefly from Egypt—though they were unwilling to admit it. I believe it is therefore appropriate to provide a short account of this wonderful Egyptian people first, in order to show where this obscurity began. This confusion eventually became so widespread that the Greeks largely lost sight of their own origins and became wrapped in mystery and myth.

The first inhabitants of the country later called Hellas were the sons of Javan <note>Javan, the grandson of Noah, is traditionally considered the ancestor of the Greeks (Ionians).</note>, who seem to have declined very early on and to have become truly uncivilized. # HELLADIC <note>original: Helladian</note> *and other* GREEK WRITERS.

They did not consider the various traditions handed down, though they actually related to their own country and had been introduced from other <gloss>16</gloss> places. Indeed, they did not choose to distinguish between them but adopted all as their own, taking the credit for every ancient event for themselves. No people had a greater love for science, nor displayed a more refined taste in composition. Their study was always to please and to inspire admiration. Consequently, they always aimed for the marvelous <note>The "marvelous" (or *to thaumaston*) in ancient rhetoric refers to elements intended to provoke wonder or awe, often at the expense of historical accuracy.</note>, which they presented in a most winning manner. At the same time, they showed a superficial reverence for antiquity. However, their judgment was flawed, and this reverence was accompanied by little regard for the truth. <gloss>17</gloss> They had a high opinion of themselves and of their country in general. Being persuaded that they had sprung from the very ground on which they stood—and that the Arcadians were older than the moon <note>This refers to the "Proselenes," a name for the ancient Arcadians who claimed to have inhabited their land before the moon existed.</note>—they were satisfied with this and looked no further. In short, they had no love for anything authentic and no desire to be properly instructed. Their history could not be corrected without an admission that their pride would not allow them to make. They therefore devoted themselves to an idle mythology, and there was nothing so contradictory

Wherever they gained a foothold, or even a brief contact, they adapted everything in their descriptions to fit their own preconceived ideas. There surely was never any nation so uninterested in and indifferent to the truth. This has led to the contradictions and inconsistencies that plague <note>original: embarrassed</note> their history.

Consequently, they believed their own writings would be just as welcome if they included historical events they had neither seen, heard, nor learned from any reliable source. They proceeded solely on the principle that they would be most likely to please the public's imagination <note>original: "fancy"</note> by resorting to things that were marvelous and new. 

For this reason, we can more safely trust **Hesiod** and **Homer** when they present us with a list of demigods and heroes—and even the tragic poets—than **Ctesias** <note>A Greek physician and historian of Persia (5th century BC)</note>, **Herodotus**, **Hellanicus** <note>An early Greek historian (5th century BC)</note>, and writers of that sort. # DISSERTATION upon the [HELLADIAN and other GREEK WRITERS]

The writers who must necessarily be consulted were in constant opposition and contradicted one another. And how, asks **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC–24 AD)</note>, could it be otherwise? For if they erred so shamefully when they had eyewitness proof, how could they speak with certainty when they were led only by hearsay? <sup>33</sup>

In another place, <sup>34</sup> he excuses the mistakes of the ancient poets, saying that we must not wonder if they sometimes drifted from the truth, given that people in more enlightened ages were so ignorant and so devoted to everything marvelous and incredible. Previously, he had even given the poets preference over other writers, but in this, his enthusiasm carried him too far. The first writers were the poets, and the problems began with them. They were the first to corrupt tradition, mixing it with allegory and myth. **Athenagoras** <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist</note> accuses them of this very justly; he says <sup>35</sup> that the greatest distortions of true knowledge originated with them. "I maintain," says this learned Church Father, "that we owe to **Orpheus**, **Homer**, and **Hesiod** the fictitious names and genealogies of the pagan spirits <note>original: *Dæmons*; in this context, the lesser gods or spirits of Greek religion</note> whom they are pleased to call gods; and I can pro—" <note>The sentence continues on the next page: "—prove..."</note>

# HELLADIAN and other GREEK WRITERS

—duce **Herodotus** as a witness to what I assert. He informs us that **Homer** and **Hesiod** lived about four hundred years before his own time, and no more. These, he says, were the people who first framed the <term>theogony</term> <note>The origin or genealogy of a group of gods</note> of the Greeks. They gave names to their deities and assigned them their several ranks and departments. At the same time, they described them as having different appearances; for until their time, there was no representation of the gods in Greece, either in sculpture or painting, nor any specimen of the statuary's art exhibited. No such substitutes were even thought of in those times.

The ancient history and mythology of Greece was partly transmitted by the common traditions of the natives and partly preserved in those original Doric hymns which were universally sung in their <term>Prutaneia</term> <note>The town hall or central administrative building of a Greek city, containing the sacred hearth</note> and temples. These were in the ancient Amonian language <note>original: "Amonian language"; the author’s term for an ancient root language he connects to the descendants of Ham or "Amun"</note> and were said to have been introduced by <gloss>36</gloss> **Pagasus**, **Agyieus**, and **Olen**. This last figure is represented by some as a Lycian, by others as a <term>Hyperborean</term> <note>A member of a mythical race of people living in the far north</note>, and by many he was esteemed an Egyptian. They were chanted by the *Purcones*, or priests of the Sun, and by the female <term>Hierophants</term> <note>Priests or priestesses who interpret sacred mysteries</note>, of whom the chief on record were <gloss>37</gloss> **Phaënnis**, <gloss>38</gloss> **Phaëmonoë**, and **Bœo**. The last of these mentions **Olen** as the inventor of verse and the most ancient priest of **Phoebus** <note>A name for Apollo, the god of the sun and prophecy</note>.

Such were the principles which gave birth to the mythology of the Greeks <note>original: "Grecians"</note>; from which their ancient history was in great measure derived. As their traditions were obsolete and filled with external <note>original: "extraneous"</note> matter, it was impossible for them to properly arrange the principal events of their country. They did not separate and distinguish events; instead, they often took credit for transactions which occurred at an earlier date and in another land. These they adopted and made their own. Hence, when they came to organize <note>original: "digest"</note> their history, it was entirely confused. They were embarrassed by numerous contradictions and absurdities which were impossible to ⁴³ remedy. For their vanity, as I have shown, would not allow them to correct their mistakes using the authority of more ancient and more learned nations. For truths passed down through tradition cannot be preserved for long without undergoing some change in themselves and picking up unrelated details. This accumulation of added material grows with every age until, in the end, only a few outlines of the original event remain. Many have maintained that the Greeks <note>original: "Grecians"</note> possessed writing very early, but upon investigation, this appears to be a baseless notion. Those ancient writers who examined the matter more carefully had no hesitation in dismissing these claims. ⁴⁵ Josephus, in particular, notes their early claim but cannot accept it. *Those*, ⁴⁶ *says this learned historian, who want to push the introduction of letters among the Greeks back to the earliest date, very solemnly tell us they were brought over by the Phoenicians <note>original: "Phenicians"</note> and Cadmus. It is certain that the Helladians <note>Helladians: An archaic term for the people of Hellas, the ancient name for Greece.</note> had no inclination toward learning until they were awakened by the Asiatic Greeks. Even then, it was some time before writing was in general use, or any histories—or even records—were attempted. For if writing had been common, and the materials for writing easily available and in frequent use, why is it that we do not have a single example older than the reign of Cyrus? <note>Cyrus: Cyrus the Great (reigned c. 559–530 BC), the founder of the Persian Empire.</note> And how is it possible, if the Greeks had any records, that they would be so ignorant about some of their most famous men?

How little is known of Homer! And of what has been passed down, how little can we actually rely on! Seven places in Greece claim him as their own, while many doubt whether he was even of Greek origin. It is said of Pythagoras that, according to <gloss>51</gloss> Hippobothrus, he was from Samos. However, Aristoxenus (who wrote his life story) as well as Aristarchus and Theopompus, identify him as a Tyrrhenian <note>Tyrrhenian: An ancient term for the non-Greek peoples of Italy, often specifically the Etruscans.</note>. According to Neanthes, he was from Syria, or perhaps a native of Tyre.

In the same way, Thales was said by Herodotus, Leander, and Duris to have been a Phoenician, though others claimed he was from Miletus in Ionia. It is reported of Pythagoras that he visited Egypt during the time of Cambyses <note>Cambyses: Cambyses II, King of Persia (reigned 530–522 BC).</note>. From there, he went to Croton in Italy, where he is supposed to have lived until the last year of the seventieth Olympiad <note>Seventieth Olympiad: Approximately 497 BC.</note>. Consequently, he could not have lived more than thirty or forty years before the birth of Aeschylus and Pindar. What credit can we give to a people for histories dating many ages back, when they were so ignorant in matters of—

Another reason can be given for the obscurity of Greek history, even after writing had been introduced among them. They had a childish dislike for every foreign language and were equally biased in favor of their own. This has gone largely unnoticed, yet it resulted in disastrous consequences for historical accuracy. They were misled by the excessive sensitivity of their hearing and could not tolerate any term that seemed to them "barbarous" <note>barbarous: Originally, the Greeks used this term for anyone who did not speak Greek, as foreign tongues sounded like "bar-bar" to them.</note> or uncouth. Because of this, they either rejected foreign <gloss>53</gloss> names entirely or so modified and changed them that they became essentially different in both sound and meaning. And as they were deeply attached to their own country and its customs, they assumed that the origins of everything were to be found among themselves. They did

<page-num>168</page-num>
<header>DISSERTATION upon the</header>

...did not consider that the titles of their gods, the names of cities, and their terms of worship were imported; that their ancient hymns had become obsolete; and that time had brought about a great change. They explained everything through the language currently in use, without the slightest consideration for history or context, and all names and titles from other countries were subject to the same rule. If a name sounded harsh or was disagreeable to their ears, it was rejected as "barbarous" <note>barbarous: A term the Greeks used for anything non-Greek, implying it was uncouth or unintelligible.</note>. However, if it sounded even slightly similar to a word in their own language, they changed it to that Greek word—even if the name was of Syriac origin or had been introduced from Egypt or Babylonia. 

By these means, the meaning of the term was changed, and the history that depended upon it was either distorted or completely erased. For example, when the title *Melech*, which signified a "king," was rendered as *Meilichos* and *Meilichios*, meaning "sweet and gentle" <note>original: Μειλιχος and Μειλιχιος. These Greek words sound like the Semitic "Melech" but have entirely different meanings related to being mild or honey-like.</note>, it referred to an idea quite different from the original. But this did not concern them; they blindly continued their practice. Some legend was immediately invented as a result of this misunderstanding <note>original: misprision</note>—perhaps some story about bees and honey—to make the mistake seem somewhat believable. 

This is a matter of great importance and deserves our serious attention. I will have the opportunity to speak of it repeatedly and will present the reader with entire treatises on the subject.
