# DISSERTATION *upon the*

...they did not consider that the titles of their gods, the names of cities, and their terms of worship were imported; that their ancient hymns had grown obsolete; and that time had wrought a great change. They explained everything by the language currently in use, without the least retrospect or allowance for the past. All names and titles from other countries were subject to the same rule. If the name was dissonant and disagreeable to their ear, it was rejected as barbarous; but if it was at all similar in sound to any word in their own language, they changed it to that word, even if the name was of Syriac origin or introduced from Egypt or Babylonia.

But this gave them no concern; they still blindly pursued their purpose. Some legend was immediately invented in consequence of this mistake <note>original: misprision</note>—perhaps some story about bees and honey—and the mistake was rendered in some degree plausible. 

This is a circumstance of much consequence and deserves our great attention. I shall have occasion to speak of it repeatedly and to lay before the reader some entire treatises upon the subject. For this failure is of such a nature that, when detected and fairly explained, it will lead us to the solution of many dark and enigmatic <note>original: enigmatical</note> histories with which the mythology of Greece abounds. <header>DISSERTATION upon the</header>

It may seem strange to use the mistakes of any people as a foundation to build upon; yet these very failures will support my system to some degree. At the least, by detecting these errors, I hope to gain much insight. Since Greek writers were consistent in their mistakes—following a clear rule and method of deviation—it is very possible to decipher what is being secretly alluded to once this method is well understood. By these means, we can arrive at the truth. If the paths in a forest or labyrinth are random, we might wander forever; but if they are designed with a discernable method, that pattern serves as a clue to lead us through the maze. Once we know that what the Greeks in their mythology called a "wolf" was actually the Sun; that a "dog" meant a prince or deity; and that "bees" signified an order of priests—these terms, however misapplied, can no longer mislead us. They are like symbols carved in stone, which a native of Egypt would recognize as emblems regardless of how they were described in writing.

I have found it necessary to state this at the outset, as our knowledge must come to us through the hands of the Greeks.⁵⁶

---

...they have turned [foreign terms] into "corpses" <note>original Greek: νεκυας (nekyas)</note>; and changed the city of Necho, or the "Royal City," into Nicopolis <note>original: Νικοπολις, meaning "City of Victory"</note> and Necropolis <note>original: Νεκροπολις, meaning "City of the Dead"</note>.

Lysimachus, in his Egyptian history, changed the name of Jerusalem to Hierosyla <note>original Greek: Ιεροσυλα, meaning "Temple-robbers"</note>. He assumed the city was named this because the Israelites, during their march to Canaan, used to plunder temples and steal sacred things. See Josephus, *Against Apion*, Book 1, Chapter 34, page 467. <note>Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish historian; *Against Apion* is his defense of Judaism against Greek slanders.</note>

⁵⁶ I do not mean to exclude the Romans, even though I have not mentioned them here; the majority of the knowledge they provide is the product of Greece.

They have, accordingly, passed down to us many valuable records <note>original: "remains"</note> which, but for them, would have been buried in oblivion. There are likewise many pagan authors to whom we are greatly indebted, but especially to Strabo and Pausanias, who in their different fields of study have provided wonderful light. Nor must we omit Josephus of Judea, whose treatise *Against Apion* must be regarded as being of inestimable value; indeed, all his writings are of consequence if read with a proper critical perspective <note>original: "allowance"</note>.

I have mentioned that it is my purpose to give a history of the first ages and to show the origin of many nations whose descent has been mistaken or else remains totally unknown. I shall speak particularly of one great family which spread itself over many parts of the earth, from whom the rites, mysteries, and almost the entire science of the Gentile <term>Gentile: in this context, the non-Jewish or "pagan" world of antiquity</term> world were borrowed. But as I venture onto an uncharted path <note>original: "unbeaten track"</note> and into a wilderness which has been little visited, I shall first take it upon myself to treat things close at hand before I advance to more distant discoveries. I shall, therefore, speak of those rites and customs, and of the nations where they prevailed; by these means, I will be led gradually <note>original: "insensibly"</note> to the discovery of the people from whom they were derived. By a similarity of customs, as well as by the same religious terms observed in different countries, it will be easy to show a relationship which existed between such people, however widely dispersed. They will be found to have been colonies of the same family and to have come ultimately from the same place. As my course will be, in large part, an uphill struggle, I shall proceed in the manner I have mentioned;

It is appropriate to mention to the reader that the following treatises were not written in the order in which they now appear, but rather as the subject matter presented itself to me. Since many sections that were composed first will appear last, I have been forced to anticipate some of the arguments and quotations they contained, as I found it necessary <note>original: "expedient"</note>. Consequently, there will be a few instances of repetition. However, I hope this will not cause any great frustration <note>original: "disgust"</note>, as the repeated material was so interwoven into the argument that I could not easily remove it from the text where it occurs a second time.

There will also be some instances where I disagree with my own previous statements or contradict positions taken in a former treatise. These are very few and of little importance <note>original: "no great moment"</note>, being the type of details that would likely escape the reader's notice. However, I believe it is more honest <note>original: "ingenuous"</note>, and indeed my strict duty, to acknowledge my mistakes and point them out rather than to pass over them in silence or pointlessly <note>original: "idly"</note> defend them.

We must never derive the <term>etymology</term><note>The study of the origin of words and the way in which their meanings have changed throughout history.</note> of an Egyptian or Eastern term from the Greek language. Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and Archbishop of Thessalonica known for his extensive commentaries on Homer.</note> well observes: "If the name is foreign, one should not seek a Greek etymology for it" <note>original: Ει βαρβαρον το ονομα, ȣ χρη ζητειν ‘Ελληνικην ετυμολογιαν αυτȣ</note>.

The Greeks adopted all foreign history and assumed it had originated in their own country.

They mistook temples for deities and places for persons.

# RULES and OBSERVATIONS

They [the Greeks] changed every foreign term to something similar in their own language: they chose words similar in sound, however remote in meaning, being guided solely by the ear.

They constantly mistook titles for names: and from these titles, they multiplied the number of their deities and heroes.

All terms of family relationship between the deities are to be disregarded <note>The author suggests that when myths say one god is the "son" or "wife" of another, it is often a later Greek invention to explain titles they did not understand.</note>.

Because the Greeks were mistaken, it is worth our while to observe their patterns of error and the consistency of their mistakes. By paying attention to this, we may bring things back to their primitive state and discover the original meaning in ancient terms.

We must pay attention to the <term>oblique cases</term><note>Grammatical cases other than the nominative (subject), such as the genitive (possession) or accusative (object).</note>, especially in <term>imparisyllabic</term><note>Nouns that have a different number of syllables in the nominative case than in the other cases (for example, the Latin 'rex' has one syllable, but the genitive 'regis' has two).</note> nouns, when we have an ancient term passed down to us from either the Greeks or Romans. In both languages, the <term>nominative</term><note>The base form of a noun used as the subject of a sentence.</note> is often shortened; because of this, the original term is to be deduced from the <term>genitive</term><note>The grammatical form of a word that shows possession or origin, often translated with "of."</note> case or from the possessive form. This is found to be true even in common names. From *veteris* [of the old], we find *veter* was the true term; from *sanguinis* [of the blood], we find *sanguen*. That this is correct, we may prove from Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), a writer often considered the father of Roman poetry.</note>, who says:

<margin>
$^{57}$ Ennius, *Annals*, Book 2.
$^{58}$ Ibid, Book 1.
</margin>

> $^{57}$ "O father, O creator, O blood descended from the gods!" <note>original: O! pater, O! genitor, O! sanguen diis oriundum.</note>
> $^{58}$ "When the aged Priam fell under the Pelasgian war." <note>original: Cum veter occubuit Priamus sub marte Pelasgo. 'Pelasgian' refers to the Greeks.</note>

So *mentis* [mind], and not *mens*, was the true nominative to the forms *mentis*, *menti*, and *mentem*, as we may learn from the same author.

# HELLADIAN AND OTHER GREEK WRITERS

<margin>$^{59}$ From the fragments of Ennius <note>original: *Apud Ennii fragmenta*</note>.</margin>
$^{59}$ The fire there is taken from the sun, and it belongs to the mind <note>original: *Istic est de sole sumptus ignis, isque mentis est*</note>.

In a similar way, *Plebes* was the <term>nominative</term><note>The base form of a noun used as the subject of a sentence.</note> case for *Plebi* and *Plebem* <note>The author is demonstrating how the spelling of words for "the common people" changed across different grammatical cases in ancient Latin.</note>.

->Nourishing Ceres fails, and the common people possess no bread. <note>original: *Deficit alma Ceres, nec plebes pane potitur*</note> — Lucilius.<-

All the common roles assigned to the Deities should be set aside as inconsistent and pointless. You will find that Pollux was considered a judge; Ceres a lawgiver; Bacchus the God of the year; Neptune a physician; and Aesculapius the God of thunder. This information comes not just from the poets, but from the best Greek mythologists—those who wrote professionally on the subject.

I have observed before that the Greeks, when dealing with foreign words, often changed the final *Nu* (the letter 'n') to a *Sigma* (the letter 's'). For *Keren*, they wrote *Keras*; for *Cohen*, *Kons*; for *Athon*, *Athos*; for *Boun*, *Bos*; for *Sain*, *Saïs* <note>The author argues that many famous Greek names and places are actually corrupted versions of older Phoenician, Hebrew, or Egyptian words.</note>.

In ancient times, people were called the children of the God whom they worshiped. Because of this, they were eventually thought to be that god's actual physical offspring, and the god was looked upon as their true parent. On the other hand, Priests were described as foster-fathers to the Deity they served; and Priestesses were called *tithēnai* <note>original: τιθηναι</note>, or "nurses," and also "daughters."

Colonies always set out under the protection and name of a specific Deity. In later times, this guiding God was mistakenly believed to have been the actual, physical leader of the expedition.

### THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

...diffused, will still taste of the fountain <note>original: "favour of the fountain," meaning the water still carries the qualities of its source.</note>. Moreover, as people were guided in their choice of holy places by those supernatural phenomena of which I have previously taken notice, if there is any truth in my system, there will be found a uniform analogy between the name of the temple, its rites, and its situation; so that the etymology may be confirmed by the history of the place. The same will appear in respect to rivers and mountains, especially those that were esteemed sacred and were named after the Sun and fire. 

I therefore flatter myself that the etymologies which I shall lay before the reader will not stand alone and unsupported, but that there will be an apparent analogy throughout the whole work. The connection will not be casual or remote, nor will it be obtained by improper grammatical changes and distortions. However complicated a name may appear, it will easily resolve itself into its original terms; and once resolved, the truth of the etymology will be confirmed by the accompanying history. Whether the subject is a deity or another personage, the truth will appear from their office and role, or from the attributes assigned to them. 

To begin then with ancient Latium <note>Latium was the region of central Italy where Rome was founded.</note>. If I should have occasion to speak of the goddess Feronia <note>Feronia was an ancient Italian goddess associated with wildlife, fertility, and health; her sanctuary was at the foot of Mount Soracte.</note> and of the city named after her, I would derive the name from *Fer-On*, meaning "the fire of the Sun God" <note>original Latin: *ignis Dei Solis*</note>. I would suppose the place to have been devoted to the worship of the Sun and the rites of fire. I accordingly find from the ancient geographers Strabo and Pliny that rites of this sort were practiced there. One custom, which remained even until the time of Augustus, consisted of a ceremony where the priests used to walk barefoot over burning coals: *For with bare [feet]...* <note>original Greek: Γυμνοις γαρ [ποσι]</note>

### THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

The custom passed westward to Greece, Italy, and the extremities of Europe. As proof of this, the following inscription is to be found in Gruter <note>Jan Gruter (1560–1627), a scholar known for his massive collection of ancient Roman inscriptions</note>:

->In Vascania <note>modern Basque Country</note> in Spain<-
->TO THE DIVINE FOUNTAIN.<-

We learn from Seneca how much this practice prevailed among the Romans. <margin>12</margin> "We venerate the sources of great rivers; the springs of hot waters are worshipped; and certain pools are held sacred due to their darkness or immense depth" <note>original Latin: Magnorum fluviorum capita veneramur — coluntur aquarum calentium fontes; et quædam ſtagna, quæ vel opacitas, vel immenſa altitudo ſacravit</note>. It mattered not what the nature of the water might be, provided it had some peculiar quality. At Thebes in Ammonia <note>the region around the Temple of Ammon in the Libyan desert</note> was a fountain which was said to be cold by day and warm at night. <margin>13</margin> It was named the *fountain of the Sun* <note>original Greek: Ἡ κρηνη καλειται τȣ ἡλιȣ</note>.

In Campania <note>a region in southern Italy</note> was a fountain named Virena. I would judge this to be a compound of *Vir-En*, signifying "fire fountain" <note>original: ignis fons</note>, because it was dedicated to the deity of fire on account of some particular quality. Accordingly, I find in <margin>14</margin> Vitruvius <note>a famous Roman architect and engineer</note> that it was a medicinal spring of a strong vitriolic <note>mineral-rich or acidic</note> nature.

The Corinthians had in their Acropolis a <margin>15</margin> Pirene, which has the same meaning as the Virena just mentioned. It was a beautiful fountain sacred to Apollo, whose <margin>16</margin> image stood at the head of the water within a sacred enclosure. We read also of a Pyrene, which

### THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

...was a fountain of another nature, yet of the same etymology, however differently expressed. It was a mountain and gave its name to the vast ridge called the *Pyrenees* <note>original: Saltus Pyrenæi</note>. It is undoubtedly a compound of <margin>17</margin> *Pur-ain*, and signifies a "fountain of fire." I should imagine, even without knowing the history of the country, that this mountain once flamed, and that the name was given due to this circumstance. Agreeably to this, I find from Aristotle’s *On Marvelous Things Heard* <note>original: de Mirabilibus</note> that there was formerly an eruption of fire here. The same is mentioned by Posidonius in the writings of Strabo, and also by Diodorus, who adds: <margin>18</margin> "The mountains were called Pyrenean because of what had happened" <note>original Greek: Τὰ μὲν ὄρη διὰ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς κληθῆναι Πυρηναῖα</note>.

Mount *Ætna* is very truly derived by Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> from *Aituna*, meaning a furnace <note>original Latin: fornax</note>, as it is a reservoir of molten matter. There was another very ancient name, *Innessa*, by which the natives called the hill as well as the city that was toward the bottom of it. The name is a compound of *Ain-Es*, like Hanes in Egypt, and signifies a "fountain of fire." It is called *Ennesia* by Diodorus, who says that this name was afterwards changed to *Ætna*. He speaks of the city, but the name was undoubtedly borrowed from the mountain, to which it was primarily applicable and upon which it was originally conferred: <margin>19</margin> "And they took possession of the place now called Etna, which was previously called Ennessia" <note>original Greek: Καὶ τὴν νῦν οὖσαν Αἴτνην ἐκτήσαντο, πρὸ τούτου καλουμένην Ἐννησίαν</note>. Strabo expresses the name as *Innessa* and informs us more precisely that the upper part of the mountain was so called. <margin>20</margin> "But the inhabitants of Etna, having [retreated]..." <note>original Greek: Οἱ δὲ Αἰτναῖοι παρα- [catchword: χωρησαντες]</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the city of Hanes (or On) and its connection to Sun worship, clarifying the geographical distinctions between various cities called "On" or "Heliopolis" in Egypt and Arabia.</meta>

### THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

The other was the city of On in Arabia, also called Hanes. These cities were within eight or nine miles of each other and are both mentioned together by the prophet $^{25}$ Isaiah: *For his princes were at Zoan; and his ambassadors came to Hanes.* Because both cities practiced a similar form of worship, the Greeks translated the names of both as $^{26}$ Heliopolis <note>literally, "City of the Sun"</note>. This has caused significant confusion in the history of Egypt. 

The second of these was the Iänis—or *Ianysos* <note>original Greek: Ἰανυσος</note>—of the Greeks. It was named after Hanes, the great fountain of light, the Sun, who was worshiped under that title by both the Egyptians and the Arabians. Today, it lies completely in ruins near the village of Matarea, which has risen from its remains. Its location is so clearly identified that there can be no mistake. Furthermore, it is a remarkable circumstance that the Arabs still call it *Ain El Sham*, meaning "the fountain of the Sun"—a name with exactly the same meaning as Hanes. The learned geographer D’Anville and others inform us of this, though various travelers spell the name differently. $^{27}$ "This city, almost buried under ruins and located near—according to Abulfeda—a small place called Matarea, retains in Arabic geographies the..." <note>original French: Cette ville presque ensevelie sous des ruines, et voisine, dit Abulfeda, d'un petit lieu nommé Matarea, conserve dans les géographies Arabes le...</note>

I have previously noted an objection likely to be made: the assumption that if *Hanes* signified the *fountain of light*, as I have suggested, it would have been expressed differently in the Hebrew language. This is a strange fallacy, yet it is very common. Without doubt, those learned men who have preceded me in these researches would have been on the verge of noble discoveries had they not been too limited and biased in their notions. But as far as I am able to judge, most of those who have engaged in inquiries of this nature have ruined the purpose of their labors through some prevailing prejudice. They have not considered that every other nation we can access, or from whom we have any history, appears to have expressed foreign terms differently from the natives in whose language those terms were found. # THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

—ferently from the people of that country; and they do the same in respect to us. What we call London, they express as *Londres*; England they style *Angleterre*. What some call Basel <note>original: "Bazil"</note>, they pronounce *Bal*; München, *Munich*; Mainz <note>original: "Mentz"</note>, *Mayence*; and Regensburg <note>original: "Ravenspurg"</note>, *Ratisbon*. The same variation was observable in ancient times. *Carthago* to the Romans was *Carchedon* <note>original: "Carchedon," the Greek name for Carthage</note> among the Greeks. Hannibal was rendered as *Annibas*; Hasdrubal <note>original: "Asdrubal"</note> as *Asdroubas*; and probably neither was consistent with the Punic <note>the language of the Carthaginians</note> way of speaking.

If a prophet were to rise from the dead and preach to any nation, he would use terms adapted to their specific idiom and usage, without looking back at the origins of those terms, whether they were local or foreign. The sacred writers undoubtedly followed this rule for the people they wrote for, and they varied their expression of foreign terms as the people's usage changed. For the Jewish nation at times differed from its neighbors and even from its own past forms of speech. 

We may be morally certain that the place they called *Ekron* was called *Achoron* by its natives; this is the *Accaron* <note>Greek: Ακκαρων</note> mentioned by Josephus and the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>. What they called *Philistim* was *Pelestin*; *Eleazer*, in their own language, they changed to *Lazar* and *Lazarus*; and from the Greek *sunedrion* <note>original Greek: συνεδριον; a council or assembly</note> they formed the word *Sanhedrim*. From this, we can be certain that the Jews and their ancestors—as well as all nations on earth—were likely to express foreign terms with variations, led by the natural peculiarities of their own way of speaking. Therefore, those who try to derive the spelling <note>original: "orthography"</note> of all ancient words from Hebrew, and who test every foreign term by that standard, are surely to be blamed. It requires no great insight into

The learned Michaelis <note>Johann David Michaelis (1717–1791), a famous German biblical scholar and teacher of linguistics.</note> has taken notice of this fatal attachment to Hebrew roots, and speaks of it as a strange illusion. He says *that it is a widespread influence <note>original: "influenza," used here in the sense of a contagious or prevailing trend of thought</note>, to which all are liable who make Hebrew their principal study* <margin>Dissertation on the influence of opinion upon language, and of language upon opinion. Section 6, page 67 of the translation.</margin>.

The only way to obtain the hidden meaning <note>original: "latent purport"</note> of ancient terms is through a fair analysis. This must be discovered by an apparent analogy and supported by the history of the place or person to whom the terms relate. If such help can be obtained, we may determine very truly the etymology of an Egyptian or Syriac name, even if it appears contrary to the spelling <note>original: "repugnant to the orthography"</note> of the Hebrews. 

The term *Hanes* is not so uncommon as may be imagined. Zeus was worshiped under this title in Greece and styled *Zeus Ainesios* <note>original Greek: Ζευς Αινησιος</note>. The commentator <note>original: "Scholiast," an ancient commentator on classical texts</note> upon Apollonius Rhodius mentions his temple and calls it *the temple of Zeus Ainesios, which is also mentioned by Leon in his "Circumnavigation" and by Demosthenes in his "On Harbors"* <note>original Greek: Διος Αινησιου ἱερον, οὗ μνημονευει και Λεων εν περιπλῳ, και Δημοσθενης εν λιμεσι</note> <margin>Scholia upon Apollonius. Book 2, verse 297.</margin>. It is also noted by Strabo, who speaks of a mountain Hanes where the temple stood. *The greatest mountain in it is Ainos (read: Aines), in which is the temple of Zeus Ainesios* <note>original Greek: Μεγιστον δε ορος εν αυτῃ Αινος (lege Αινης), εν ᾧ το του Διος Αινησιου ἱερον</note> <margin>Strabo. Book 10, page 700.</margin>. The mountain of Zeus Ainesius must have been Aines and not Ainos, though it appears that way in our present copies of Strabo. The commentator mentioned above quotes a verse from Hesiod, where the poet styles the deity *Aineïos* <note>original Greek: Αινηϊος</note>.

Aineïus and Ainesius both come from *Hanes*, the deity of Egypt, whose religious ceremonies can be traced in various regions. There were places named Aineas and Ainesia in Thrace that share this same origin. This title sometimes appears with the prefix *Ph'anes*; early theologians believed the deity called by this name was of the highest antiquity. They considered him identical to Ouranus <note>Uranus</note> and Dionysus, even going so far as to credit him with creative power and claiming that all things originated from him. <margin>^34 Orphic Fragment 7.</margin> <margin>^35 "The theologians... praised the creative cause in Phanes." <note>original Greek: Οἱ Θεολογοι—εν γε τῳ Φανητι την δημιουργικην αιτιαν ανυμνησαν</note>. Orphic Fragment 8, from Proclus's commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*.</margin>

From *Phanes*, the Greeks derived the title *Phanaios* <note>original Greek: Φαναιος, meaning "the bringing of light" or "the revealer"</note>, which they applied to both Zeus and Apollo. <margin>^36 "To me, you have come as Zeus the Bringer of Light." <note>original Greek: Συ μοι Ζευς ὁ Φαναιος ἡκεις</note>. Euripides, *Rhesus*, line 355. "Phanaios Apollo among the people of Chios." <note>original Greek: Φαναιος Απολλων εν Χιοις</note>. Hesychius <note>an Alexandrian grammarian who compiled a dictionary of rare Greek words</note>.</margin> This was not unusual, as they were both regarded as the same god. In northern Italy, there was a district called *Ager Pisanus* <note>original Latin: "the Pisan territory"</note>. <margin>^37 Pliny, Book 2, chapter 106, page 120.</margin> The origin of this name is the same as *Hanes* and *Phanes*, though the terms are reversed. It means "source of fire" <note>original Latin: *ignis fons*</note>. To confirm this etymology, I have found that the place was famous for its hot springs, which the Roman author Pliny refers to as the *Aquæ Pisanæ* <note>original Latin: "the Pisan waters"</note>.

Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 18, chapter 14.</margin> Its medicinal waters are well-known and were called the *Aquæ Cumanæ* <note>original Latin: "the Cuman waters"</note>. Cappadocia, where there stood one of the most noble fire-temples <note>original: Puratheia</note> in Asia. The deity worshiped there was represented as a female and named *Anaït* and *Anaïs*; the latter name is the same as *Hanes*. She was well known also in Persia <note>original: Persis</note>, Mesopotamia, and at Ecbatana <note>original: Egbatana</note> in Media. Both *An-ait* and *An-ais* signify a "fountain of fire." Of the latter, the geographer Strabo gives an account, describing the fiery matter found near it: ^45 "Near Arbela is also the city of Demetrias; then the naphtha spring, and the fires (or fire-temples), and the temple of Anaia." <note>original Greek: Περι Αρβηλα δε εστι και Δημητριας πολις· ειθ’ ἡ τε ναφθα πηγη, και τα πυρα (or πυρεια), και το της Αναιας ἱερον.</note>

In Arcadia, near Mount Lyceus, there was a sacred fountain into which one of the nymphs who nursed Jupiter was supposed to have been transformed. It was called *Hagnon*, which is the same as *Ain-On*, the "Fountain of the Sun." From *Ain* (fountain), a word used by the Amonians <note>Bryant’s term for the ancient peoples he believes spread sun worship from Egypt and Babylon</note> and expressed as *Agn*, came the Greek word *hagnos* <note>original: ἁγνος</note>, which signified anything pure and clean, or "pure or chaste" <note>original: purus sive castus</note>. From this were derived the terms for "holy, as a fountain," "holy, or pure," and "holy, or clean," <note>original Greek: ἁγνειον, πηγαιον· ἁγναιον, καθαρον· ἁγνη, καθαρα</note> as we may learn from the lexicographer Hesychius. Pausanias calls the fountain ^46 *Hagno*, but it was originally *Hagnon*, the fountain of the Sun. From this we learn in another passage of Hesychius that the word *agnopoleisthai* <note>original: ἁγνοπολεισθαι</note> means to be purified or treated as holy.

Thucydides and other Greek writers call them Phoenicians <note>original: Phenicians</note> ⁵⁰: "And Phoenicians also lived all around Sicily" <note>original Greek: Ωικουν δε και Φοινικες περι πασαν μεν Σικελιαν</note>. Furthermore, the term "Phoenician" was not a proper name but a title, which was adopted by people from various regions, as I will demonstrate. The small district to which the Greeks applied this name could not have provided enough people to inhabit all the many regions the Phoenicians were said to have occupied. It was a name <note>original: appellation</note> that the ancient and original inhabitants of Canaan never used for any part of their land; nor was it ever accepted or used until the Greeks took control of the coast. Even then, it was limited to a small area—the coast of Tyre and Sidon.

If so many examples can be found in the west, many more will appear as we move toward the east, where these terms originated. Almost all the place names in Greece have an Oriental <note>Eastern</note> etymology, or at least come from Egypt. I suspect that the name of Methane in the Peloponnese <note>original: Peloponnesus</note> relates to a fountain, being a compound of *Meth-an*—the "fountain of the Egyptian deity, Meth," whom the Greeks called Metis <note>original: Μητις</note>.

Colophon is *Col-Oph On*, the mound of the Python Sun God <note>original Latin: *tumulus Dei Solis Pythonis*</note>, and corresponds with the character given. The river into which this fountain ran was sacred and named Halesus; it was also called <gloss>55</gloss> Anelon: *An-El-On*, the Fountain of the Sun God <note>original Latin: *Fons Dei Solis*</note>. Delos was famed for its oracle and for a fountain sacred to the prophetic Deity. It was called <gloss>56</gloss> Inopus. Places named Asopus, Elopus, and the like, follow the same logic <note>original: analogy</note>. The God of light, Orus <note>Horus</note>, was often styled *Az-El*; from which we encounter many places named Azelis, Azilis, Azila, and by shortening the end of the word <term>apocope</term>, Zelis, Zela, and Zeleia. Chimæra is a compound of *Cham-Ur*, the name of the Deity whose altar stood towards the top of the <gloss>59</gloss> mountain. At no great distance stood Mount Argaius, which was a part of the great ridge called Taurus. This Argaius may be derived either from *Har*, a mountain, or from *Aur*, fire. We may suppose Ar-gaius to signify a **hollow mountain** <note>original Latin: *Mons cavus*</note> or rather a **hollow of fire** <note>original Latin: *ignis cavitas*</note>, or **house of Vulcan** <note>original Latin: *Vulcani domus*</note>—a name given because it was hollow and, at the same time, a reservoir of fiery matter. The history of the mountain may be seen in Strabo, who says that it was immensely high and ever covered with snow; it stood in the vicinity of Comana, Castabala, Caesarea, and Tyana, and all the country about it abounded with fiery <gloss>60</gloss> eruptions. But the most satisfactory idea of this mountain may be obtained from coins which were struck in its vicinity and particularly <gloss>61</gloss> describe it as both a hollow and an inflamed mountain.

In Thrace was a region called Pæonia, which seems to have had its name from P'Eon, the God of light <gloss>62</gloss>. The natives of these parts were styled both Pæonians and Pierians; these names equally relate to the Sun. Agreeably to this, Maximus Tyrius tells us that they particularly worshiped that luminary, and adds that they had no image;

...a people, a tribe of the Chaldeans. This area was the source of fire-worship, and the entire country was filled with bitumen and fire. There was a region, <sup>75</sup> *Hyrcania*, inhabited by the Medes, which seems to have had the same flammable nature. The people were called *Hyrcani* and *Astabeni*; the latter name signifies the "fountain of fire" <note>original Latin: fons of fire</note>. Cellarius mentions a city called *Hyrcania* in <sup>76</sup> *Lydia*. There were certainly people styled *Hyrcani*, and a large plain called the *Hyrcanian Plain* <sup>77</sup> in the same part of the world. It seems to have been a part of that parched and burning region called *Katakekaumene*, named for the fires with which it abounded <note>original Greek: κατακεκαυμενη, meaning "the burnt region"</note>. It was near *Hierapolis*, *Caroura*, and the *Fossa Charonea*, all of which were famous for fire.

It may seem extraordinary, yet I cannot help thinking that the *Hercynian* forest in Germany was none other than the *Hyrcanian*, and that it was named after the god *Ur-can*, who was worshiped here as well as in the East. It is mentioned by Eratosthenes and Ptolemy under the name of the *Orcunian forest* <sup>78</sup>, which is undoubtedly the same name as the one mentioned above <note>original Greek: δρυμος Ορκυνιος (drymos Orkunios)</note>. One would infer that it was named this way from the same circumstance <note>the name Pyrene is derived from the Greek "pyr," meaning fire</note>. Since the worship of the Sun—the deity of fire—prevailed greatly at places of this nature, I have no doubt that Hercynia (which Ptolemy writes as *Orkunia* <note>original Greek: Ὀρκυνία</note>) was named after Or-cun, the god of that element.

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that European geographical names and religious customs—specifically in the Alps and Germanic regions—originated from an ancient "Amonian" culture (descendants of Ham) who spread sun-worship and specific titles across the continent.</meta>

->### THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 212<-

The passage through the mountains was generally attributed to a single person. This mountain pass is therefore said by some to have been the work of Hercules; others attribute it to Cottus or Cottius. From this, this particular branch of the mountains received the name of the Cottian Alps <note>original: Alpes Cottiæ</note>, and the country was called the Cottian Region <note>original: Regio Cottiana</note>, which contained about twelve major cities <sup>85</sup>. Posidonius states that some members of that ancient and sacred nation, the Hyperboreans <note>a mythical people who lived in the far north "beyond the North Wind"</note>, settled in these parts: "The Hyperboreans... dwell around the Alps of Italy" <note>original Greek: Τους Ὑπερβορεους—οικειν περι τας Αλπεις της Ιταλιας</note> <sup>86</sup>. The Taurini lived here, and one of their chief cities was Comus. Strabo calls the country the land of Ideonus and Cottius <sup>87</sup>. 

These names will later be shown to be quite remarkable. In fact, many Alpine place-names were Amonian <note>referring to the descendants of Ham, whom the author believes spread an ancient solar religion</note>, as were their religious rites. The same pattern can be observed in many parts of Gaul <note>modern France</note>, Britain, and Germany. Among other evidence, the worship of Isis and her sacred ship should be noted, as it was practiced by the Suevi <note>a large group of Germanic tribes</note>. Tacitus writes: "A portion of the Suevi also sacrifices to Isis. I have discovered little regarding the cause and origin of this foreign rite, except that the symbol itself, shaped like a Liburnian galley <note>a small, fast type of warship; original: Liburnæ</note>, shows that the religion was imported" <note>original Latin: Pars Suevorum et Isidi sacrificat: unde causa et origino peregrino sacro, parum comperi; nisi quod signum ipsum in modum Liburnæ figuratum docet advectam religionem</note> <sup>88</sup>. The ship of Isis was also reverenced...

### OF
# WORSHIP AT CAVERNS,
### AND OF
## THE ADORATION OF FIRE IN THE EARLY AGES.

---

As soon as religion began to lose its purity, it deteriorated very rapidly. In place of a reverential awe and a pleasing sense of duty, there followed a fearful gloom and an unnatural horror, which were continually intensified as superstition increased. In the earliest ages, people traveled <note>original: "repaired"</note> either to the lonely summits of mountains or to caverns in the rocks and hollows within the depths <note>original: "bosom"</note> of the earth, which they believed were the residences of their gods. At the entrances of these, they raised their altars and performed their vows. Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose works often discussed the history of religious rituals and symbolism.</note> notes how much this mode of worship prevailed...

<summary>This page describes how early religious practices shifted from pure devotion toward superstitious rituals held in dark, remote locations like mountain peaks and caverns, which were believed to be the homes of gods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient sites of worship, specifically focusing on how geological features like caves and mountains were interpreted as temples or deities in antiquity.</meta>

-> THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. <-

It has been observed that the Greek term *koilos* <note>original: κοιλος</note>, meaning "hollow," was often substituted for *Coëlus*, the word for heaven. I believe it will be shown that it was used in this way in the following history, which describes the worship of the Atlantians <note>The ancient inhabitants of the Atlas Mountains region in North Africa.</note>. 

Mythologists claimed that Atlas supported the heavens; one reason for this idea was that a temple dedicated to *Coëlus* (Heaven) stood upon Mount Atlas. This is mentioned by Maximus Tyrius in one of his dissertations, where—as in many other instances—the name is changed to *koilos* <note>original: κοιλος</note>, or "hollow." The temple was undoubtedly a cavern, but the name should be understood in its original sense as *Co-el*, the "house of God," to which the natives paid their devotion. 

This style of worship among the Atlantians reveals great antiquity, as the temple seems to have been merely a vast hollow in the side of the mountain. It contained no image, pillar, stone, nor any other physical object of worship: 

<note>original Greek: Εστι δε Ατλας ορος κοιλον, επιεικως ὑψηλον. — Τετο Λιβυων και ἱερον, και θεος, και ὁρκος, και αγαλμα.</note>
"This Atlas (of which I have been speaking) is a mountain with a cavity and of a reasonable <note>original: tolerable</note> height, which the Libyans regard as both a temple and a deity; it is the great object by which they swear and to which they pay their devotions." 

The cave in the mountain was certainly named *Co-el*, the house of God, which is equivalent to the *Coëlus* of the Romans. The people made their offerings to this site, and this was the "heaven" that Atlas was thought to support. This seems to have been a common term among the North Africans. There was a city in Libya <note>original: Lybia</note> named Coël, which the Romans called Coëlu.

Syria; and one large province was consequently named *Curesta* and *Curestica*, from *Kur Heros*, or "Hestian Sun" <note>original Latin: *Sol Hestius*. Hestia was the Greek goddess of the hearth and sacred fire.</note>.

In *Cappadocia* <note>A historical region in central Turkey.</note> there were many *Puratheia* <term>Puratheia</term> <note>Fire temples or open-air altars where a perpetual fire was kept burning.</note>; and the people followed the same manner of worship as was practiced in *Persis* <note>Persia.</note>. The rites that prevailed may be inferred from the names of places, as well as from the history of the country. One city seems to have been named after its guardian <note>original: "tutelary"</note> deity and called *Castabala*. This is a plain compound of *Ca-Asta-Bala*, the place or temple of *Asta Bala*; the same deity as the Syrians called *Baaltis*. *Asta Bala* was the goddess of fire, and the same customs prevailed here as at *Feronia* in *Latium* <note>A region in central Italy.</note>. The female attendants in the temple used to walk with their feet bare over burning $^{48}$ coals.

Such is the nature of the temple named *Istachar* <note>Likely referring to Istakhr, near Persepolis.</note>, and of the caverns in the mountains of *Chusistan* <note>Khuzestan, a province in southwestern Iran.</note>. Such was the painful exercise which Mir Mahmud <note>original: Maghmud. Mir Mahmud Hotaki (1697–1725) was an Afghan ruler who conquered Persia.</note> undertook in January of this year; for this purpose, he chose an underground vault. In the beginning of the next month, when he emerged, he was so pale, disfigured, and emaciated that they hardly recognized him. But this was not the worst effect of his devotion. Solitude, which is often dangerous to someone with a melancholy temperament, had—under the circumstances of his restlessness and the strangeness of his penance—damaged his sanity. He became restless and suspicious, often jumping at small things. In one of these fits of madness, he determined to put to death the entire family of his predecessor, Shah Husayn <note>original: Sha Hussein</note>. Among them were several brothers, three uncles, and seven nephews, besides that prince's children. All these, numbering above a hundred, the tyrant cut to pieces with his own hand in the palace yard, where they had been assembled for that bloody purpose. Only two small children escaped through the intervention of their father, who was wounded while trying to shield them.

The respect paid to caves and grottos arose from a notion that they were a representation of the <note>53</note> world, and that the chief deity whom the Persians worshiped emerged from a cave. Such was the tradition they had received, and it contained matter of great importance. The term *Omphi* <term>Omphi</term> <note>The author uses this term to refer to a divine or oracular voice, often associated with the Greek "omphi" (divine voice) or "omphalos" (navel/center).</note> is of great antiquity and denotes an oracular influence by which people obtained an insight into the secrets of the future. I have noted with what reverence men in the earliest ages went to <note>original: repaired to</note> rocks and caverns, viewing them as places of particular sanctity. Here they thought that the Deity would most likely reveal himself either by a voice, a dream, or some other supernatural <note>original: præternatural</note> sign. Many for the same purpose worshipped on hills and on the tops of high mountains, imagining that they thereby obtained a closer communication with heaven. In Japan, most of their temples today are constructed upon high ground, and often upon the slopes of high mountains. They are all, says Kaempfer <note>Engelbert Kaempfer (1651–1716), a German naturalist and traveler known for his descriptions of Japan.</note>, most beautifully situated: an interesting view of the adjacent country, a spring and stream of clear water, and the neighborhood of a grove with pleasant walks are the necessary requirements for the spots of ground where these holy structures are to be built. They say that the Gods are extremely delighted with such high and pleasant places. <margin>¹⁰</margin>

This practice in early times was almost universal, and every mountain was considered holy. <margin>¹¹</margin> The people who practiced this method of worship enjoyed a soothing influence <note>original: "infatuation"</note> which appealed to their superstitious nature. The high places to which they retreated were lonely and silent, and seemed to be perfectly suited for contemplation and prayer. Those who frequented them were raised above the lower world and imagined that they were brought into the vicinity of the powers of the air, and of the Deity who resided in the higher regions. But the chief reason for which they were frequented was the *Omphi*, expressed as *omphē* <note>original: ομφη</note> by the Greeks, and interpreted as a "divine voice" <note>original: Θεια κληδων, vox divina</note>, being regarded as a particular revelation from heaven. <margin>¹²</margin> In short, they were looked upon as the specific places where God deliv—

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

...upon to be prophetic; and were supposed to be the residence of the chief Deity, under whatever name he was identified, which was generally the God of Light. For these oracles, no place was more famous than the hill at Delphi, called *Omphi-El*, or the "Oracle of the Sun" <note>Bryant derives this from *Omphi* (oracle) and *El* (a common Semitic name for God or the Sun).</note>. 

But the Greeks, who changed *Al-omphi* to *Olympus*, distorted these terms in an even stranger way. Finding them somewhat similar in sound to a word in their own language, their whims immediately led them to think of *omphalos* <note>original: ὀμφαλός</note>, meaning a "navel," which they substituted for the original word. They did this consistently in all parts of the world, and they always invented some story to justify their mistake. Therefore, whenever we encounter a frivolous story about a "navel," we can be fairly certain it is an allusion to an oracle. 

Regarding Delphi, they assumed it was the *umbilicus* <note>Latin for "navel," used here to mean the center.</note>, or the center of the entire earth. The poets accepted this notion without any hesitation. Sophocles calls it the $^{16}$ "prophetic center of the Earth" <note>original: μεσόμφαλα Γῆς μαντεῖα (mesomphala Gēs manteia)</note>, and Euripides asserts that it was the exact center of the earth:

Libya was called Olympia. — *Stephanus of Byzantium*.

The Earth itself was called *Olympia* by Plutarch, who mentions the "Temple of the Prophetic Earth" <note>original: της Γης Ολυμπιας ἱερον</note> in his biography of *Theseus*.

->$^{21}$ For there was neither a middle navel of the earth, nor of the sea.<-
<note>original Greek: Οὔτε γὰρ ἦν γαίης μέσος ὀμφαλός, οὐδὲ θαλάσσης (Oute gar ēn gaiēs mesos omphalos, oude thalassēs). Plutarch, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*.</note>

But even if we assume that this name and character had some connection to Delphi, how are we to explain other places being called by the same name? They could not all be umbilical <term>umbilical: relating to the navel, or occupying a central point</term>; the earth cannot be thought to have many different centers. Nor could the places named this way always be situated so as to be central to the nation or the province where they were located. Writers try to explain it this way, yet they do not seem satisfied with the reasoning. The contradictory accounts show the absurdity of the idea. It was a term borrowed from Egypt, which was itself an "Omphalian" region <note>The author argues "Omphalos" derives from "Omphi," an Egyptian term for an oracle, rather than the Greek word for "navel."</note>. What the Greeks called *Omphalus* was certainly *Ompha-El*, the same as *Al-Ompha*, and related to the oracle of Ham or the Sun. ...ancient city $^{29}$ **Alphira**; a grove of **Artemis** $^{30}$ **Alpheionia**, and the entire region was watered by the sacred river **Alpheus**. All these names are derived from *El*, the prophetic Deity, the Sun; and more directly from his oracle, *Alphi*. The Greeks traditionally claimed that every place was named after some historical person. Accordingly, Plutarch describes Alpheus as $^{31}$ "one of those who traced their descent from the Sun." <note>original Greek: Εις των το γενος αφ’ ἡλιου καταγοντων (Heis tōn to genos aph’ hēliou katagontōn)</note>. The term *Alphi*, from which the Greeks formed the names *Alphira*, *Alpheionia*, and *Alpheus*, has essentially the same meaning as *Amphi*. Since Ham was esteemed by his descendants as the Sun, or *El*—and also as *Or*, the same as the Egyptian god Horus—his oracles were consequently styled not only *Amphi* and *Omphi*, but also *Alphi*, *Elphi*, *Orphi*, and *Urphi*.

I have previously noted several cities called **Omphalian**, and I have observed that they generally contained oracular temples. However, the Greeks almost universally assumed these places were named after a "navel" <term>original: omphalos; the Greeks believed certain sites were the physical center or 'navel' of the world</term>. There was a place called $^{32}$ **Omphalian** in **Thessaly**, and another in **Crete**, which had...

We encounter other places in history styled **Omphalian**. The temple of **Jupiter Ammon** <note>The famous oracle in the Libyan desert where the Egyptian god Amun was equated with the Greek Zeus/Jupiter</note> was esteemed to be of the highest antiquity, and we are informed that there was an *omphalus* <term>Greek: "navel"; here referring to a sacred stone or ritual center</term> there; and that the Deity was worshipped under the form of a navel. **Quintus Curtius**, who copied his history from the Greeks, gives us the following strange account in his life of **Alexander**, which he has embellished with some coloring of his own:

> ³⁶ "That which is worshipped as a god did not have the same appearance that artists commonly assign to the gods. Its form is most like a navel, joined together with emeralds and gems. The whole of this is a misuse of terms, which the author did not understand and has totally misapplied. One would imagine that so improbable a story—that of an umbilical Deity with his silver basins, even if patched up with gold and emeralds—would have refuted itself. Yet **Schottus**, in his notes upon Curtius, has been captivated by this motley description; and, in opposition to all reliable history, thinks that this idle story of a navel relates to the compass. **Hyde** too has adopted this notion, and proceeds to show how each circumstance may be made to agree with the properties of the magnet:

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 247

...as a certain **inspired object** <note>original Latin/Greek: *quam ενθεον (entheon) quoddam*</note> that was worshipped because of its divine help: namely, because there was a magnetic needle within it, like a god dwelling inside, directing the course of ships in the middle of the sea. <note>This refers to the theory that the "navel" mentioned by Quintus Curtius was actually an early magnetic compass used in sacred processions.</note> These learned men were endowed with a ready faith; they not only accept what they have been told, but contribute largely to establishing the mistake. The true history is this: Most places in which there was a supposed oracle of a deity, the Greeks (as I have previously mentioned) called *Olympus*, *Olympia*, and *Olympiaca*; or else *Omphale*, *Omphalia*, and the province *Omphalian territory* <note>original Greek: *χωριον Ομφαλιον (chorion Omphalion)*</note>. These terms were thought to relate to a **navel** <note>Greek: *omphalos*</note>. However, even if such an interpretation could have been made to match the history of any one single place, that history could not have been repeated in so many locations; nor could places so widely distant have all had the same reference. The term that was ended as **omphalos** was originally **Omph-El** <note>Bryant argues this is a compound of "Omph" (voice/oracle) and "El" (God)</note>, the oracle of God, the seat of divine influence. Likewise, **Al-Omphi** was a name given to mountains and high places for the same reason. An oracle was given to Pelias in Thessaly; and from where did it proceed? From the well-wooded *omphalus* <term>navel/oracle</term> of his mother Earth.

> There came to him a chilling oracle in his wise heart. <note>original Greek: Ηλθε δε οἱ κρυοεν Πυκινῷ μαντευμα θυμῷ; from Pindar, Pythian Ode 4.</note>

In other words, it proceeded from the stately grove of Hestia <note>The goddess of the hearth, often associated by Bryant with the earth or sacred fire</note>, where an oracular temple stood.

Regarding the *omphalus* <term>navel or oracle</term> of Ammon, which the Roman historian Quintus Curtius translated as *umbilicus* <note>Latin for "navel"</note> and described as decorated with gold and jewels, the whole idea arises from a mistake in terminology, as in many previous instances. It was actually *Omphi El*, the oracle of Ham (or the Sun). The shrine from which the oracle was supposed to come was carried in a boat. The *Paterae*, which have been traditionally described as silver basins, were in reality the interpreters of the oracle. They were the priests who walked on each side during the sacred processions, supporting both the image and the boat in which it was carried. They are said to have been eighty in number, and they claimed to carry the deity around, going wherever they were directed by divine impulse. <margin><sup>40</sup> Diodorus Siculus <note>A 1st-century BC Greek historian</note>.</margin> Diodorus says, "*The God is carried around in a ship of gold by eighty of his priests. They bear him upon their shoulders and follow their path by instinct, just as the divine automaton happens to direct them.*" These people who officiated were probably the same as the *Petipharae* of the ancient Egyptians, but were called *Paterae* by the Greeks. This was a name and an office by which the priests of Delphi, and many other places besides those in Egypt, were distinguished; and the...

In his drawings <note>original: "specimens"</note>, the largest number of attendants shown is twenty: eighteen support the boat, one leads with a type of scepter, and another follows at the rear holding a rod or staff, which undoubtedly had a symbolic <note>original: "mystic"</note> meaning. The entire scene seems to have been symbolic; as will be shown later, it related to a great act of preservation that was religiously recorded and became the primary theme of all their sacred mysteries. The person within the shrine was their chief ancestor <note>In the author's "Arkite" theory, this refers to Noah</note>, and the entire ceremony was a memorial of the Great Flood <note>original: "deluge"</note>. The history of this event must have been quite recent when these works were created in Egypt.

From these shrines of Amon mentioned above, we can trace the history of all oracles. These oracles were named after the deity supposed to speak through them, called *Omphi* and *Amphi* (as I have shown), as well as *Alphi*, *Elphi*, *Orphi*, and *Urphi*, derived from *El* <note>A Semitic word for God</note> and *Orus* <note>Horus, the Egyptian god</note>. The Greeks strictly followed ancient terms, even when they were obsolete or difficult to understand. They kept the name *Amphi* despite not knowing its meaning, as the term had become archaic before the Greeks even had a written alphabet. It is clear that the term originally related to oracular revelation because it is always attached to the names of places famous for such prophecies. It also appears in the names of men renowned as priests and prophets <note>original: "augurs"</note> who were believed to possess the gift of foresight. The city of Amphicleia in Phocis had Dionysus for its guardian deity, whose orgies were celebrated there and whose shrine was oracular.

I believe that this sacred influence, known by the name "Amphi," is often mentioned in the introductions <term>original: exordia; the opening parts of a speech or composition</term> of poets—especially by the writers of dithyrambic poetry <term>Dithyrambic: a passionate, wild, and choral hymn often dedicated to Dionysus or Apollo</term> when they address Apollo. When taken in its usual sense of "around" or "concerning" <note>original Greek: αμφι (amphi); original Latin: circum</note>, the word has no meaning in this context. # THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

We can see from what has been said that the word *Amphi* was an ancient term; its true meaning was no longer understood, yet the sound was kept by the Greeks and used as a common exclamation. Regarding the more ancient introductions <note>original: "exordia"</note> quoted above, especially that of *Terpander*, I believe the words are an imitation rather than a translation of a hymn sung at Delphi in the ancient *Amonian* <note>Amonian: Bryant’s term for the language or culture of the descendants of Ham, often associated with solar worship</note> language. The sound was copied rather than the meaning, and then adapted to modern terms with different definitions. I have no doubt that many ancient hymns were preserved in those oracular temples; these were kept and sung for a long time even when their meaning was very poorly understood. They were mostly composed in praise of *Ham*, or the *Sun*, and were sung by the *Homeridae* and *Iamidae* <note>Homeridae and Iamidae: lineages or guilds of poets and prophetic singers</note>. They were named after his titles—*Ad*, *Athyr*, and *Amphi*—which the Greeks expressed as *Dithyrambi*. These were songs of joy and celebration accompanied by grand processions. From the same term *dithyrambus* came the Greek *thriambos* <note>original: θριαμβος</note> and the Roman *triumphus* (triumph). We are told that triumphs were first established by ⁶⁷ *Bacchus*, who was actually *Chus* <note>Chus: In Bryant's system, the biblical Cush, son of Ham, whom he identifies with the god Bacchus</note>; therefore, the history of the term must be sought among the *Cuseans* (Cushites). It is clear that the word was composed of titles, as *Varro* states it was a ⁶⁸ name, and one that...

When people spoke specifically of *the oracle*, it was expressed as *P'omphi* and *P'ompi*—the source of the Greek word *pompe* <note>original Greek: πομπη</note>. From this, the god Hermes <term>Hermes</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Hermes is the messenger of the gods, but Bryant argues his titles have much older, oracular origins</note> received the name *pompaios* <note>original Greek: πομπαιος</note>, which was misinterpreted as "the messenger" and "conductor." Consequently, the deity was made into a servant of the gods and an attendant for the dead. 

However, *pompaios* properly related to divine influence, and *pompe* was an oracle. An ox or a cow was considered very sacred and oracular by the Amonians <term>Amonians</term> <note>Bryant's term for the descendants of Ham (Amon), whom he believes established the first great civilizations and religious systems</note>. Accordingly, Cadmus was said to have been directed by the *pompe boos* <note>original Greek: πομπη βοος; meaning "the guidance or oracle of the cow"</note>.

The Romans supposed these places were named after Pompey the Great <note>Pompeius Magnus</note>, but they were too numerous and too remote to have been named after him or any other Roman. This pillar was not the work of Pompey the Great <note>original: Pompeius Magnus</note>; nor could it relate to his history at all, for the time of its rebuilding was not long before the age in which he lived. The original work must therefore have been much earlier. The pillar in Egypt is undoubtedly the same one built upon the ruins of a former structure by Sostratus of Cnidus, before the time of Pompey. <note>original Greek: ΣΩΣΤΡΑΤΟΣ ΚΝΙΔΙΟΣ ΔΕΞΙΦΑΝΟΥΣ ΘΕΟΙΣ ΣΩΤΗΡΣΙΝ ΥΠΕΡ ΤΩΝ ΠΛΩΙΖΟΜΕΝΩΝ</note>

The narrow strait into the Euxine Sea <note>The Black Sea</note> was a passage of difficult navigation. This was the reason why, on each side, temples and sacred columns were erected to the deity of the country in order to obtain his assistance. There is reason to believe that these pillars and obelisks were used as beacons <term>beacon</term> <note>A fire or light set up in a high or prominent position as a warning or signal to sailors</note>, and that every temple was a Pharos <term>Pharos</term> <note>A lighthouse; named after the famous Great Lighthouse of Alexandria located on the island of Pharos</note>. They seem to have been erected at the entrance of harbors and upon high ground along the coasts in most countries. The Pillars of Hercules <note>The promontories that flank the entrance to the Strait of Gibraltar</note> were of this sort and were undoubtedly for the same purpose. They were not built by him but were erected in his honor by people who worshiped him and who were called Herculeans. ⁸¹ For it was an ancient custom to place such... <note>original Greek: Εθος γαρ παλαιον ὑπηρξε το τιθεσθαι τοιουτους</note>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

"...mountain, just as the people of Rhegium placed the pillar that stands by the strait, like a tower. And the tower called Pelorus stands opposite this pillar." <note>original Greek: ὄρος, καθαπερ οἱ Ῥηγινοι την στηλιδα εθεσαν, την επι τῳ πορθμῳ κειμενην, πυργον τι. Και ὁ Πελωρος λεγομενος πυργος αντικειται τῃ ταυτῃ στηλιδι</note>

"For it was a custom," says Strabo, "among the ancients to erect these kinds of landmarks, such as the pillar at Rhegium near the foot of Italy. This is a kind of tower and was raised by the people of Rhegium at the strait <note>original: freight; likely referring to the Latin *fretum*, meaning strait</note> where the passage leads to Sicily." Directly opposite stood another building of the same sort, called the tower of Pelorus. Such pillars were called "Herculean" by the Iberians because they were sacred to Hercules, under which title they worshiped their chief deity. 

Some of these were near Gades and Onoba <gloss>82</gloss>, "near Onoba in Iberia" <note>original Greek: Κατ' Ονοβαν της Ιβηριας</note>; others were erected even further north, on the coast of Lusitania <note>Modern-day Portugal</note>. This caused a pointless dispute between Eratosthenes, Dicæarchus, and <gloss>83</gloss> others, who tried to determine which were the genuine Pillars of Hercules—as if they were not all equally genuine, all named after the deity of that country. 

Two of the most celebrated stood on each side of the Mediterranean at the famous passage called the Strait of Gades <note>original Latin: fretum Gaditanum</note>, "at the extremities of the strait" <note>original Greek: κατα τα ακρα του πορθμου</note>. The one on the Mauritanian <note>North African</note> side was called Abyla, from *Ab-El*, "Father Sun" <note>original Latin: parens Sol</note>. The other in Iberia <note>Spain</note> had the name of <gloss>84</gloss> Calpe. This was an obelisk or tower, and its name is a compound of *Ca-Alpe*, signifying the house or cavern of the same oracular god; for it was built near a cave;

"Nobody," says <gloss>85</gloss> Arrian, "will venture to quit his harbor without paying due offerings to the Gods and invoking their favor." O, ever crowned with altars, ever blessed,
Lovely Asteria <note>Asteria is an ancient name for the island of Delos</note>, in how high repute
Stands your fair temple among the various tribes
Who sail the Aegean. Though their business claims
Immediate dispatch; though the inviting gales
Hardly tolerate the lingering mariners’ delay:
Soon as they reach your soundings, down at once
Drop the slack sails, and all the naval gear.
The ship is moored: nor do the crew presume
To quit your sacred limits, until they have passed
A painful penance: with the stinging whip
Lashed three times around your altar.

This island was greatly esteemed for its sanctity, and there used to be a wonderful gathering <note>original: "concourse"</note> of people from all nations continually visiting its temple. Consequently, the priests had hymns composed in almost all languages. It is moreover said of the female attendants that they could imitate the speech of various people and were well-versed in the histories of foreign parts and of ancient times. Homer speaks of these extraordinary qualifications as if he had been an eyewitness:

<margin>88</margin> And besides this, there is a great wonder, whose fame shall never perish:

Who, when they have first sung in praise of Apollo,
And then of Leto and Artemis, the pourer of arrows,

They know how to imitate the voices and rhythmic speech
Of all people; you would say each person was

The Delian nymphs, who tend Apollo's shrine,
When they begin their tuneful hymns, first praise
The mighty God of day <note>Apollo</note>: to his they join
Latona's <note>Leto</note> name, and Artemis, far-famed
For her fleet arrows, and unerring bow.
Of heroes next, and heroines they sing,
And deeds of ancient prowess. Crowds around,
Of every region, every language, stand
In mute applause, soothed with the pleasing lay.
Versed in each art, and every power of speech,
The Delians mimic all who come: to them
All language is familiar: you would think
The natives spoke from every different clime.
Such are their winning ways: so sweet their song.

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

> "The tribes of the Iapygians <note>Ancient inhabitants of the 'heel' of Italy</note> are stretched out as far as the coastal Hyria—Hyria, where the Adriatic salt water is swept along."
> <note>original Greek: Φυλα τ᾿ Ιηπυγιων τετανυσμενα, μεσφ᾿ Ὑριοιο Παῤῥαλιης, Ὑριης, τοθι συρεται Ἀδριας ἁλμη.</note> ^91

The more difficult the navigation was, the more places of sanctity were erected upon the coast. The *Bosporus* was esteemed a dangerous pass; and for that reason, it abounded with *cippi* <term>monumental pillars or landmarks</term> and altars. These were originally mounds of earth and sacred to the Sun; for that reason, they were called *Col-On*, or altars of that deity <note>Bryant suggests this is derived from 'Col' (hill) and 'On' (an ancient name for the Sun)</note>. From this is derived the term *Colona* and *Kolōnē* <note>original Greek: Κολωνη</note>. It came at last to denote any headland <note>original: "nees"</note> or foreland; but it was originally the name of a sacred hill and of the pillar which was placed upon it. To say the truth, in ancient times there was hardly any headland that did not have its temple or altar. The *Bosporus* in particular had many of them serving as sea-marks <note>Early navigational aids or landmarks for sailors</note> as well as for sacred purposes; and there were many upon the coast of **Greece**. Hence **Apollonius** says of the Argonauts:

> "And as they journeyed, the peak <note>original Greek: κολωνη (kolōnē), meaning hill or mound</note> of Athos rose up before them." ^92
> <note>original Greek: Ηει δε νισσομενοισιν Αθω ανετελλε κολωνη.</note>

> <note>original Greek: Φαινεται ηεροεν στομα Βοσπορου, ηδε κολωναι Μυσιας.</note>

A similar instance occurs in the *Orphic Argonautica*, where Peleus points out the home of the Centaur Chiron:

> "O friends, behold the mound that projects from the lookout point, shaded on the central headland, where Chiron—the most righteous of Centaurs—dwells in a cave." ^94

These *Colonae* <term>sacred hills or mounds</term> were sacred to the Apollo of Greece. Because they served as sea-marks and beacons standing on high ground near the mouths of rivers and the entrances of harbors, they were called *oria* <term>boundaries or landmarks</term>, *ourea* <term>mountains</term>, and *hormoi* <term>anchorages or havens</term>. Homer provides a beautiful description of such hills and headlands, and of the coastline stretching out in a stunning landscape below. In a passage of enchanting poetry, he describes how all these places rejoiced at the birth of Apollo:

> "All the watchtowers were pleasing to you, and the high peaks of the lofty mountains; the rivers flowing forth to the sea, the shores sloping to the deep, and the harbors of the ocean." ^95
> <note>original Greek: Πασαι δε σκοπιαι τοι α´δον, και πρωνες ακροι Ὑψηλων ορεων, ποταμοι θ' άλα δε προρεοντες, Ακται τ' εις άλα κεκλιμεναι, λιμενες τε θαλασσης.</note>

->In that happy hour<-

> The lofty cliffs, that overlook the main,
> And the high summits of the towering hills,
> Shouted in triumph: down the rivers ran
> In pleasing murmurs to the distant deep.
> The shelves, the shores, the inlets of the sea,
> Witnessed uncommon gladness.

Because of this connection, Apollo was often called *epaktios* <term>original Greek: επακτιος; meaning "on the shore"</term>, or the protective God of the coast, and he received specific offerings for that reason.

It was not only upon rocks and high ground that these *Cippi* <term>small pillars or boundary posts</term> and Obelisks were placed by the ancients. They were also to be found in their temples, where for many ages a rough post or stone served as a representation of the Deity. They were sometimes quite shapeless, but generally of a conical figure, of which we find many examples. Clement of Alexandria ^97 takes notice of this kind of worship; and Pausanias, in describing the temple of Hercules at Hyettus in Boeotia ^98, tells us that there was no statue in it, nor any work of art, but merely an unworked stone in the manner of the ancient ages. Tertullian gives a similar description of Ceres and Pallas: "The Pallas of Athens and the Phrygian Ceres—who stand without an image, as a rough stake and a formless shape." ^99 Juno of Samos was little better than a wooden post ^100. Trees bear a faint likeness to the human form <term>original: "fabric"</term>; roots and branches are also often so strange in their shapes that they suggest a remote resemblance. The ancients seem to have taken advantage of this imagined similarity, which they enhanced with a bit of art; their first attempts at creating statues were made from these rough and decaying materials. In his account of the Argonauts <note>The mythical heroes who sailed with Jason to find the Golden Fleece.</note>, Apollonius Rhodius describes a monument of this type, which they erected in a dark grove on a mountainous part of Bithynia <note>An ancient region in what is now north-western Turkey.</note>. They built an altar of rough stones and placed near it an image of Rhea <note>An ancient mother goddess in Greek mythology.</note>, which they carved from the limb or stump of an ancient vine.

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

Instead of an image made of a stump, the poet Dionysius <note>Dionysius Periegetes, a Greek geographer and poet.</note> suggests that a temple was built beneath the trunk of a decayed tree.

> There the Amazons once built a temple to the Goddess
> Beneath the trunk of an elm, a great wonder to men. 
> — verse 827.
<note>original Greek: Ενθα Θεη ποτε νηον Αμαζονιδες τετυχοντο / Πρεμνῳ ὑπο πτελεης, περιωσιον ανδρασι θαυμα.</note>

It is notable that the Chinese, as well as the people of Japan, still retain something of this custom. When they encounter an unusually shaped <term>original: "uncouth"</term> root or branch of a tree, they indulge the strange form <term>original: "humour the extravagance"</term>; and by adding a face, they give it the appearance of a Joss <note>A Chinese religious statue or idol.</note> or Bonze <note>A term used by early European travelers for a Buddhist monk or religious figure.</note>, just as their imagination directs them.

The vine was considered sacred to both Dionysus and Bacchus; for they were two different figures, though the Greeks confused them. Indeed, the titles of all those who were originally called Baalim <note>The plural of Baal, a general term for "Lord" or deity in ancient Semitic languages.</note> are blended together. This tree therefore had the name of *Ampel*—which the Greeks rendered as *Ampelos*—derived from the Sun-god, Ham, whose specific plant it was. This title is the same as *Omphel* mentioned previously, and relates to the oracular deity of the pagan world; it was under this character that Ham was mainly represented. The Greeks in Egypt and Asia Minor had some imperfect traditions about Ham and Chus <note>Cush, the son of Ham in biblical tradition.</note>; they regarded the latter as Bacchus. 

Because the term *Ampelus* did not originally refer to the vine, but was a sacred name transferred from the deity, they had some vague idea of this fact. However, since it was their custom to create a new mythological character out of every title, they imagined Ampelus to be a youth of great beauty whom Bacchus especially favored. Thus Nonnus <note>A Greek epic poet of the 5th century AD, author of the *Dionysiaca*.</note> depicts Ampelus begging Selene <note>The goddess of the moon.</note> not to envy him this happiness.

<summary>Bryant argues that the names of sacred plants like the vine (Ampelus) were originally titles for the deity Ham, which the Greeks later misunderstood as distinct mythological characters.</summary>

The place called *Ampelus* at *Mycale* in *Ionia* was admittedly named so because it was a sacred ^13 place, rich with springs of water. It was believed that those who drank from these waters became inspired. These waters are mentioned in an ancient oracle quoted by Eusebius ^14: "In the hollows of *Didyma* <note>a famous sanctuary and oracle site in Ionia</note>, the *inspired* water of *Mycale*." <note>original Greek: Εν Διδυμων γυαλοις Μυκαλησιον ΕΝΘΕΟΝ υδωρ</note> I have previously mentioned that all fountains were considered sacred, but especially those that possessed any supernatural quality or emitted vapors <note>original: "exhalations"</note>. It was a universal belief that a divine energy proceeded from these vapors <note>original: "effluvia"</note>, and that the people who lived near them were gifted with prophetic abilities. Young women were styled Nymphs by later Greeks and Romans, but improperly. The word *Nympha* (the Greek *Nymphe*) was not originally specific to a virgin or girl; instead, it denoted a part of the body. Just as the Egyptians named every animal, stone, bush, and herb with a divine title, it was their custom to denote every limb and part of the human body with such a title. Hence they called the heart *Ath*, the womb *Mathyr* or *Mether*; and the "female fountain" <note>the source of life</note>, like other fountains, they designated by the name *Ain Omphe* <note>meaning "Fountain of the Oracle"</note>, which the Greeks called *nymphe*. This was derived by the Greeks from the Egyptians. Thus we read: "*Nymphe*: a fountain, and a newly married woman; they call her a nymph," etc. <note>original Greek: Νυμφη πηγη, και νεογαμος γυνη, νυμφην δε καλουσι κτλ</note> Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>.

...fountain of *Ades* <note>original: "Ades", referring to the Sun in the author's system</note>, or the Sun. In a similar way, this name was changed to *Naiades* <note>original Greek: Ναϊαδες; Naiads, a type of water nymph</note>, a species of deities of the same class. Fountains of bitumen in Susiana and Babylonia were called *Ain-Aptha*, the fountains of *Aptha*, the God of fire. The Greeks converted this name into *Naptha* <note>Naphtha</note>, a name given to ^19 bitumen. Just as they changed *Ain Omphe* to *Nympha*, a Goddess; they accordingly named the place itself *Nymphæum* <note>original Greek: Νυμφαιον</note>. Wherever a place of that name occurs, you will find something unusual in its circumstances. We are told by ^20 Pliny that the river Tigris, being stopped in its course by the mountains of Taurus, disappears underground and rises again on the other side at *Nymphæum*. According to Marcellinus, it seems that it is at *Nymphæum* where the river sinks into the earth. Regardless of which is the case, he tells us that this is the place where that fiery matter called naphtha was produced—which is undoubtedly where the place got its name. ^21 "Bitumen is produced near Lake Sosingites, in whose channel the Tigris is swallowed up..." <note>original Latin: Bitumen nascitur prope lacum Sosingitem, cujus alveo Tigris voratus</note>

The same word is shortened by Gregory of Nyssa and called *Pthes* <note>original Greek: Φθης</note> in the Ionic style: "just as that which is called *Pthes* is set on fire" <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ ὁ καλύμενος Φθης εξάπτεται</note>. *On the Soul* <note>original Latin: Liber de animâ</note>. However, they are guilty of no mistake; they simply use the word without its prefix. *Ain-Aptha*, shortened to *Naphtha*, was properly the fountain itself. The matter that came out of it was called *Apthas*, *Pthas*, and *Ptha*. This was one of the titles of the God of fire, called *Apha-Astus*, which became the *Hephaestus* of the Greeks; this inflammable substance was sacred to him.

...the religious system, which was so widely spread, was due to one great family who expanded almost everywhere. Their colonies went abroad with the authorization and guidance of their priests, carrying with them both the rituals and the records of their homeland. Celsus <note>a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and critic of early Christianity</note> noticed this and thought that people paid too little attention to historical records of this nature. He specifically mentions the oracular temples at Dodona, Delphi, and Claros, along with those of the Branchidae <note>an ancient line of priests who served the oracle of Apollo at Didyma</note> and the Amonians <note>priests and followers of the oracle of Ammon in Libya</note>. At the same time, he overlooks many other places whose priests and followers seem to have populated the entire earth³¹: "The prophecies delivered by the Pythian oracle, or at Dodona, or Claros, or among the Branchidae, or in the temple of Ammon, and by countless other prophets—by which the whole earth was effectively settled—these things they hold in no account" <note>original Greek: Τα μεν ὑπο της Πυθιας, η Δωδωνιων, η Κλαρις, η εν Βραγχιδαις, η εν Αμμωνος, ὑπο μυριων τε αλλων θεοπροπων προειρημενα, ὑφ' ὡν επιεικως πασα γη κατωκισθη, ταυτα μεν ουδενι λογῳ τιθενται</note>.

As colonies went abroad under the influence and direction of their guardian deities, those deities were called *Hegemones* <note>original: Ἡγεμονες; meaning "leaders" or "guides"</note> and *Archegetai* <note>original: Αρχηγεται; meaning "founding leaders"</note>. Furthermore, the colony was named after some sacred title of the god. For example, a colony was established at Miletus, where the guiding deity was Diana³²: "For Neleus made you his Guide" <note>original Greek: Σε γαρ ποιησατο Νηλευς Ἡγεμονην</note>. This goddess is called *Polypolis* <note>original: πολυπολις; meaning "of many cities"</note> because this role was specifically attributed to her, and she had many places under her protection. Accordingly, Jupiter tells her:
