## PATOR AND PATRA.

I cannot help thinking that the word *pater* <note>original Greek: πατηρ</note>, or *pater* <note>Latin for father</note>, when used in the religious addresses of the Greeks and Romans, did not mean a father or parent, as is generally supposed. Instead, it related to the divine influence of the Deity, called *Pator* by the people of the East, as I have already shown <gloss>1</gloss>. From this, I would infer that two words, originally very distinct, have been rendered as one and the same <gloss>2</gloss>. The word *pater*, in its common meaning, might be applicable to Saturn; for he was supposed to have been the father of all the gods, and was therefore titled so by the ancient poet Sulpitius.

> ->Father Janus, watchful Janus, two-headed god, two-formed,<-
> ->O, wise creator of all things, O, beginning of the gods.<-
> <gloss>3</gloss> <note>original Latin: Jane pater, Jane tuens, Dive biceps, biformis, O, cate rerum sator, O, principium Deorum.</note>

But when it became a title that was bestowed upon gods of every denomination, it caused Jupiter to observe with some...

...some warmth upon the impropriety, if we may believe the poet Lucilius:

> <note>original Latin: Ut nemo sit nostrum, quin pater optimus Divôm est: Ut Neptunus pater, Liber, Saturnus pater, Mars, Janus, Quirinus, pater, omnes dicamur ad unum.</note>
> "So that there is not one of us who is not called 'Best Father of the Gods'; just as Neptune is called 'Father,' and Liber, Saturn, Mars, Janus, and Quirinus are all called 'Father'—we are all referred to by that name, every single one of us."

And it was not only the gods who were called this, but also the Hierophants <note>original: Hierophantæ; priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> in most temples. Those priests in particular who were busy with the celebration of mysteries were styled *Fathers* <note>original: Patres</note>. Therefore, it was undoubtedly a religious term imported from Egypt, the same as the words *Pator* and *Patora* mentioned before. I have noted that the *Paterae* mentioned by the historian Curtius <note>Quintus Curtius Rufus</note> were the priests of Hammon <note>original: Hamon; the Egyptian god Amun</note>, but that writer was unfamiliar with the true meaning of the word, as well as with its pronunciation, which seems to have been stressed on the next-to-last syllable <note>original Latin: penultimâ productâ</note>.

The worship of Ham, or the Sun, was both the most ancient and the most universal religion in the world. It was initially the prevailing religion of Greece and was spread along all the sea coasts of Europe, from where it extended into the inland provinces. It was established in Gaul and Britain, and it was the original religion of this island, which the Druids adopted in later times. That it reached far into the north is evident from Ausonius <note>a 4th-century Roman poet</note>, who noted its existence in his own time. He had relatives who were priests of this order and title, and he complimented them for that reason in his ode to the Orator <note>original: Rhetor</note> Attius Patera.

Since the ancient Greeks used the terms *Petros* and *Petra* <note>original: "Petros, and Petra" — Greek for a stone or a rock.</note>, we can easily explain why that word appears so frequently in the accounts of his worship. Furthermore, the scholarly commentaries mentioned above will lead us to discover where the strange idea arose regarding the famous Anaxagoras of Clazomenae; he is said to have prophesied that a stone would fall from the Sun. All that he had actually asserted can be seen in the account by the commentator mentioned earlier, which amounts only to this: that *Petros* was a name for the Sun. It was a word of Egyptian origin, derived from *Petor*, which is the same as Ham, the *Iämus* of the ancient Greeks. 

Some of his countrymen understood this *Petros* in a different sense and claimed he had foretold that a stone would drop from the Sun. Some people were foolish enough to think that this had actually happened, and as a result, they even pretended to show the very stone $^{24}$ at Aegospotamos which was said to have fallen. A similar story was told about a stone at Abydus on the Hellespont, and here too, Anaxagoras was supposed to have been the prophet $^{25}$. "In the gymnasium of Abydus, for that reason, a modest stone is still worshipped today; it is said that Anaxagoras predicted this stone would fall in the center of the earth." <note>original: "In Abydi gymnasio ex eâ causâ colitur hodieque modicus quidem (lapis), sed quem in medio terrarum casurum Anaxagoras prædixisse narratur."</note>

Because of this, they were mistakenly thought to have been located in the center of the inhabited world. They were also called *Sun-reaching Rocks* <note>original: Ηλιβατοι Πετραι (Elibatoi Petrai)</note>. The Greeks derived the word *Elibatos* from the verb "to descend" <note>original: βαινω (baino)</note>; on this account, these *Petra* (rocks) were thought to have fallen from the Sun $^{26}$. "The natural philosophers say that the sun is called a stone <note>original: "λιθος" (lithos); it should be "πετρα" (petra, or rock)</note>. Some understand what is said in the history about the stone as relating to the Sun: and they suppose that it was the Sun which hung over his head to his terror and confusion. We may from this learn the reason why so many deities were styled *Petræi* <note>original: "Πετραιοι"; meaning "of the rock"</note>. We read of $^{34}$ Mithras, "the God out of the rock" <note>original: "Μιθρας, ὁ θεος εκ πετρας"</note>, whose temple of old was actually a rock or cavern. The same worship seems to have prevailed to some degree in the west, as we may judge from an ancient inscription at Milan, which was dedicated $^{35}$ "To Hercules in the Rock" <note>original: "Herculi in Petrâ"</note>. 

But all deities were not worshiped in this way; the very name *Petra* was nothing other than the sacred term *Petora*, given to a cavern because it was esteemed in the first ages as an oracular temple. Some reverence for places of this sort was kept up for a long time. We may, from this, understand the reason for the prohibition given to some of the early converts to Christianity: that they should no longer $^{36}$ "offer vows at the rocks" <note>original: "ad petras vota reddere"</note>. ...passage in Homer, where he speaks of persons entering into agreements under oaks and rocks as places of <note>original: "security"</note> safety. The oak was sacred to Zeus and called *Sar-On*; and *Petra*, in its original sense being a temple, it must be looked upon as an asylum <note>A place of protection or sanctuary</note>. But this term was not confined to a rock or cavern: every oracular temple was styled *Petra* and *Petora*. From this, it followed that so many gods were called *Theoi Petraioi* <note>original: "Θεοι Πετραιοι"; Gods of the Rock</note> and *Patrooi* <note>original: "Πατρωοι"; Ancestral Gods. Bryant argues this title relates to "Petra" (temple/rock) rather than "Pater" (father)</note>. Pindar speaks of *Poseidon Petraios* <note>original: "Παι Ποσειδανος Πετραιε"; O Son of Poseidon of the Rock</note>, under which title Neptune was worshiped by the Thessalians; but the latter <note>Patroos</note> was the more common title. We meet in Pausanias with Apollo *Patroüs*, and with *Zeus Meilichios* <note>original: "Ζευς Μειλιχιος"; Zeus the Gracious</note>, and *Artemis Patroä* <note>original: "Αρτεμις Πατρωα"; Ancestral Artemis</note>; also *Bacchus Patroüs*, *Zeus Patroüs*, and *Vesta Patroä*, together with other instances.

$^{37}$ "There is no way now to converse with him from an oak or a rock, like a youth and a maiden—as a youth and a maiden converse with each other." <note>original: Homer, Iliad. Book 22, v. 126. Bryant likely cited Book 10 by mistake or used a different numbering system.</note> 
"Stone-swearers, public speakers, swearing upon the stone." <note>original: "Λιθωμοται, δημηγοροι, επι τω λιθῳ ομνυντες." Hesychius.</note>
$^{38}$ Pindar, Pythian Ode 4. p. 248. 
"Poseidon Petraios is honored among the Thessalians." <note>original: "Πετραιος τιμαται Ποσειδων παρα Θετταλοις." Ancient Commentary (Scholia) on Pindar.</note>

$^{40}$ Pausanias, Book 1, p. 104.

***

According to the interpretation in which I understand the term, we may explain why so many places in the East were styled *Petra*. Persia <note>original: "Persis"</note> and India did not abound with rocks more than Europe; yet in these parts, as well as in the neighboring regions, there is continual mention made of *Petra*: such as the *Rock of Sisimithrae* in Sogdiana, *Petra Aornon* in India, "and the Rock of Oxus, while others say of Arimazes." <note>original: "και την τε Οξυ (Πετραν), οἱ δε Αριαμαζε." Strabo, Book 11, p. 787.</note> *Petra Abatos* in Egypt, and *Petra Nabataea* in Arabia. Many places called *Petra* occur in the history of Alexander the Great: "To take even very strong rocks [fortresses] through betrayal." <note>original: "Ελειν δε και Πετρας ερυμνας σφοδρα εκ προδοσεως." Strabo, Book 11, p. 787.</note> They were in reality sacred eminences where people worshiped in ancient times, which in later ages were fortified. Every place styled *Arx* <note>Latin: citadel</note> and *Acropolis* <note>Greek: high city</note> was originally of the same nature. The same is to be observed of those styled *Purgoi* <note>original: "Πυργοι"; towers</note>.

The Greeks, whenever they encountered this term, even in the most remote regions, always gave it an interpretation according to their own preconceptions. It would be entirely unnecessary to say of a Persian prince that the homage he paid was to Persian deities; that is a matter of course and should be taken for granted unless there is specific evidence to the contrary. Rather, his vows were made to Mithras <note>The Persian god of the sun and light</note>, who was called *Pator* by the eastern nations. His temples were called *Patra* and *Petra*, and his festivals were the *Patrica*. # THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 298

...house of the Sun, ⁵⁰ *Cauones* <note>original Greek: Χαυωνες</note>. From *Pur-Ham* and *Pur-Amon*, they were named *Puramoun* ⁵¹ <note>original Greek: Πυραμυν</note>. From *Ob-El*, the Serpent God <note>original: "Pytho Deus"</note>, came ⁵² *Obelia*. If the place was a *Petra* or *Petora*, they had offerings of the same sort called *Petora*, which the Greeks expressed as ⁵³ *Pitura* <note>original Greek: Πιτυρα; Pitura usually refers to bran or husks</note>.

One of the titles of the Sun was *El-Aphas*, the Sun God of fire <note>original Latin: Sol Deus ignis</note>. The Greeks rendered this *El-aphas* as *Elaphos* <note>original Greek: ελαφος</note> and supposed it related to a deer. Similarly, the title *El-Apha-Baal*, given by the Amonians to the chief deity, was changed to *elaphebolos* <note>original Greek: ελαφηβολος</note>, a term with an entirely different meaning <note>In Greek, "elaphebolos" means "deer-slayer," an epithet often given to Artemis</note>. *El-aphas* and *El-apha-baal* actually related to the god Osiris, the deity of light. Sacred cakes <note>original Latin: liba</note> were made at his temple, similar to those mentioned above, and were named after him *Elaphor* <note>original Greek: Ελαφοι</note>. In the writings of Athenaeus, we have an account of their ingredients, which consisted of fine meal and a mixture of sesame and honey: ⁵⁴ "The *Elaphos* is a cake made of wheat, honey, and sesame" <note>original Greek: Ελαφος πλακους δια σιτος και μελιτος και σησαμυ</note>.

One species of sacred bread which used to be offered to the gods was of great antiquity and was called *Boun*. The Greeks, who often changed a final *N* into an *S* <note>original: "Nu final into a Sigma"</note>, expressed this in the nominative case as *bous* <note>original Greek: βους; this is also the Greek word for an ox or cow</note>; but in the accusative case, it is more accurately rendered as *boun* <note>original Greek: βουν</note>.

The *Patrica* <note>Ancestral or fatherly rites</note> were not only rituals of Mithras, but also of Osiris, who was in reality the same deity. We have a curious inscription regarding this matter, and a visual representation, which was first presented by the learned John Price in his observations on Apuleius <note>A Roman novelist and rhetorician, c. 124–170 AD</note>. It is copied from an original that he saw at Venice, and there is an engraving of it in the edition of Herodotus by ⁶² Gronovius <note>Jacobus Gronovius, a Dutch classical scholar</note>, as well as in the one by ⁶³ Wesseling <note>Peter Wesseling, a German-born Dutch philologist</note>. However, they are strangely mistaken about its purpose <note>original: purport</note>. They suppose it relates to a daughter of Mycerinus, the son of Cheops <note>Pharaohs of the Egyptian Old Kingdom; Mycerinus is credited with the third pyramid at Giza</note>. It seems she died, and her father was so affected by her death that he made a gilded wooden image of a cow and buried his daughter inside it. Herodotus says that he saw the image Mycerinus made and that it referred to this story. But despite the authority of this great author, we may be certain that it was a symbolic <note>original: emblematical</note> representation. And regarding the sculpture mentioned above and the characters depicted in it, the whole scene is a religious ceremony. It relates to an event of great antiquity that was commemorated in the rituals of Osiris. I shall discuss this later; for now, it is enough to observe that the sacred procession is carried out before a temple. On the temple is a Greek inscription, though written in provincial characters: "I carry the Fatherly Festival within" <note>original Greek: Ενδον Πατρικην Ἑορτην Φερω</note>. How can a "Fatherly Festival" <note>original Greek: Ἑορτη Πατρικη</note> relate to a funeral? It denotes a festival in

The Egyptians were the most extravagant of all nations in their <gloss>65</gloss> grief. If anyone died in a family of consequence, the women used to show their concern by smearing their heads with the mud of the river and disfiguring their faces with filth. In this manner, they would run up and down the streets half-naked, whipping themselves as they ran; the men likewise whipped themselves. ### AN
# ACCOUNT
### OF THE
## GODS of GREECE;
### To show that they were all originally one GOD, the SUN.

Since I shall have much to say concerning Greek theology <note>original: Grecian Theology</note> throughout this work, it will be necessary to first take some notice of their gods, both in respect to their origins <note>original: original</note> and to their intended meaning <note>original: purport</note>. Many scholars <note>original: learned men</note> have gone to great lengths <note>original: infinite pains</note> to classify the specific deities of different countries and to point out which were the same. However, they would have saved themselves much labor if, before they had bewildered themselves in these useless investigations <note>original: fruitless enquiries</note>, they had considered whether all the deities of which they treat were not originally the same—all coming from one source, then branching out and becoming diversified in different parts of the world. I have mentioned that the nations of

<meta>This page continues the argument that ancient Eastern religions originally worshiped only the Sun, but later developed complex systems of polytheism through the use of divine titles and attributes—systems which the Greeks eventually adopted without fully understanding.</meta>

<page-num>306</page-num>

<margin>
¹ Cyril against Julian <note>original: Cyril contra Julian</note>, p. 15. It is related somewhat differently in the *Timaeus* of Plato. Vol. 3. p. 22. See also Clement of Alexandria <note>original: Clemens Alexandr.</note>, *Stromata*, Book 1, p. 356.
</margin>

The East originally acknowledged only one Deity, the Sun. However, when they began to give the titles of Orus, Osiris, and Ham <note>original: Cham</note> to some of the heads of their families <note>ancestral figures</note>, these individuals also, in time, were looked up to as Gods and were worshiped individually as the Sun. This was practiced by the Egyptians; but this nation, being very prone to refinement in their worship, made many subtle distinctions. Supposing that there were certain "emanations" of divinity, they chose to distinguish each one by a specific title and to worship the Deity through his various attributes. 

This gave rise to a multitude of Gods; for the more inquisitive they were in their investigations <note>original: disquisitions</note>, the greater the number of these substitutes became. Many of them at first were intended as mere titles; others, as I mentioned before, were outpourings <note>original: απορροιαι—emanations or derivatives</note>. All of these, in time, were esteemed as distinct beings and gave rise to a most inconsistent system of Polytheism. 

The Greeks <note>original: Grecians</note>, who received their religion from Egypt and the East, misinterpreted everything that was imported and added significantly to these absurdities. They adopted Deities whose supposed attributes were totally unknown to them and whose names they could neither pronounce nor spell. They did not know how to arrange the linguistic elements of which the words were composed. Because of this, Solon the Wise could not escape the sharp but fair criticism of the priest in Egypt, who accused both him and the Greeks in general of the grossest childishness <note>original: puerility</note> and ignorance: ¹ "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; there is no such thing as an old Greek; you are all young in your souls; you possess no [ancient tradition...]" <note>original: Ω Σολων, Σολων, Έλληνες εστε παιδες αει, γερων δε Έλλην ουκ εστι, νεοι τε ψυχας απαντες· ουδεμιαν... This famous passage from Plato’s *Timaeus* records an Egyptian priest telling the lawgiver Solon that the Greeks lack the deep historical memory of the Egyptians.</note>

"...for you have no ancient tradition among yourselves, nor any knowledge grown gray with time" <note>original: γαρ εν ἑαυτοις εχετε παλαιαν δοξαν, ουδε μαθημα χρονῳ πολιὸν ουδεν</note>. The truth of this claim can be proven both by the uncertainty and the inconsistency of the ancient writers in their accounts of their deities. Herodotus takes note of this uncertainty: "From where each of the gods came, or whether they had all existed forever, and what kind of forms they had, was not known until just the other day, so to speak" <note>original: Ενθενδε εγενετο ἑκαστος των θεων, ειτε δ’ αει ησαν παντες, ὁποιοι δε τινες τα ειδεα, ουκ ηπιστατο μεχρι οὑ πρωϊν τε και χθες, ὡς ειπειν λογῳ</note>. <margin>² Book 2, chapter 53. The evidence of Herodotus must be considered early, and his judgment valid. What could provide a more tragic account of the doubt and darkness in which humanity was enveloped than these words from the historian? How clearly he shows the necessity of divine intervention <note>original: interposition</note> and the revelation that follows it!</margin> He credits Homer and Hesiod with creating the various names and distinctions of the gods, as well as the endless polytheism that prevailed: "These are the ones who created a genealogy <note>original: θεογονιαν—theogony</note> of the gods for the Greeks, gave the gods their titles, assigned them their honors and skills, and described their forms" <note>original: Οὑτοι δε εισι, οἱ ποιησαντες θεογονιαν Ἑλλησι, και τοισι θεοισι τας επωνυμιας δοντες, και τιμας τε και τεχνας διελοντες, και ειδεα αυτων σημαντες</note>. <margin>³ Herodotus, Book 2, chapter 53.</margin>

This ignorance regarding their own theology—and that of the countries from which they borrowed—led them to misapply the terms they had received and to create a separate god out of every title. But regardless of how they may have separated and distinguished them as different characters, they can all be clearly traced back to a single deity: the Sun. The same can be observed regarding the gods of the Romans. This can be largely proven by the common accounts of their own writers, if we pay close attention to what they say; however, it becomes even more obvious from the writings of those who had visited Egypt and based their accounts on that country. > One Zeus, one Hades, one Sun, one Dionysus; one god is in them all. <note>original: 'Εις Ζευς, εις Αΐδης, εις Ήλιος, εις Διονυσος, 'Εις θεος εν παντεσσι. Orphic Fragment 4.</note>

It was therefore pointless for the ancients to debate the identity of any god as compared with another, or to assign him to Jupiter rather than to Mars, or to Venus rather than Diana. "Some," says Diodorus, "think that Osiris is Serapis; others that he is Dionysus; others still that he is Pluto. There was originally nowhere near the diversity that is imagined, as Sir John Marsham has very correctly observed: "For the polytheism <term>original: πολυθεοτης; the worship of many gods</term> of the nations was not as great as the polyonymy <term>original: πολυωνυμια; the use of many names</term> of the gods." <note>original: Neque enim tanta πολυθεοτης Gentium, quanta fuit Deorum πολυωνυμια.</note> It is mentioned above that some thought Osiris was Jupiter, and others thought he was Pluto. But among the best theologians, Pluto was considered the same as Jupiter—and indeed, the same as Proserpine, Ceres, Hermes, Apollo, and every other deity.

We learn this from Pausanias, who says, <margin>17</margin> "Purcon was the servant of Poseidon for his oracles." <note>original Greek: Ποσειδωνι δ᾽ ὑπηρετην ες τα μαντευματα ειναι Πυρκωνα.</note> He mentions a verse to the same purpose: "Along with him was Purcon, the attendant of the famous Earth-shaker <term>Ennosigaios, a common title for Poseidon</term>." <note>original Greek: Συν δε τε Πυρκων αμφιπολος κλυτȣ Εννοσιγαιο.</note> **Purcon** means "Lord of fire or light" <note>original Latin: Ignis vel lucis dominus</note>; and we may know the department of the god from the name of the priest. He was no other than the supreme deity, the Sun, from whom all were supposed to be derived. Hence Poseidon (or Neptune), in the Orphic verses, is styled the father of gods and men, just like Zeus.

Nonnus, who was deeply read in the mythology of these countries, makes all the various roles of the other gods, as well as their titles, center in him. He describes him in some good poetry as the head of all.

## PHOENIX and PHOENICES.

Since there has been much uncertainty about the meaning and extent of these terms, and because they are of great consequence in the course of history, I will endeavor to state their true meaning. *Phoinic*, or *Poinic*, was an Egyptian and Canaanite term of honor. From this term, the Greeks formed the words *Phoenix*, *Phoenicians*, and *Phoenikoeis* <note>original Greek: Φοῖνιξ, Φοίνικες, Φοινικόεις</note>, and the Romans formed *Phoinic*, *Poinicus*, and *Poinicius*. These were later changed to *Phoenix*, *Punicus*, and ¹ *Puniceus* <note>Terms relating to the Carthaginians and the color purple, often associated with the Phoenicians.</note>. 

Originally, it was a title that the Greeks used as a name for a province; however, it was never accepted as such by the people to whom it was applied until the Greeks took possession of the country. Even then, it was only partially accepted. For although mention is made of the coast of Phoenicia <note>original: Phœnice</note>, we find the natives still called Sidonians, Tyrians, and ² Canaanites as late as the days of the Apostles. It was an honorary title, compounded of the word *Anac* <note>Likely referring to the Anakim or a title for "lord."</note> with an Egyptian prefix; it was translated at various times as both *Phoinic* and *Poinic*. It signified—

---

¹ In all ancient Roman accounts, the term was expressed as *Poini* and *Poinicus*. "The Carthaginians pay the taxes. The Carthaginians were accustomed to sacrifice their young boys." <note>original Latin: Poinei stipendia pendunt. Poinei sunt solitei fos sacrificare puellos.</note> — Ennius, *Annals*, Book 7. It was later changed to *Poenus* and *Punicus*.
² Simon the Canaanite. Matthew, chapter 10, verse 4. Also the woman of Canaan. Matthew, chapter 15, verse 22.

<summary>This page analyzes the origins of the word "Phoenix" and "Phoenician," arguing they were originally titles of honor derived from Egyptian and Canaanite roots rather than native names for the region.</summary>

<keywords>Phoenix, Phoenicians, etymology, Canaanites, Punic, Romans, Ennius, Anac, linguistics, ancient history</keywords>

--- Page 364 ---
<meta>This page continues the etymological discussion of the term "Phoenic" or "Ph'anac," showing how this title of honor was applied to gods, colors, and the palm tree.</meta>

<header>THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.</header>

[This word] signified a lord or prince and was particularly used by the sons of Cush <note>original: Chus</note> and Canaan. The Mysians seem to have kept closest to the original pronunciation, as they gave this title to the god Dionysus <note>original: Dionusus</note> and called him Ph'anac.

> ³ "Ogygia calls me Bacchus,
> Egypt thinks me Osiris,
> The Mysians call me Phanax."
> <note>original Latin: Ogygia me Bacchum vocat, Osiris Ægyptus putat, Mysi Phanacem.</note>

It was also bestowed upon many things that were considered princely and noble. Because of this, red or scarlet—a color reserved for great and honorable personages—was called *Phoinic*. The palm tree was also called *Phoinic* <note>original Greek: Φοινιξ</note>, and the ancients always described it as a stately and noble tree. It was regarded as an emblem of honor and used as a reward for victory. "A man of many palms" <note>original Latin: *Plurimarum palmarum homo*</note> was a proverbial expression among the Romans for a soldier of merit. Pliny speaks of various species of palms and the high regard in which the Babylonians held them. He says that the noblest among them were called the "Royal Palms," and he assumes they were named so because they were set aside for the king's use. However, they were an emblem of royalty from a very early period, a fact reflected in their original name. ...men. And as it was a mere title, the sacred writers of the Old Testament never use it to distinguish either the people or the country. This part of Canaan is never called Phoenicia by them; yet others did call it so, and the natives were styled Phoenicians even before the birth of Homer. However, this was a mistake, for it was never used by the natives as a provincial name. I have shown that it was a title of another sort—a mark of rank and preeminence. On this account, it was adopted by other people and given to other places. For this reason, it is never mentioned by any of the sacred writers before the Babylonian captivity, in order to avoid ambiguity. The Gentile <note>meaning non-Jewish or pagan</note> writers made use of it, and we can see what mistakes have followed. There were "Phoenicians" from various countries. <meta>This page continues the argument that "Phoenician" was originally a title used by Egyptian migrants rather than a native name for the inhabitants of Canaan. It identifies "Phoenix" and "Belus" as titles of honor used by colonizing groups.</meta>

<header>THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.</header>

"...there is a race of people called Phoenicians among the Athenians" <note>original Greek: γενος τι Αθηνησι</note>. In short, it was a title introduced at Sidon and the adjoining coast by people from Egypt. Who the people were that brought it may be known from several passages in ancient history, but particularly from an extract in Eusebius: "Phoenix and Cadmus, leaving Thebes in Egypt for Syria, ruled over Tyre and Sidon" <note>original Greek: Φοινιξ και Καδμος, απο Θηβων των Αιγυπτιων εξελθοντες εις την Συριαν, Τυρου και Σιδωνος εβασιλευον</note>. It is said that Belus <note>a title often associated with the Babylonian god Bel or Marduk, here used as a name for a leader</note> led a colony to the same regions; and it hardly needs explanation from which part of the world Belus must be supposed to have come. Euripides styles Cepheus, the king of Ethiopia, as the son of Phoenix; meanwhile, Apollodorus identifies him as the son of Belus. 

From this, we may infer that Belus and Phoenix were the same. This does not mean there were actual persons named Phoenix and Belus, for they were certainly titles. Under the characters of those two personages, colonies named the Belidae and Phoenicians went abroad and settled in different parts. Their history and names may be traced from Babylonia to Arabia in Egypt, and from there to Canaan and the regions in the West. It is therefore regrettable that the terms "Phoenix" and "Phoenicia" have ever been used in their common meaning—at least when the discussion turns toward the more ancient history of Canaan.

--- Page 368 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that "Phoenicia" was a name applied externally by the Greeks to the coast of Tyre and Sidon, and should not be confused with the native identity of the region's much older inhabitants.</meta>

When the Greeks took possession of the coast of Tyre, they called it Phoenicia; from that time onward, it may be accepted as a provincial name. Consequently, the writers of the New Testament do not hesitate to use the term, but they always do so with proper geographic precision, for the geography of the Scriptures is wonderfully exact. However, Greek and Roman writers often speak of it with much greater latitude, including Judea and Palestine within its borders, and sometimes even adding Syria and Idumea <note>original: Idume; the region south of Judea inhabited by the descendants of Esau</note>. Yet these countries were all separate and distinct, and Phoenicia comprised only a small portion of them.

Small as it may have been, many learned men have believed that all the colonies which settled at various times along the coast of the Mediterranean came from this region, and that all science was of Phoenician origin <note>original: original</note>. But this is not true according to their understanding <note>original: acceptation</note> of the term. While it is true that colonies did settle and science did come from the East, they did not originate merely from the Sidonians <note>the people of Sidon, a major Phoenician city</note>. I shall show that this progress was principally due to an earlier and superior branch of the family.

### OF THE
# TERM CAHEN,
## The COHEN, כהן, of the HEBREWS.

I have previously noted that the term *Cahen* denoted a priest or a president, and that it was a title often conferred upon princes and kings. Nor was it restricted to men alone; we find it frequently attached to the names of deities to signify their rule and supervision over the earth. From these gods, the title was passed down to their attendants and to all people of a prophetic or sacred character. 

The meaning of the term was so obvious that one would imagine no mistake could have occurred; yet, such is the perversity of human intellect that we find it was constantly misapplied by the Greeks and Romans. Because the sound of the word closely resembled the Greek *kyon* <note>original: κυων; meaning dog or hound</note> and the Latin *canis*, they could not help imagining that it referred to that animal. Consequently, due to this unfortunate resemblance, they continually misinterpreted it as a *dog*. For this reason, we are told by ¹ Ælian—

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

In ancient hieroglyphics, the figure of a dog occurs. I believe the meaning of this history can be determined with a little attention. The Egyptians were more sophisticated in their superstitions than any other nation in the world. They bestowed the names and titles of their deities upon plants and animals of every species, as well as upon parts of the human body and even the passions of the mind. Whatever they considered beneficial <note>original: "salutary"</note> or of great value, they labeled "Sacred" and dedicated it to some <gloss>10</gloss> god. 

This becomes clear when looking at words borrowed from Egypt. The Laurel (*Laurus*) was named after *Al-Orus* <note>Horus, the Egyptian sky god</note>. The berry was termed *bacca* after *Bacchus*. *Myrrh* (Μυῤῥα) was derived from *Ham-Ourah*. *Cassia* came from *Chus*. The crocodile was called *Caimin* and *Campsa*. The lion was *El-Eon*, the wolf was *El-Uc*, and the cat was *Al-Ourah*—from which the Greeks formed their own words: *leon* (lion), *lykos* (wolf), and *ailouros* (cat). 

The Egyptians styled myrrh as *Baal*; balsam as *baal-samen*; camphire <note>an archaic spelling of camphor</note> as *Cham-phour* (the Greek *kamphora*); and opium as *Ophion*. The sweet reed of Egypt was named <gloss>11</gloss> *Canah*, and *Conah* by way of eminence; it was also called <gloss>12</gloss> *Can-Osiris* <note>original: Χενοσιρις (Chenosiris); a plant title associated with the god Osiris</note>. Cinnamon was named after *Chan-Amon*; cinnabar (κινναβαρις) from *Chan-Abor*; and the sacred beetle (*Cantharus*) from *Chan-Athur*. The harp was styled *Cin-* <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "nor" suggests the full word is "Cinnor," a type of ancient lyre.</note>

From this arose the error of Horus Apollo <note>Referring to Horapollo, the supposed author of a late antique treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>. It is possible that in later times, Greek artists and the various mixed populations of Egypt may have depicted them this way; they were "led by the ear" <note>meaning they relied on the sound of words rather than their true meaning</note> and did not investigate the hidden meaning <note>original: "latent purport"</note> of the theology passed down to them. From this, we can perceive how little the later native Egyptians actually knew of their own rites and history.

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

It is said of the *Cunocephali* <note>Dog-heads</note> that when one part was dead and buried, the other still survived. This can relate to nothing else but a society, or a "body politic," where there is a continual decrease in members, yet a part always remains; the whole institution is maintained through succession. It is a puzzle that particularly relates to the priesthood in Egypt, for the sacred office there was hereditary, being entrusted to certain families. When some members died, a residue still <sup>26</sup> survived who admitted others to take the place of the deceased. <sup>27</sup> "Whenever someone dies, his son is appointed in his place" <note>original Greek: *Επεαν δε τις αποθανη, τουτου ὁ παις αντικαθισαται*</note>. We find that the sons supplied the place of their fathers; therefore, the group itself never became extinct, as it was kept up by a regular succession. 

As for the story that the *Cunocephali* gave <term>Hermes</term> <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Thoth, patron of wisdom and science</note> the first hint of dividing the day into twelve parts based on the exactness observed in their <sup>28</sup> bodily evacuations, it is a theory almost too trivial to be discussed. I have shown that the *Cunocephali* were a sacred college whose members were people of great learning, and their society seems to have been a very ancient institution. They were particularly dedicated to astronomical observations; and by contemplating the heavens—which they called *Ouran*—they learned to distinguish the seasons and to divide the day into parts. However, through a strange misconception, the Greeks changed the term *Ouran* to *ourein* <note>to urinate; original Greek: *ουρειν*</note>. They have made similar mistakes in other instances; and from this abuse of terms, the silly fable took its [rise]...

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that various ancient people groups and celestial names, often misinterpreted by the Greeks as being related to "dogs" (kunos), actually derived from sacred Egyptian titles for the Sun or their deities.</meta>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

The history of the *Cunodontes* <note>original: "dog-teeth"</note> is similar to the history of the *Cunocephali* <note>Dog-heads</note> and the *Acephali* <note>Headless ones</note>. They are a people mentioned by Solinus and Isidorus, who supposed them to have had the teeth of dogs. Yet, like those mentioned above, they were probably named after the object of their worship: the deity *Chan-Adon*. The Greeks expressed this name as *Kunodon* <note>original Greek: Κυνοδων</note> and called his followers <sup>32</sup> *Cunodontes*.

<margin>32 Solinus, chapter 4; and Isidorus, *Etymologies* <note>original: Origin.</note>, Book 9, "On Portents" <note>original Latin: de Portentis</note>.</margin>

The Greeks claimed that they had used the celestial sphere and were acquainted with the zodiac and its constellations <note>original: asterisms</note> very early on. However, it is plain from their mistakes that they actually received the knowledge of these things very late, at a time when the original terms were obsolete and their true meaning could no longer be obtained. They borrowed all the systems by which the stars are organized from the Egyptians, who had created them in ancient times and named them after aspects of their own religion and mythology. 

The Egyptians had specifically granted the titles of their deities to those stars which appeared brightest in their hemisphere. One of the most remarkable and brilliant stars they called *Cahen Sehor*; another they termed *Purcahen*; a third *Cahen Ourah*, or *Cun Ourah*. These were all misunderstood and changed by the Greeks: *Cahen Sehor* became *Canis Sirius* <note>The Dog Star</note>; *Purcahen* became *Procyon* <note>The star "before the dog"</note>; and *Cahen Ourah* became *Cunosoura* <note>Cynosure, or the Little Ursa</note>, which they interpreted as "the dog’s tail." Regarding this last name, I think that based on how it is applied in other instances, we may be certain that its accepted meaning could not be what the Greeks would persuade us; nor did it have any relation to a dog. The ancients very gratefully attributed the merit of every useful and beneficial <note>original: "salutary"</note> invention to the gods. Ceres was supposed to have discovered corn and bread to men; Osiris showed them the use of the plough; Cinyras, the harp; and Vesta taught them how to build. Every deity was looked up to as the source of some blessing.

The Tyrians and Sidonians <note>People of the Phoenician cities Tyre and Sidon</note> were famous for the manufacture of purple. The dye was very exquisite, and its discovery was attributed to Hercules of Tyre—the same figure who is styled "Hercules the Philosopher" <note>original Greek: Ἡρακλῆς Φιλόσοφος</note> by Palaephatus. However, some will not allow him this honor, but instead say that the dog of Hercules was the discoverer. According to the story, while accidentally feeding upon the *Murex* <note>A sea snail from which the dye was extracted</note>, with which the coast abounded, the dog stained its mouth with the fluid <note>original: "ichor"</note> of the fish; from this, the first hint of dyeing was taken. This gave birth to the proverbial expression:

> The venerable purple is the discovery of a dog. <note>original Greek: Εὑρημα κυνος ἡ σεβαση πορφυρα.</note>

Nonnus mentions the particular circumstance of the dog staining its mouth:

> He purpled his snowy cheeks with the blood of the shellfish. <note>original Greek: Χιονεας πορφυρε παρηϊδας αἱματι κοχλȣ.</note>

Such is the story, which at first sight is too childish to be believed. It is not likely that a dog would feed upon shell-

Plutarch thought that by this clever explanation <note>original: "refinement"</note>, he could remove the embarrassment of giving such a lowly name to a god. <meta>This page continues the argument that Greek deities and their attributes were often the result of linguistic misunderstandings of ancient Egyptian titles. Specifically, it explores how the title "Cahen" was misinterpreted to mean "dog" or "gaping."</meta>

<page-num>346</page-num>

<meta>catchword: But</meta>

He was the Egyptian *Cahen* <note>a title meaning a priest or prince</note> mentioned above; but this sacred title was carelessly changed to a "dog and a goose" <note>original Greek: κυνα και χηνα, *kuna kai chēna*</note> because of a similarity in sound. It is clear from Plato that he was referring to the Egyptian deity, as Plato acknowledges that he swore "by the dog, the god of the Egyptians" <note>original Greek: μα τον κυνα τον Αιγυπτιων Θεον, *ma ton kuna ton Aigyptiōn Theon*</note>. $^{47}$ By this, we are to understand a *Cahen* of Egypt. Porphyry explicitly states that it was the god Hermes, the son of Zeus and Maia: "He made his oath by the child of Zeus and Maia" <note>original Greek: Κατα τον του Διος και Μαιας παιδα εποιειτο τον ορκον</note>. $^{48}$

I cannot explain by any other principle than the one I have followed why there are strange representations of Apollo and Bacchus "gaping" with open mouths. It seems they were described this way in some places. Clement of Alexandria mentions from Polemon that Apollo was exhibited in this manner: "Polemon knew of a statue of a gaping Apollo" <note>original Greek: Πολεμων δε κεχνηοτος Απολλωνος οιδεν αγαλμα</note>. $^{49}$ We are also told that a "gaping" $^{50}$ Bacchus was particularly worshiped at Samos. Both were the same as the Egyptian Orus <note>Horus</note>, who was styled *Cahen-On*, meaning "Prince," or "God of the Sun." From this *Cahen-On*, the Greeks seem to have formed the word *Chainon* <note>original Greek: Χαινων, meaning 'gaping' or 'yawning'</note>; as a result, these two deities were represented with their jaws widely extended. 

This term was sometimes changed to *koinos* <note>original Greek: κοινος</note>, meaning "common." This is why we so often find "common gods" <note>original Greek: κοινοι Θεοι</note> and "common altars" <note>original Greek: κοινοι βωμοι</note> on coins and marbles, as well as "Hermes the common" <note>original Greek: κοινος Ερμης</note>. And since Hermes was the reputed god of profit and gain, everything found by chance was judged to be *koinos*, or "common" <note>a Greek legal concept where a find is shared</note>.

I am confident that anyone who considers the strange names of deities, men, and places in the way I have suggested—while paying attention to the mythology passed down about them—will be able to trace them back to their original meanings.

It seems clear to me that what the Greeks so often interpreted as "dogs" <note>original Greek: κυνες (*kunes*)</note> was actually an ancient Amonian <note>relating to the worship of Amon, a major Egyptian deity</note> title. Therefore, when I read about the "brazen dog" of Vulcan, or the dogs of Erigone, Orion, Geryon, Horus, Hercules, Amphilocus, and Hecate, I must conclude that these were titles for various deities, or perhaps for their priests, who were named after their religious office. 

In short, the *Cahen* <note>priests</note> of Egypt were no more dogs than the *Paterae* of Amon were basins <note>the author argues *Patera* was a title for a priest, later confused with a ritual bowl</note>. And although Diodorus Siculus does say that at the great festival of Isis the entire procession was led by dogs, I am convinced that they were actually the priests of the goddess.

It would be an endless task to list every instance of this nature.

I am confident that anyone who considers the strange names of deities, people, and places in the light I have recommended—and pays attention to the mythology passed down about them—will be able to trace them back to their original meanings using these clues. It seems clear to me that what the Greeks so often interpreted as "dogs" <note>original Greek: κυνες (*kunes*)</note> was actually an ancient <term>Amonian</term> <note>Bryant's term for the descendants of Ham, specifically referring here to the ancient Egyptians and their religious descendants</note> title. 

Therefore, when I read about the "bronze dog" of Vulcan, or the dogs belonging to Erigone, Orion, Geryon, Orus <note>Horus</note>, Hercules, Amphilocus, or Hecate, I must conclude that these were actually titles for those deities, or perhaps for their priests, who were named according to their office. In short, the <term>Cahen</term> <note>priests</note> of Egypt were no more "dogs" than the <term>Paterae</term> <note>sacred shallow bowls used for libations</note> of Amon were simply "basins." And although Diodorus Siculus says that during the grand festival of ⁵⁴ Isis, the whole procession was preceded by dogs, I cannot help being convinced that they were actually the priests of the Goddess.

The subject which I have been treating was greatly misapplied by being so uniformly referred to dogs; yet I do not mean to imply that it did not sometimes relate to them. They were distinguished by this sacred title and were held in some degree of $^{64}$ veneration: but how far they were revered is not easy to determine. Herodotus, $^{65}$ speaking of the sanctity of some animals in Egypt, says that the people in every family where a dog died shaved themselves all over; and he mentions it as a custom still continuing in his own time. Plutarch $^{66}$ differs from him. He allows that these animals were at one time esteemed holy, but it was before the time of Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, the Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE</note>. From the era of his reign, they were seen in another light; for when this king killed the sacred Apis <note>The sacred bull of Memphis</note>, the dogs fed so greedily upon his entrails without making a proper distinction that they lost all their sanctity. It is of little consequence which account is more accurate. They were certainly of old looked upon as sacred and esteemed emblems of the Deity. And it was perhaps with a view to this, and to prevent the Israelites from retaining any notion of this nature, that a dog was not allowed to come within the precincts of the temple at $^{67}$ Jerusalem. In the Mosaic law, the price of a dog and the hire of a harlot are put upon the same level. $^{68}$ *You shall not bring the hire of a prostitute, or the*

Among the different branches of the great Amonian family <note>The descendants of Ham (Amon), according to Bryant’s historical framework.</note> who spread themselves abroad, the sons of Chus <note>In the Bible, Chus (or Cush) was the eldest son of Ham and the father of Nimrod.</note> were the most significant and, at the same time, the most enterprising. They gained access to countries widely distant from one another, where they may be traced under different names, but more particularly by their family title. We might expect the Greeks to have rendered this title as *Chusos*, and to have named the people *Chusaei* <note>original: Χυσαῖοι (Chusaei).</note>.

[Colchis was said] to have abounded with gold; and the same was claimed of the Hermus and Pactolus rivers in Ionia. Not only the poets, but many of the more serious historians speak of their golden sands. Yet there is reason to doubt this; for not one of them provides any good evidence for what they assume. They do not mention any trade being conducted, nor any riches resulting from this lucky circumstance. Therefore, there is no reason to think that even one grain of gold was gathered from these famous streams. Among the several islands occupied by this people <note>The Chuseans or descendants of Cush.</note> were Rhodes and Delos. # THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

Chus <note>The biblical Cush, son of Ham.</note> was styled *Or-Chus* and *Chus-Or* by the Egyptians and Canaanites. The Greeks expressed the latter name as *Chrusor* <note>original: Χρυσωρ</note>, following the same pattern as the examples mentioned previously. We learn from the historian Eusebius, citing Philo, that *Chrusor* was one of the principal deities of the Phoenicians and a great benefactor to mankind; some even supposed him to be the same as Hephaestus <note>The Greek god of fire and metalworking, known to the Romans as Vulcan.</note>. Both the Tyrians and Sidonians were undoubtedly a mixed race, and they preserved the memory of Ham and Chus just as much as they did the memory of Canaan.

This name, so often rendered as *Chrusos* <note>Greek for "gold."</note> and *Chrusor*, was sometimes changed to *Chrusaor* <note>original: Χρυσαωρ</note>. It appears in many places where the Cuthites <note>The descendants of Cush.</note> were known to have settled. We have already seen that they lived in Egypt for a long time, and we read of a *Chrusaor* in those parts who is said to have arisen from the blood of Medusa.

> "Great Chrusaor and the horse Pegasus sprang forth." <note>original: Εξεθορε Χρυσαωρ τε μεγας, και Πηγασος ιππος. Hesiod, *Theogony*, line 281.</note>

We meet with the same *Chrusaor* in the regions of Asia Minor, especially among the Carians. In these areas, he was particularly worshipped and was said to have been the first mortal to be deified. The great assembly <note>original: Divan</note> of that nation was called the *Chrusaorium*; there was also a city named *Chrusoaris*, and a temple of the same

Chus <note>The biblical Cush, son of Ham and father of the Cuthites.</note> was called Or-Chus and Chus-Or by the Egyptians and Canaanites. The Greeks expressed the latter name as *Chrusor* <note>original: Χρυσωρ</note>, following the same patterns we have seen before. We learn from Eusebius (quoting Philo of Byblos) that Chrusor was one of the primary deities of the Phoenicians. He was considered a great benefactor to humanity and was thought by some to be the same as Hephaestus <note>The Greek god of fire and craftsmanship.</note>. The people of Tyre and Sidon were undoubtedly a mixed race, and they preserved the memory of Ham and Chus just as much as they did that of Canaan. <note>original: "Tyrians and Sidonians"</note>

This name, which was so often rendered as *Chrusos* or *Chrusor*, was sometimes changed to *Chrusaor* <note>original: Χρυσαωρ</note>. It appears in many places where the Cuthites are known to have settled. We have already seen that they lived in Egypt for a long time, and we read of a figure named Chrusaor in those regions who was said to have been born from the blood of Medusa.

->Great Chrusaor leaped forth, and the horse Pegasus.<-
<note>original: "Εξεθορε Χρυσαωρ τε μεγας, και Πηγασος ιππος." Hesiod, *Theogony*, line 281.</note>

We encounter this same Chrusaor in the regions of Asia Minor, especially among the Carians <note>An ancient people of southwestern Anatolia.</note>. In these parts, he was specifically worshipped and was said to have been the first mortal to be deified. The great assembly <note>original: "Divan," a term for a high council or court.</note> of that nation was called the *Chrusaorium*, and there was a city called *Chrusoaris* and a temple of the same

...of the sons of Chus. The Greeks borrowed this term and applied it to Apollo; and from this title, *Chrysaor*, he was named the God of the Golden Sword. Accordingly, Homer calls him $^{18}$ "Apollo Chrysaor" <note>original: Απολλωνα Χρυσαορα (*Apollona Chrysaora*)</note>. This title cannot possibly refer to the weapon suggested, for it would be pointless to call an infant the "God of the Golden Sword." A sword was a weapon that was never attributed to him at any time. I do not believe he is ever represented with one on an engraved gem or a marble statue. Instead, he is described as wishing for a lyre <note>original: harp</note> and for a bow:

> $^{21}$ "May the lyre and the curved bow be dear to me." <note>original: Ειη μοι κιθαρις τε φιλη, και καμπυλα τοξα (*Eiē moi kitharis te philē, kai kampula toxa*)</note>

And his mother is said to have been pleased that she brought him into the world as an archer:

> $^{22}$ "Leto rejoiced, because she bore a powerful son who carries a bow." <note>original: Χαιρε δε Λητω, Ουνεκα τοξοφορον και καρτερον υιον ετικτεν (*Chaire de Lētō, Houneka toxophoron kai karteron huion etikten*)</note>

These items of equipment <note>original: habiliments</note> are often specified, but I do not recall any mention of a sword. Furthermore, the term *Chrysaor* did not originate from Greek etymology.

Now, what is this description but a misuse of terms that were poorly understood and shamefully misapplied? Philostratus had heard of a region in India whose history he wanted to make seem miraculous. The country where Apollonius is supposed to have gone was a province of the Indo-Cuthites, who were found in various places under the title of Oreitae. Chus was the son of Ham. Although the names of the Greek deities are not used consistently, Ham is generally regarded as Helios <note>original: Ἥλιος</note>, the Sun, and held the titles Dis and Dios. For this reason, the city of Amon in Egypt was translated as Diospolis <note>City of Zeus/God.</note>. If, then, *Chrusos* and *Chrusor* are indeed Chus (as I have supposed), the person so named must have been—according to the more ancient mythology—the son of Helios and Dios. We find accordingly that this was the case. ...that we never saw a swan. There are some here and there toward the marshes, which make a low, dull noise. But as for any musical harmony, a rook or a jackdaw, in comparison to them, might be considered a nightingale.

Such are the witty criticisms <note>original: "strictures"</note> of Lucian regarding the story of Phaethon and Cycnus, as described by the poets. Whatever the real origins of this fiction might have been, they were certainly unknown to the Greeks. They misinterpreted the little information that reached them and, from those misunderstandings, they invented these fables. 

The story, as we have it, is not told consistently. Some, like Lucian, speak of swans in the plural and imagine them to have been the ministers and attendants of Apollo who assisted at his concerts. Others mention only one person, called Cycnus, who was the reputed brother of Phaethon and was transformed into the bird of that name <note>Cycnus is the Greek word for "swan."</note> upon his death. The fable remains the same regardless of how it is told, and its overall meaning is also the same. 

There is one mistake in the story that I must correct before I continue, as it may be important for my inquiry. Many poets represent Phaethon as the child of the Sun, or Apollo: <note>original Latin: "Sole satus Phaethon," meaning "Phaethon, born of the Sun"</note>. However, this was a mistake found primarily among the Roman poets. Phaethon actually *was* the Sun. It was a title for Apollo, given to him as the god of light. This is evident from the testimony of the earlier Greek poets, particularly Homer, who uses the name in this sense.

...they <margin>original: "^4 removed it"</margin> moved it to the stronghold of Tyre. This place was soon developed into a mighty city, which was very memorable in its day. The <term>Canaanites</term> <note>The descendants of Canaan, son of Ham; often associated with the Phoenicians.</note>, being a sister tribe of the <term>Mizraim</term> <note>The biblical name for the Egyptians.</note>, were extremely similar to them in their rituals and religion. They held a heifer, or cow, in high veneration, in accordance with the ^5 customs of Egypt. Their chief deity was the Sun, whom they worshiped together with the <term>Baalim</term> <note>Plural of "Baal," meaning "lords" or "gods."</note>, under the titles of Ourchol, Adonis, and Thamuz. 

It was a custom among the Greeks at the celebration of their religious festivals to conclude everything with hymns of praise and the most joyful exclamations. But the Egyptians were of a gloomy turn of mind, which influenced the entirety of their worship. Their hymns were always composed in melancholy, moving melodies and consisted of lamentations for the loss of Osiris, the mystical flight of Bacchus, the wanderings of Isis, and the sufferings of the gods. <term>Apuleius</term> <note>A Roman writer and philosopher (c. 124 – c. 170 AD).</note> notes this difference in the rituals and worship of the two nations: ^6 "The Egyptian shrines of the deities are full of wailing; the Greek ones are mostly full of dances." <note>original: "Ægyptiaca numinum fana plena plangoribus: Græca plerumque choreis."</note> Hence the author of the *Orphic Argonautica*, speaking of the initiations in Egypt, mentions:

->^7 "The wailing of the Egyptians, and the sacred libations for Osiris." <note>original: "Θρῆνος τ’ Αἰγυπτίων, καὶ Ὀσίριδος ἱερὰ χύτλα."</note><-

The Canaanites at Byblus, Berytus, Sidon, and afterwards at

The father of this people is represented in the Mosaic <note>Referring to the books of Moses in the Bible, specifically Genesis.</note> history, according to our version, as Canaan. However, there is reason to think that by the Egyptians and other neighboring nations, the name was expressed as *Cnaan*. This was rendered by the Greeks as *Chnaas* <note>original Greek: Χναας</note> and *Chnas* <note>original Greek: Χνας</note>; and in later times *Chna* <note>original Greek: Χνα</note>. $^{14}$ "Chna: this was what Phoenicia was called—the ethnic name was Chnaos" <note>original Greek: Χνα, οὑτως ἡ Φοινικη εκαλειτο—το εθνικον Χναος</note>. We are told by Philo <note>Philo of Byblos, an antiquarian who translated the works of Sanchoniathon.</note>, citing Sanchoniathon <note>A Phoenician author believed to have lived before the Trojan War.</note>, that $^{15}$ Isiris <note>A variant of the name Osiris.</note> the Egyptian, who discovered three letters, was the brother of Chna. By this, it is meant that Mizraim <note>The biblical ancestor of the Egyptians and brother of Canaan.</note> was the brother of Canaan. 

I have noted more than once a particular term, *Uc* <note>original Greek: Υκ</note>, which has been overlooked by most writers; yet it is found in the composition of many words, especially those of Amonian <note>Relating to the descendants of Ham (often identified with the Egyptian god Amun).</note> origin. The tribe of Cush was called by Manethon <note>An Egyptian priest and historian who wrote in the 3rd century BCE.</note>, before the passage was corrupted, *Uc-Cussos* <note>original Greek: Υκκουσος</note>. *Uch*, says this author, signifies a $^{16}$ king in the sacred language of Egypt. Because of this, it was bestowed as a title upon the god Sehor <note>A name for the god of the Nile, often associated with Osiris.</note>, who, as we may infer from Manethon and $^{17}$ Hellanicus <note>A Greek historian from the 5th century BCE.</note>, was called *Ucsiris* and *Icsiris*; but by the later Greeks...

<meta>This page continues the etymological analysis of the name "Canaan" and its variations, exploring how the Greeks adapted foreign titles into their own mythology and language, specifically linking Canaan to the names Ichnaia, Themis, and Cucnus.</meta>

<page-num>374</page-num>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

The Greeks altered the name to Isiris and Osiris. Not only was the god Sehor, or Sehoris, expressed in this way, but Cnas, or Canaan, held the same title and was styled Uc-Cnas. The national name or possessive form was Uc-cnaos <note>original Greek: Υκ-κναος</note>; for as we learn from Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century geographer.</note>, "the national name was Chnaos" <note>original Greek: το εθνικον γαρ Χναος</note>. 

The Greeks, who usually adapted every foreign name to something similar in their own language, changed Uc-cnaos <note>original Greek: Υκκναος</note> to Cucneios <note>original Greek: Κυκνειος</note>; and from Uc-cnas <note>original Greek: Υκ Κνας</note> they formed Cucnus <note>original Greek: Κυκνος; the Greek word for "swan." The author argues the mythical "Swan" stories originated from a corruption of the name Canaan.</note>. Some traces of this word still remain, though they are almost erased, and can be seen in the name of the goddess Ichnaia. Instead of Uc-Cnaan, the son of Ham, the Greeks substituted a feminine version of this figure, whom they portrayed as the daughter of the Sun. Lycophron mentions her in this light:

$^{18}$ "The judge of Ichnaia, the daughter of the Sun" <note>original Greek: Της Ηλιου θυγατρος Ιχναιας βραβευς</note>.

They likewise changed Thamuz and Thamas of Canaan and Egypt into the feminine goddess Themis, and called her Ichnaia Themis. She is styled this way by Homer:

> $^{19}$ "All the goddesses were inside, 
> as many as were the best: Dione, Rhea, 
> Ichnaia Themis, and loud-moaning Amphitrite" <note>original Greek: Θεαι δ’ εσαν ενδοθι πασαι, Οσσαι αρισται εσαν, Διωνη τε, ‘Ρειη τε, Ιχναιη τε Θεμις, και αγασονος Αμφιτριτη.</note>.

*Ichnaia* <note>original Greek: Ιχναια</note> is used here as an adjective. *Ichnaia Themis* signifies the Themis, or Thamuz, of $^{20}$ Canaan.

He also mentions "Arachnaion, a mountain in Argos" <note>original Greek: Αραχναιον ορος Αργους</note>. *Ar-Achnaion* is the hill of Canaan, or the Canaanite mountain.

<margin>21 See Radicals, page 89.</margin>

There was another factor that likely helped perpetuate this error: a Canaanite temple was called both *Ca-Cnas* and *Cu-Cnas*, and the adjective form <margin>21 See Radicals, page 89.</margin> was *Cu-Cnaios*. There is reason to believe these terms were rendered in Greek as *Cycnus* and *Cycneios* <note>original Greek: Κυκνος and Κυκνειος. "Cycnus" is the Greek word for swan.</note>. In addition to all this, the swan was undoubtedly the emblem <note>original: insigne</note> of Canaan, just as the eagle and vulture were symbols of Egypt, and the dove represented Babylonia. It was certainly the hieroglyphic symbol of the country. These factors contributed to the creation of many frivolous legends, which poets then greatly expanded upon. 

Therefore, it is notable that wherever we might imagine colonies from Canaan settled and founded temples, there is usually some story involving swans. When the Greeks referred to the hymns of these people, instead of saying *Ucnaon asma* <note>original Greek: Υκναον ασμα</note>, meaning "the music of Canaan," they introduced the phrase *cycneion asma* <note>original Greek: κυκνειον ασμα</note>, meaning "the song of swans." Furthermore, instead of describing the death of the god Thamuz being lamented by the *Cucnaans* (the priests), they claimed that swans sing their own funeral song <note>original: dirge</note> and foretell their own deaths. 

Wherever the Canaanites traveled, they introduced their national worship. Part of this, as I have shown, consisted of chanting hymns in honor of their local god. He was the same as the Greek god Apollo. Because of this, the writer Lucian <note>A 2nd-century AD Syrian-Greek satirist.</note>, following the popular belief of his time, says that the *Cycni* (the Swan-people) were once the attendants and ministers of that deity. By this, we are to understand that people known by this name were, in ancient times, his priests. 

One region of the world where this belief about swans was common was in Liguria, on the banks of the River Eridanus <note>The ancient name for the River Po in Italy.</note>. According to myth, this is where Phaethon <note>The son of the Sun god who died while trying to drive his father's chariot.</note> met his downfall, and here his brother Cycnus...

In these parts, some Amonians <note>The author's term for descendants of Ham/Ammon</note> settled very early; among whom it appears there were many from Canaan. They can be tracked by the massive engineering projects they undertook, for they drained the river toward its mouth and constructed vast canals called the *Fossae Philistinae* <note>Latin: "Philistine Ditches"</note>. Pliny, speaking of the entrance into the Eridanus <note>The ancient name for the River Po in Italy</note>, says: <gloss>22</gloss> "From there are the full mouths [of the river], the Carbonaria, and the Philistine excavations—which others call the Tartarus—all created by the overflow of the Philistine canal" <note>original Latin: "Inde ostia plena, Carbonaria, ac fossiones Philistinæ, quod alii Tartarum vocant: omnia ex Philistinæ fossæ abundatione nascentia."</note>. These canals were undoubtedly the work of the Canaanites, and particularly of some of the Caphtorim <note>A biblical people often associated with the origins of the Philistines</note> who came from Philistia. For this reason, these outlets of the river were named the Philistine canals.

The river reveals its origins through its name, as it has no connection to the Celtic language, but is clearly of Egyptian or Canaanite etymology. This is obvious from the terms that compose it: for it is a combination of *Ur-Adon*, or *Orus Adonis* <note>Orus is a version of the Egyptian god Horus; Adonis is the Greek name for the Semitic lord Adon</note>; it was sacred to the God of that name. On its own, the river was simply called Adon or Adonis. It should be noted that this is also the name of one of the major rivers in Canaan. That river flowed near the city of Byblos, where the death of the god Thamuz <note>A Mesopotamian/Canaanite deity whose death and rebirth were celebrated annually</note> was especially mourned. This circumstance is noted by many authors and most movingly described by Milton:

> The Syrian damsels to lament his fate

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that mythological transformations of gods into animals were actually poetic metaphors for the movements and actions of specific nations or priestly groups, specifically identifying the eagle with Egypt and the swan with Canaan.</meta>

<page-num>379</page-num>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

In early times, colonies were often called by the name of the deity they worshipped, or by the name of the insignia <term>original: insigne; a badge or emblem</term> and hieroglyphic symbol by which their country was known. Every raid or conquest made by such people was attributed to the deity represented by that symbol. This was the way poets described events, and in those days, almost all history was written in verse. Consequently, instead of saying that the Egyptians, Canaanites, or Tyrians landed and kidnapped certain people, they said it was done by Jupiter in the form of an eagle, a swan, or a bull. They substituted an eagle for Egypt, a swan for Canaan, and a bull for the city of <gloss>30</gloss> Tyre. It is said of the Telchines—who were Amonian priests <note>Priests of the Egyptian god Amun</note>—that they came to Attica led by Jupiter in the shape of an eagle.

<gloss>31</gloss> "An eagle led the way through the air, a representation of Jupiter." <note>original Greek: Αιετος ηγεμονευε δι’ αιθερος αντιτυπος Ζευς. From Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, Book 24, page 626.</note>

By this, the author means they were Egyptian priests, and an eagle was likely the emblem on their military standard as well as the national symbol of their country.

Some members of the same family were also found among the Atlantes of Mauritania and are described as having the form of swans. Prometheus, in the play by Aeschylus, speaks of them in the instructions he gives to Io: <gloss>32</gloss> *“You must go,” says he, “as far as...*

...as far as the city of Cisthene in the Gorgonian plains, where the three Phorcides reside. These are ancient, honorable ladies who are said to be in the shape of swans and have but one eye, which they use in common. This history relates to an Amonian <term>Amonian: belonging to the lineage of Ham or the Egyptian god Amun</term> temple founded in the remote parts of Africa. In this temple, there were three priestesses of Canaanite race; for that reason, they are described as being in the shape of swans. The idea that they had only one eye among them originated from a hieroglyphic very common in Egypt, and probably in Canaan: this was the representation of an eye, which was said to be engraved upon the pediment <note>The triangular upper part of the front of a classical building</note> of their <gloss>33</gloss> temples. As the land of Canaan was so well-positioned for trade, and because emigrants from most parts of the world traveled under their guidance, their history was widely known. 

They navigated the seas very early and were necessarily familiar with foreign regions. At one point, they must have moved to these regions in great numbers when they fled before the sons of Israel. In all the places where they settled, they were famous for their hymns and music. The Greeks transferred all these qualities to birds and assumed that they were literal swans who were gifted with this harmony. Yet, as sweet as their songs are said to have been, I do not believe there is a single person on record who was ever an actual witness to it.

<margin>"The Phorcides were three—they had the form of swans." <note>original Greek: Ἀι μεν Φορκιδες τρεις— ειχον ειδος Κυκνων.</note> Scholia on the same passage. It is certainly all a fable. When, therefore, Plutarch tells us that Apollo was pleased with the music of swans <gloss>34</gloss> <note>original Greek: mousikē te hēdetai, kai kyknōn phōnais — "he is delighted with music and the voices of swans"</note>; and when Aeschylus mentions them singing their own funeral dirges, they are certainly referring to Egyptian and Canaanite priests, who mourned the deaths of Adonis <note>original: Adon</note> and Osiris. This could not have been a complete secret to the Greeks, as they often seem to refer to such an idea. Socrates called swans his "fellow-servants"; in doing so, he was referring to the ancient priests known as *Cycni* <term>Cycni: Latin for "swans," here used as a title for priests</term>. These priests were members of the temple choir and served the same deities that Socrates claimed to serve. Because of this, Porphyry assures us <gloss>35</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ou paizōn homodoulos autou elegen tas kyknous (Sōkratēs) — "Socrates was not joking when he called the swans his fellow-servants"</note> that Socrates was very serious when he mentioned swans as his fellow-servants. 

Therefore, when Aristophanes speaks of the <gloss>36</gloss> Delian and Pythian swans <note>referring to the priests at Apollo's sacred sites in Delos and Delphi; original Greek: Kyknō Pythiō kai Dēliō</note>, he is referring to the priests of those places. And when Plato says that the soul of Orpheus, out of a disgust for women, led the life of a <gloss>37</gloss> swan, the meaning is certainly that he retired from the world to a cloister and lived a life of celibacy, like a priest. For the priests of many countries—but particularly those of Egypt—were recluses and devoted themselves to <gloss>38</gloss> celibacy; indeed, monasticism <term>monkery: the practice of living as a monk or in a religious community</term> originated in Egypt. ## TEMPLE SCIENCE.

The Egyptians were very famous for their knowledge of geometry. Because all the low-lying parts of their country were flooded every year, it is reasonable to assume that they used this science to survey their lands and re-establish their various property claims once the waters receded. Many, indeed, have thought that the confusion over property ownership—which must have prevailed for a time—gave birth to practical geometry as a way to remedy the problem. Consequently, it is believed that charts and maps were first drawn in this country. <margin>Herodotus, Book 2, chapter 109.</margin> We can imagine that these did not relate only to private estates <note>original: "demesnes," meaning landed property or territory</note>, but also included the various branches of the Nile, the entire sea coast, and the inlets that bordered Lower Egypt. <note>"The Egyptians became the inventors of geometry." original Greek: *Γεωμετρίας τε αυ ευρεται γεγόνασιν (ό Αιγυπτιοι)*. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book 1, page 361.</note>

It is quite certain that the people of Colchis <note>Colchis was an ancient kingdom on the coast of the Black Sea (modern-day Georgia), which the author identifies as an Egyptian colony.</note>, who were a colony from Egypt, possessed charts of this sort. These included written descriptions of the seas and shores wherever they traded, and at one time they conducted a most extensive commerce. We are told, says the commentator <note>original: "Scholiast," an ancient scholar who provided explanatory notes on classical texts.</note> on Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Rhodes (3rd century BC), author of the *Argonautica*.</note>, that the Colchians still retain the laws and customs of their ancestors: <margin>Book 4, verse 279.</margin>

<summary>Bryant discusses the Egyptian origins of geometry and cartography, explaining how the annual flooding of the Nile necessitated the development of surveying and map-making to settle land disputes.</summary>

<note>original Greek: Εχει δε τε Κιονας αυτος / Μακρας, αἱ Γαιην τε και Ουρανον αμφις εχυσιν. From Homer’s *Odyssey*.</note>

They also had long pillars, or obelisks, which referred to the sea, and upon which was illustrated the whole system of both heaven and earth; *amphis* <note>original Greek: αμφις</note>, meaning all around, both on the front of the obelisk and on the other sides. The Greeks, in their accounts, have made the history obscure by substituting a single person for an entire people—a history which would otherwise be very easy to understand.

...contained descriptions of both the heavens and the earth. From Phrygia, these records eventually reached Hellas <note>Ancient Greece.</note>, where they were introduced by Anaximander. He is said to have been the first to publish a geographical map <note>original Greek: Εκδουναι πρωτον γεωγραφικον πινακα</note>. Or, as Laertius expresses it, he produced a "delineation of the circumference of the land and sea" <note>original Greek: Γης και Θαλαττης περιμετρον</note>—essentially a map of the known world.

Although the origin of maps can be traced back to Egypt, they were not created by the native Egyptians. Instead, these types of drawings were the invention of the Cuthites, also known as the "Shepherds." <note>The author refers to the "Shepherd Kings" or Hyksos, whom he identifies as descendants of Cush (Cuthites).</note> They were known by several titles, including Saïtae, and they introduced both astronomy and geometry to those regions. With immense labor, they drained the lower provinces, built massive structures, and erected towers at the mouths of the Nile which were perfectly located for navigation. 

While the Mizraim <note>The descendants of Mizraim; a biblical term for the indigenous Egyptians.</note> were not typically devoted to commerce, trade was pursued by other families besides the Cuthites who lived in the lower provinces near the sea. The towers built there served as lighthouses and were simultaneously temples dedicated to various titles of the Deity, such as Canoph, Caneph, and Cneph, as well as Perses, Proteus, Phanes, and Canobus. Sailors frequently visited these sites to leave offerings, and the temples became repositories for geographical knowledge. Charts of the coast and records of Nile navigation were kept there—originally engraved on stone pillars and, in later times, sketched onto Nile papyrus. There is likewise reason to

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that the myths of Theseus and Ariadne were misinterpretations of much older historical records. # THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

...with Ariadne. If we are to believe Plutarch²⁷, Theseus, as soon as he had reached manhood, followed the advice of his mother Aethra and went from Troezen in search of his father Aegeus at Athens. This occurred some years after the Argonautic expedition, at a time when Medea had already left Jason and placed herself under the protection of this same Aegeus. After being acknowledged by his father, Theseus went on his expedition to Crete; it was there he is said to have first seen Ariadne and carried her away. All of this, I must point out, supposedly happened after Jason had married Medea and had children with her—and after she had left him and arrived in Athens.

However, the story of Ariadne described in the specimen mentioned previously is treated as a fact of a much older date. It happened prior to the arrival of Medea in Greece, and even before the Argonautic expedition. It is spoken of as a matter of the highest antiquity; consequently²⁸, Theseus could not have been involved in it in any way.

There is also an account in Nonnus <note>Nonnus of Panopolis (5th century AD): An Egyptian-Greek poet known for his epic poem the *Dionysiaca*.</note> of a robe or *Pharos* <note>original: Pharos. A recurring theme in this text is that "Pharos" could mean both a cloak and a lighthouse tower.</note>, which Harmonia is supposed to have worn when she was visited by the Goddess of Beauty <note>Aphrodite.</note>. Delineated upon this garment—just as in those mentioned before—were the earth, the heavens, and all the stars. The sea and the rivers were also represented, and the whole image was surrounded at the bottom by the ocean.

*...a copy and imitation of all the celestial appearances.* The entire collection was housed in a *Pharos* <note>original: Pharos. While commonly referring to a cloak or a lighthouse, the author argues here that it refers to a specific type of sacred tower or observatory.</note> on the seashore, upon which the rising sun cast its earliest rays, and whose turrets sparkled with the dew. This vast body of water surrounded the building like a belt and offered a magnificent sight. This, I believe, is the solution to the mystery.

# TAR, TOR, TARIT.

<margin>1 Bochart, *Sacred Geography*, Book 1, chapter 228, page 524, regarding *Tor* <note>original: תור</note>.</margin>
I have noted the fears and anxieties that the first navigators must have felt when they sailed across unknown seas and were at risk of becoming trapped among the rocks and sandbanks <note>original: shelves</note> of the deep. I also mentioned the methods they used to avoid such difficulties and to make the coast less dangerous. Upon every hill and promontory where they conducted trade or established a settlement, they built obelisks and towers, which they dedicated to some deity. These served a dual purpose: both as landmarks by day and as beacons by night. Since people in those times only made coasting voyages <note>trips following the shoreline</note>, they frequently went ashore with offerings to obtain the help of whatever god presided there. For these towers were temples, often richly furnished and endowed. They were sometimes built on artificial mounds, but usually on natural heights <note>original: eminences</note>, so that they might be seen from a great distance. They were called *Tar* and *Tor* by the Amonians <note>A group the author identifies as descendants of Ham (Amun), whom he credits with spreading early civilization and sun worship</note>, who first built them. This is the same as the *Tor* <note>original: תור</note> of the Chaldeans <note>original: Chaldees</note>, which signified both a
