As I often quote from Palæphatus, it may be proper to say something concerning him. He wrote early and seems to have been a serious and sensible person—one who saw the absurdity of the fables upon which the theology of his country was founded. The very meaning of his name signifies an "antiquarian" <note>The name Palæphatus literally means "one who speaks of ancient things."</note>, a person who dealt in researches into the remote past. While it is possible that this correspondence between his name and his writings occurred by chance, I think it is hardly probable. Since he wrote against the mythology of his country, I would imagine that *Palæphatus* was an assumed name, which he took as a disguise in order to shield himself from persecution; the nature of his writings made him liable to much ill will. One little treatise by <gloss>33</gloss> Palæphatus regarding Orion is quoted word-for-word by the commentator <term>Scholiast</term> <note>An ancient commentator or annotator of classical texts.</note> upon <gloss>34</gloss> Homer, who speaks of it as a quotation from Euphorion. I should therefore think that Euphorion was the true name of this writer; but as there were many learned men called by that name, it may be difficult to determine which one was the author of this treatise.

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument that mythological giants were originally physical structures like towers. Here, he examines the poetic descriptions of Homer and Pindar regarding the giants Otus and Ephialtes, suggesting they represent ruined edifices rather than living beings.</meta>

Homer's poetry, ever crafted from the strangest materials, is full of allegory and mysterious descriptions. He often introduces imaginary characters, basing his concepts on buildings, hills, and fountains—anything that carried an air of wonder and antiquity. He seems at times to blend two different aspects of the same thing—one borrowed and one real—to make the true history (if there is any truth at the root of it) seem even more extraordinary and entertaining.

I cannot help thinking that Otus and Ephialtes, those gigantic youths so celebrated by the poets, were actually two lofty towers. They were being built to *Alohim* <note>A Hebrew name for God, which Bryant believes was adapted by the Greeks</note>, called $^{35}$ Aloeus, but were probably toppled by an earthquake. They are described by the poet Pindar as the sons of Iphimedeia and are supposed to have been killed by Apollo on the island of Naxos.

<meta>This page continues the argument that the "giant" Orion was originally a reference to a lighthouse or temple tower. Specifically, it discusses the promontory of Pelorus in Sicily, which was named after Orion (under the name Alorus) and served as both a landmark and a place of worship.</meta>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

The promontory was called ^40 Pelorus because it was sacred to Alorus, who was the same as ^41 Orion. There was also a river named after him, which Lycophron calls ^42 Elorus. This tower is mentioned by the geographer Strabo, but more detailed information is provided by Diodorus Siculus. He informs us that, according to local tradition, Orion lived there; and that among other works, he raised this very mound and promontory, called Pelorus and Pelorias, along with the temple that was situated upon it. ^43 "Orion raised the mound at the promontory situated near Pelorias, and constructed the sanctuary of Poseidon, which was held in exceptional honor by the local inhabitants." <note>original Greek: Ωριωνα προσχωσαι το κατα την Πελοριαδα κειμενον ακρωτηριον, και το τεμενος το Ποσειδωνος κατασκευασαι, τιμωμενον ὑπο των εγχωριων διαφεροντως.</note> From this, we find that there was a tower of this sort which belonged to Orion. The word *Pelorion* was a term borrowed from these massive buildings and used metaphorically to describe anything stupendous and large. Homer’s description is of a mixed nature: in it, he retains the ancient tradition of a giant person, but he borrows his imagery from the towers sacred to him. I have noted before that in ancient times, all temples were supposed to be oracular; the Amonians called these temples *Pator* and *Patara*. This temple of Orion was undoubtedly a *Pator* <note>original: "Pator" — a term Bryant links to "interpreters" or "oracles," suggesting the towers were centers of religious prophecy.</note>.

For this reason, it was called *Tor Pator*; when the Greeks expressed this as *Tripator* <note>original Greek: τριπατωρ</note>, it gave rise to the idea that this earth-born giant had three fathers.

> ^44 "Orion, three-fathered, sprang from Mother Earth." <note>original Greek: Ωριων τριπατωρ απο μητερος ανθορϵ γαιης.</note>

These towers near the sea were used to predict the weather and to observe the heavens. Those belonging to cities were generally located in the Acropolis, or the higher part of the town. The Amonians called such a place *Bosrah* <note>original: "Bosrah" — a Semitic word for a fortress or citadel, famously used for the citadel of Carthage.</note>, and the citadel of Carthage, as well as those of other cities, is known to have been named this. However, the Greeks, by an unavoidable habit of misinterpretation, consistently turned this into *Bursa* <note>original Greek: βυρσα</note>, meaning "a skin" or "hide." 

When some of the Greeks later settled in Zancle ^46 in Sicily, they found that Orion was associated with *Ouran* or *Ouranus* (the sky/heaven). Based on the temple's name (*Tripator*), they concluded he must have had three fathers, and they immediately set to work to reconcile these different ideas. They accordingly changed *Ouran* to *ourein* <note>original Greek: ουρειν — a verb meaning "to urinate."</note>. Thinking the misinterpreted "hide" (*Bursa*) was a suitable vessel for their purpose, they made these three fathers cooperate in a most extraordinary way to produce this imaginary person, inventing—

<meta>This page continues Bryant’s argument that Greek myths often originated from the names of ancient physical structures. Here, he moves from the giant Orion to other figures like Tithonus, the Cyclopes, and Tethys, arguing they were originally names for lighthouses or hilltop fire-towers.</meta>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

Structures of this nature are often termed by Pausanias and Strabo as *mastoeideis* <note>original Greek: μαστοειδεις — "breast-shaped"</note> because of their resemblance to that shape. Tithonus, whose long life is so celebrated in myth, was actually nothing more than one of these structures—a lighthouse <note>original: "Pharos"</note> sacred to the sun, as his name clearly shows. *Tith-On* means "mount of the sun" <note>original Greek: μαστος ἡλιȢ — literally "breast of the sun."</note>. Because it acted as a substitute for that light-bearing star, he was said to have been beloved by Aurora (the Dawn), and through her favor to have lived for many ages. 

This is actually the opposite of the stories told about the Cyclopes, whose history also relates to physical buildings. They are said to have provoked Apollo's jealousy and were killed by his arrows; yet, at its core, the story has the same meaning. The Cyclopean towers upon the Sicilian shore faced due east, and their fires were necessarily eclipsed by the rays of the rising sun. This, I believe, is the true meaning behind Apollo "killing" the Cyclopes with his arrows <note>In mythology, Apollo’s arrows are often a metaphor for the rays of the sun.</note>. 

Tethys, the ancient goddess of the sea, was nothing more than an old tower on a mount; it was the same shape and built for the same purposes as the structures mentioned above. For this reason, it was called *Tith-Is*, meaning "mount of fire" <note>original Greek: μαστος πυρος — literally "breast of fire."</note>. Thetis seems to be a variation of the same name and was likely a lighthouse or fire-tower near the sea.

These mounds, or "breast-shaped hills" <note>original Greek: λοφοι μαστοειδεις</note>, were not only found in Greece;

<meta>This page continues Bryant’s discussion of ancient physical structures, specifically mounds and towers that were often misinterpreted in later mythology. He is moving from the discussion of "breast-shaped" hills (mastoeideis) to their practical use as fortresses and treasuries.</meta>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

These mounds were found not only in Greece, but in Egypt, Syria, and most parts of the world. They were generally constructed by hand, composed of earth raised very high and sloped gradually with great precision. The summit of each was crowned with a beautiful tower. The location of these buildings caused them to be regarded as places of great safety, and the religious reverence in which they were held added to their security. For these reasons, they served as repositories for much wealth and treasure; in times of danger, they were filled with valuable items. 

In Assyria, there was a temple named Azara, which the Parthians plundered; they are said to have carried off ten thousand talents <note>original Greek: Και ηρε ταλαντων μυριων γαζαν — "And he took away a treasure of ten thousand talents." Azara meant "treasure."</note>. The same author <note>Strabo, a Greek geographer.</note> mentions two towers of this kind of fortress in Judea, not far from Jericho, which belonged to Aristobulus and Alexander. They were called "Treasuries of the Tyrants" <note>original Greek: Γαζοφυλακια των Τυραννων — "Gazophylakia ton Tyrannon"</note> and were captured by Pompey the Great <note>original: Pompeius Magnus</note> during his war with the Jews. 

There were often two of these mounds of equal height within the same enclosure, such as those described by the historian Josephus at Machaerus, near some warm springs. He mentions a cavern and a rock there: "a cave... protected by being surrounded by the rock; and above it, two hills stand up like breasts, separated from each other by a small distance" <note>original Greek: σπηλαιον—τη πετρα περιεχεσθη σκεπομενον· ταυτης ανωθεν ωσανει μαζοι δυο ανεχουσιν, αλληλων ολιγω διεσωτες</note>. 

Solomon alludes to such structures when he has his beloved say, "I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers" <note>Song of Solomon (Canticles) 8:10.</note>. Although the Hebrew word *Chumah* <note>original Hebrew: חומה</note> or *Comah* is generally translated as "a wall," I believe that

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

In this context, it signified the ground which the wall surrounded: an enclosure sacred to Cham, the Sun, who was particularly worshipped in such places. The Egyptians <note>original: Mizraïm</note> called these hills Typhon, and the cities where they were built, Typhonian. But as they stood within enclosures sacred to Chom, they were also called Choma. This, I imagine, was the meaning of the term in this place, and in some others where the text alludes to a different nation and to a foreign mode of worship. In these temples the Sun was principally adored, and the rites of fire celebrated. This seems to have been the reason why the judgment pronounced against them is uniformly that they shall be destroyed by fire. If we suppose *Comah* to mean a mere wall, I do not see why fire should be so specifically directed against a part of a structure which is the least combustible. The Deity says:

<gloss>12</gloss> *I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus.*
<gloss>13</gloss> *I will send a fire on the wall of Gaza.*
<gloss>14</gloss> *I will send a fire on the wall of Tyre* <note>original: Tyrus</note>.
<gloss>15</gloss> *I will kindle a* <gloss>16</gloss> *fire in the wall of Rabbah.*

As the crime which brought down this curse was idolatry, and the term used in all these instances is *Chomah*, I believe it related to a temple of Chom and his high places, called by the Greeks "breast-shaped hills" <note>original Greek: λοφοι μασοειδεις — lophoi mastoeideis</note>. To these, the spouse of Solomon certainly alludes when she says, "I am a wall, and my breasts are like [towers]" <note>original Greek: εγω τειχος, και οἱ μασοι μο — ego teichos, kai hoi masoi mou. From Song of Solomon 8:10</note>.

These were hills topped with towers and must have been very beautiful to look at. Solomon takes notice of a hill-fortress of this kind upon ²⁰ *Lebanon, looking toward Damascus*, which he describes as a beautiful structure.

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

Such are the poetical depictions; but the history at its core relates to sacred towers, dedicated to the symbolic worship of the serpent, where there was a perpetual watch and a light ever burning. The Titans <note>original Greek: Τιτανες</note> were properly Titanians: a people so named from their worship and from the places where it was celebrated. They are, like Orion and the Cyclopians, represented as giants; and they were of the same race, the "children of Anak" <note>A biblical reference to a race of giants mentioned in the Old Testament.</note>. The Titanian temples were grand buildings, erected in Chaldea as well as in Lower Egypt upon mounds of earth—breast-shaped hills <note>original Greek: λοφοι μασοειδεις</note>—and were sacred to Hanes. *Titanis* and *Titanes* are compound words derived from *Tit-Hanes*; they literally signify the "breast of the sun" <note>original Greek: μασος ηλιου</note>, or the conical hill of Orus. Due to their location, these sites were strong and probably made defensible by other means.

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

...at the top between their heads was an eagle; and beneath it was a sacred carriage, called a Cemus.

> "There was a golden eagle, as if cutting through the wide air, standing upright between the heads of twin vipers, appearing on high with four wings on a four-yoked carriage <note>original: *κημῳ* (kemō), which Bryant links to "Cemus."</note>. Yellow jasper ran over it." <note>original Greek: Αιετος ην χρυσειος, ἀτε πλατυν ηερα τεμνων, Ορθος, εχιδναιων διδυμων μεσσηγυ καρηνων, Ὑψιφανης πτερύγων πισυρων τετραζυγι κημῳ. Τῃ μεν ξανθος ιασπις επετρεχε. From Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, Book 5, p. 148.</note>

The history of Tityus, Prometheus, and many other poetical characters was certainly derived from hieroglyphics that were misunderstood and poorly explained. Prometheus was worshiped by the Colchians <note>An ancient people living on the eastern coast of the Black Sea.</note> as a deity; he had a temple and a "high place" <note>A sacred site, usually on a hill or mountain, used for religious rituals.</note> called the Typhaonian Rock <note>original Greek: Πετρα Τυφαονια</note> upon Mount Caucasus. The emblem upon the entrance was Egyptian: an eagle over a heart. The immense size of these characters was derived from the vast extent of the temple enclosures. The words, "whose body is stretched over nine whole acres," <note>original Latin: *per tota novem cui jugera corpus porrigitur*. This refers to the giant Tityus in Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note> actually refer to a garden of that many acres. There were many such enclosures, as I have noted before; some of them were beautifully planted and decorated with pavilions and fountains, and were called *Paradisi* <note>Ancient Persian-style walled gardens or pleasure grounds; the root of the word "Paradise."</note>. One of this sort stood in Syria upon the river Typhon, later called the Orontes. Places of this nature are alluded to in the descriptions of the gardens of the Hesperides, the gardens of Alcinous, and the gardens of Adonis.

I have noted that the word *drakon* <note>original: δραϰων</note>, or *draco*, was a mistake for *Tarchon* (Ταρχων), which was sometimes expressed as *Trachon* (Τραχων); as is observable in the "Trachones" <note>Referring to the Trachonitis, a rugged region near Damascus; the name implies a rough or stony place.</note> at Damascus. For the *Draco* was an imaginary being, however it was afterwards accepted and understood. That the legends of these animals took their rise from the temples of the Syrians and Egyptians, and especially from the *Trachones* <note>original: Τραχωνες</note> at Damascus, seems highly probable from the accounts above. It may be rendered still more apparent from Damasenus, a supposed hero who took his name from the city Damasene, or Damascus. He is represented as an earthborn giant who encountered two dragons: "The immense son of the earth, the dragon-killing Damasenus." <note>original Greek: Και χθονος απλετον υια, δρακοντοφονον Δαμασηνα.</note> One of the monsters with which he fought is described as being of an enormous size—a "serpent in extent of fifty acres" <note>original Greek: πεντηκονταπελεθρος οφις</note>—which certainly, as I have before suggested, must refer to the grove and garden where such an Ophite <term>serpent-worshipping</term> temple stood at Damascus.

For the general measurement of all these wonderful beings by <gloss>43</gloss> *jugera* or acres proves that such an estimate could not relate to any thing of solid contents, but to an enclosure of that surface area. Of the same nature as these was the gigantic personage supposed to have been seen at Gades <note>modern Cádiz, Spain</note> by Cleon Magnesius. He made, it seems, no doubt that Tityus and other such monsters had existed; for while he was at Gades, he was ordered to go upon a certain expedition by Hercules. Upon his return to the island, he saw upon the shore a huge sea-man who had been struck by lightning and lay extended upon the ground:

-> "Here the Muses buried the Thracian Orpheus of the golden lyre," <-
-> "Whom Zeus, ruling on high, killed with a smoky bolt." <-
<note>original Greek: 45 Θρηϊ̈κα χρυσολολύρην τῆδ' Ὀρφέα Μοῦσαι ἔθαψαν, Ὅν κτανεν ὑψιμέδων Ζεὺς ψολόεντι βέλει. Diogenes Laertius, Prooemium, p. 5.</note>

All these histories relate to sacred enclosures, and to the worship of the serpent and the rites of fire that were practiced within them. Such an enclosure was styled by the Greeks a *temenos* <note>original: τέμενος</note>, and the mound or high place was called a *taphos* <note>original: τάφος</note> or *tumbos* <note>original: τύμβος</note>. These sites often had a tower upon them, which was esteemed as a sanctuary and a place of asylum. Lycophron has Cassandra say of Diomedes:

-> "The temple mound <note>original: ΤΥΜΒΟΣ</note> shall save him." <-
<note>original: ΤΥΜΒΟΣ δ' αὐτὸν ἐκσώσει. Lycophron, line 613. The literal translation is "the tomb shall save him," but the author argues it refers to a temple sanctuary.</note>

In the process of time, both the word *tumbos* and *taphos* were no longer understood in their original sense as "high places" or "sanctuaries," but were instead thought to mean only places of burial. This misunderstanding has turned many ancient temples into "tombs" in historical accounts; consequently, the deities to whom these temples were sacred have been incorrectly represented as being buried there. For example, there was an Orphic *Dracontium* <term>a temple dedicated to serpent worship</term> at Lesbos, where a serpent was...

<margin>48 Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 11, line 56.</margin>
> <margin>48</margin> "Here a wild, foreign snake attacks the head exposed on the sands, and the hair still dripping with dew. At last Apollo <note>original: Phoebus</note> appears; he blocks the creature as it prepares to bite and freezes the serpent’s open jaws into stone, hardening the wide, gaping mouth exactly as it was."
<note>original Latin: *Hic ferus expositum peregrinus anguis arenis / Os petit, et sparsos stillanti rore capillos. / Tandem Phoebus adest: morsusque inferre parantem / Arcet; et in lapidem rictus serpentis apertos / Congelat; et patulos, ut erant, indurat hiatus.*</note>

All the poetic accounts of heroes battling dragons have arisen from a misconception about these towers and temples. These heroes were actually the people who either founded those buildings or captured them in war. If the story is told about a deity, it means those buildings were erected in their honor. But the Greeks made no distinction. They were so fond of tales of heroism that they interpreted every ancient history according to their own prejudices; even in the simplest narrative, they managed to find a military achievement. No colony could settle anywhere and build an Ophite temple <note>original: Ophite; from the Greek 'ophis,' meaning serpent. These were temples dedicated to serpent worship</note> without the Greeks imagining a struggle between a hero and a dragon. As I have shown, Cadmus was described as being in conflict with such a creature near Thebes, whose teeth he sowed in the earth:

Serpents were reportedly a plague in Cyprus when the island was first settled, and a terrifying dragon was said to reside on the island of <gloss>51</gloss> Salamis. The Python of Parnassus is a well-known legend; it was said that Apollo killed this creature when he was very young, a story beautifully told by the poet Apollonius Rhodius:

-><gloss>52</gloss> "As once beneath the rocky ridge of Parnassus, he slew the giant Delphyne <note>Delphyne was another name for the dragon or serpent at Delphi</note> with his arrows, while he was yet a boy, still youthful, and still rejoicing in his long hair."<-
-><note>original Greek: Ως ποτε πετραιη ὑπο δειραδι Παρνησσοιο Δελφυνην τοξοισι πελωριον εξεναριξε, Κουρος εων, ετι γυμνος, ετι πλοκαμοισι γεγηθως.</note><-

Ultimately, this "dragon" was actually a serpent temple—a *tumbos* <note>original: *τυμβος* (tumbos), meaning a mound, barrow, or ceremonial earthwork</note> made of earth and considered in ancient times to be a place of prophecy. The author Hyginus confirms this: <gloss>53</gloss> "Python, the son of Earth, was a massive dragon. Before the time of Apollo, this creature used to give prophetic responses at the oracle on Mount Parnassus." <note>original Latin: *Python, Terræ filius, Draco ingens. Hic ante Apollinem ex oraculo in monte Parnasso responsa dare solitus est.*</note>

Plutarch also mentions that the conflict between Apollo and the Dragon was really a dispute over who had the right to control the site. <gloss>54</gloss> "The theologians of Delphi believe that a battle took place there between the God and a serpent over the ownership of the oracle." <note>original Greek: Οἱ Δελφων θεολογοι νομιζουσιν ενταυθα ποτε προς οφιν τῳ Θεῳ περι του χρηστηριου μαχην γενεσθαι.</note> From this, we can see that the serpent was actually the deity of the temple itself, even though the Greeks made a pointless distinction between the two. Furthermore, the serpent was worshiped with divine honors: <gloss>55</gloss> "In Pytho <note>another name for Delphi</note>, the Pythian Dragon is worshiped, and the festival of the Serpent is proclaimed as the Pythian games." <note>original Greek: Πυθοι μεν ουν ὁ Δρακων ὁ Πυθιος θρησκευεται, και του Οφεως ἡ πανηγυρις καταγγελλεται Πυθια.</note> It is said, moreover, that the seventh day was appointed—

We often read of virgins who were exposed to dragons and sea monsters, and of dragons that laid waste to whole provinces until they were finally encountered and slain by some person of great prowess. In those places specifically set apart for religious service, there was a fire that never went out.

<page-num>434</page-num>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

In the temple of Amon, there was an <gloss>59</gloss> unquenchable lamp <note>original Greek: *Lychnon asbeston*</note> continually burning. A similar practice was observed in other temples of the <gloss>60</gloss> Egyptians. Pausanias mentions the lamp of Minerva <note>Athena</note> <gloss>61</gloss> Polias at Athens, which never went out; the same custom was maintained in most of the <gloss>62</gloss> *Prytaneia* <note>The seat of government in ancient Greek cities, which housed the community's holy hearth</note>. The Chaldeans and Persians had sacred hearths on which they preserved a <gloss>63</gloss> perpetual fire. In the temple of <gloss>64</gloss> Apollo Carneus at Cyrene, the fire upon the altar was never allowed to be extinguished. A similar account is given by Said Ebn Batrick regarding the sacred fire that was preserved in the great temple at <gloss>65</gloss> Aderbain in Armenia. The Nubian Geographer mentions a nation in India, called <gloss>66</gloss> Caimachitae, who had large *Puratheia* <note>Fire-temples</note> and maintained a perpetual fire. According to the Levitical law, a constant fire was to be kept up upon the altar of God: <gloss>67</gloss> *The fire shall be ever burning upon the altar; it shall never go out.*

From what has preceded, we may perceive that many mythological personages have been formed out of descriptions of places. I cannot help suspecting that much more of ancient history is of this nature than I dare venture to acknowledge. I believe that almost every circumstance of the mythic age was either imported and adopted from other cultures, or else is a fable. I imagine that Chiron, who was so celebrated—

<page-num>439</page-num>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.

Memphis was located on the western side of the Nile. It was near the spot where most people of importance <note>original: "consequence"</note> were buried. There is a tower in this province called Kiroon $^{83}$ today, though it is located at some distance from the place being discussed here. Since *Charon* was a temple near the catacombs, or place of burial, an offering was made for every person brought there to be interred <note>original: "deposited"</note> upon their landing on that shore. From this practice arose the notion of "Charon’s fee" and the mythical ferryman of the same name. This building stood on the banks of a canal that connected with the Nile. However, the place now called *Kiroon* stands some distance to the west, near Lake $^{84}$ *Moeris*, where only the kings of Egypt had the right of burial <note>term: sepulture</note>. The region of the catacombs was called the Acheronian and $^{85}$ Acherusian plain, as well as the Elysian plain; the stream that ran by it was called the *Acheron*. These places are often alluded to by *Homer* and other poets when they describe the realm of departed souls. The *Amonians* <note>The author's term for an ancient race he believes spread Egyptian religion and culture across the world.</note> gave these names to other places where they settled in various parts of the world. They are, therefore, found in $^{86}$ Phrygia, $^{87}$ Epirus, $^{88}$ Hellas, and $^{89}$ Apulia <note>original: "Apu-" followed by the catchword "lia,"</note>.

The entire history of *Castor* and *Pollux*, the two *Dioscuri* <note>The "sons of Zeus," typically the twins Castor and Polydeuces</note>, is very strange and inconsistent. ...trusted as places of great security. The temple of Castor was particularly famous for this reason, as we may learn from the Roman poet Juvenal:

> ⁹⁷ Much wealth in a bronze-bound chest, and money to be deposited at the temple of watchful Castor. <note>original Latin: *Æratâ multus in arcâ / Fiscus, et ad vigilem ponendi Castora nummi*</note>

The deity who was referred to under the name of Castor was actually the Sun. He had several temples of that name in Laconia <note>A region in the southern Peloponnese, Greece, where Sparta was located</note> and other parts of Greece. His religious rites were first introduced by people from Egypt and Canaan. We may infer this, among other circumstances, from the title of *Anac* <term>Anac: a Canaanite title of honor or royalty; the author links it to the Anakim of the Bible</term> being so specifically granted to him and his brother Pollux. Consequently, their temple was called the *Anakeion* <note>original Greek: *Ανακειον*</note> in Laconia, and their festival at Athens was called the *Anakeia* <note>original Greek: *ανακεια*</note>. *Anac* was a Canaanite term of honor, which the Greeks adapted into *Anax* <note>original Greek: *αναξ*; meaning king or lord</note> and *Anakes* <note>original Greek: *ανακτες*; the plural form</note>.

I have mentioned previously that the archives of the cities and provinces where these temples stood were preserved <note>original OCR: "preferred," likely a transcription error for "preserved" based on the context of archives</note> within them. They were also frequently used as courts of law, called *prytaneia* <note>original Greek: *πρυτανεια*; public buildings where the city's "eternal flame" was kept and government business was conducted</note> and *praetoria* <note>original Latin: *prætoria*; the headquarters of a magistrate or judicial space</note>, where the ancient local residents gathered to resolve legal disputes. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Castor and Pollux, moving from the physical security of their temples to their symbolic roles as judges and supervisors of law, which the author argues were originally attributes of the Sun deity.</meta>

<page-num>443</page-num>

-> # THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. <-

Their traditional depictions agree with the general and absurd character under which they are represented: for what does horsemanship and boxing have to do with law and equity? However, these were mistaken attributes which arose from a misapplication of history. Within the precincts of their temples was a parade ground for boxing and wrestling, and often a *Hippodromus* <term>Hippodromus: an ancient Greek stadium designed for horse racing and chariot racing</term>. From this, those attributes arose by which the poets celebrated these figures:

> ⁹⁹ Castor the horse-tamer, and Pollux the brave boxer. <note>original Greek: Καστορα θ᾽ Ιπποδαμον, και πυξ αγαθον Πολυδευκεα</note>

The deity originally referred to was the Sun. As he was the chief deity, he must necessarily have been esteemed the supervisor and arbitrator of all earthly things:

> ¹⁰⁰ The Sun, who sees all and hears all. <note>original Greek: Ηελιος, ος παντ᾽ εφορᾳ, και παντ᾽ επακουει</note>

On this account, the same role of supreme judge was conferred on his substitute Castor, in conjunction with his brother Pollux. They were accordingly looked upon as the protectors of the rights of mankind. Cicero makes a noble appeal to them in his seventh oration against Verres <note>Gaius Verres was a Roman magistrate notorious for his corruption and misgovernment of Sicily</note>, and enlarges upon the great department of which they were presumed to be in charge, at the same time mentioning the treasures which were deposited in their temples:

# TAPH, TUPH, TAPHOS.

There was another name used by the Amonians <term>Amonians: A term used by the author to refer to the descendants of Ham (Ammon), specifically the ancient Egyptians and related peoples who worshiped the sun.</term> to describe their mounds or hills <note>original Greek: $\lambda o \phi o \iota$ (lophoi)</note>, or high places. This was *Taph*, which at times was written as *Tuph*, *Toph*, and *Taphos*. 

Because Lower Egypt is a flat plain and is flooded annually, the natives were forced to raise the soil on which they built their principal buildings in order to secure them from the flood. Many of their sacred towers were erected upon conical mounds of earth. However, there were often hills of the same form constructed for religious purposes upon which there was no building. These were very common in Egypt. This is why we read of *Taphanis*, or *Taph-Hanes*, *Taph-Osiris*, *Little Taph-Osiris* <note>original Latin: *Taph-Osiris parva*</note>, and *Opposite Taphias* <note>original Latin: *contra Taphias*</note>, in the writings of Antoninus <note>The *Antonine Itinerary*, an ancient register of Roman roads and stations</note>; all belonging to this country. 

In other parts of the world were *Taphiousa*, *Tape*, *Taphura*, *Tapori*, *Taphus*, *Taphofus*, and *Taphitis*. All these names relate to high altars, upon which they used to frequently offer human sacrifices. *Typhon* was one of these, being a compound of *Tuph-On*, which signifies "the hill" or "altar of the Sun." *Tophet*—where the Israelites made their children pass through fire to Moloch <note>See 2 Kings 23:10 and 2 Chronicles 28:3</note>—was a mound of this form. And there seem to have been...

[Whatever] their original name was, they were further named after some title of the deity in whose honor they were built. However, because it was common in ancient times to bury important people under heaps of earth formed in this fashion, these *Tapha* came to mean "tombs." Consequently, almost all the sacred mounds raised for religious purposes were eventually looked upon as monuments to deceased heroes.

Hence, *Taph-Osiris* was translated as *taphos* <note>original Greek: ταφὸς</note>, or the burial place of the God Osiris. As there were many such places in Egypt and Arabia sacred to Osiris and Dionysus <note>original: Dionusus</note>, the Greeks believed they were all places of sepulture <term>sepulture: burial or interment</term>. Through this mistake, many different nations were wrongly credited with having these deities interred in their country. 

The *tumulus* <term>tumulus: an ancient burial mound or low hill</term> of the Latins was misunderstood in the same manner. Originally, it was a sacred hillock and was often raised before temples to serve as an altar, such as those I have described previously. It is represented in this light by Virgil:

> There is a mound as you leave the city, and an ancient temple 
> of abandoned Ceres; and nearby stands an ancient cypress tree. 
> <note>original Latin: *Est urbe egressis tumulus, templumque vetustum Desertæ Cereris; juxtaque antiqua cupressus.* Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 2, line 713.</note>

In the course of time, the word *tumulus* was largely regarded as a tomb, and *tumulo* came to mean "to bury." -> "The Cretans are always liars; for they even built a tomb for you, O King. But you did not die, for you live forever." <note>original Greek: Κρητες αει ψευσται· και γαρ ταφον, ω Ανα, σειο Κρητες ετεκτηναντο, συ δ᾽ ου θανες, εσσι γαρ αιει. Callimachus, *Hymn to Jove*, v. 8.</note> <-

I have no doubt that there was some high place in Crete which the later Greeks—especially those who were not from that country—mistook for a tomb. However, it certainly must have been regarded differently by those who originally built it. It is not believable, no matter how blind idolatry might be, that people would enshrine individuals as immortal gods in the very places where they had the clearest evidence of their death. An inscription dedicated "To the immortal man" <note>original Latin: *Viro immortali*</note> would have been a style of flattery far too sophisticated for the simplicity of those early ages. 

If divine honors were granted to men, they were the result of time and paid from a distance, not offered on the spot at the entrance of a burial vault <term>charnel-house: a vault or building where human skeletal remains are stored</term>. Furthermore, it is evident that most of these deified figures never actually existed but were merely different titles for the supreme Deity, the Sun, as has been largely proven by the Roman author Macrobius. Nothing has been more damaging to ancient history than the assumption that the gods of the pagan <note>original: Gentile</note> world were originally natives of the countries where they were worshiped. By this mistake, they have been wrongly included in historical chronologies, and the primary focus of scholars has been to record the legends concerning them and to try to reconcile their many contradictions,

->THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY.<-

...and to arrange the entire collection into a chronological series. This is a fruitless and inexplicable labor, for there are in all these fables such inconsistencies and contradictions that no skill or hard work can remedy them. Therefore, everyone who has applied their scholarship to this purpose ends up in opposition to one another and is often at odds with their own arguments. By these means, some have turned their works—which might have been of immense use to the world—into something little better than the daydreams of Monsieur Voltaire. 

Most of Greek theology arose from misconceptions and blunders, and the stories concerning their gods and heroes were based on terms that were misinterpreted and misused. For example, from the word *taphos* <note>original Greek: ταφος; usually meaning a tomb or burial place</note>, which they adopted in a very narrow sense, they formed the notion that their gods had been buried in every place where there was a mound <term>tumulus: an ancient burial mound</term> built in their honor. This error misled Bishop Cumberland, Usher, Pearson, Petavius, and Scaliger, along with countless other learned men—and most notably, the great Isaac Newton. 

This extraordinary genius significantly weakened the excellent system he was developing by admitting these imaginary beings into historical chronology. We are so saturated in our childhood with notions of Mars, Hercules, and the rest of those celestial outcasts that we can hardly ever set them aside. We essentially argue based on pagan principles; and though we cannot believe the fables that have been passed down to us, we constantly forget ourselves and draw conclusions from them as if they were real. In short, until we regain our perspective, we are "semi-pagans." It is painful to see men of learning and character debating which "Jupiter" it was who slept with Semele, and whether it was the same one who...

...and many other learned men, supposed the gods of the heathens to have been deified mortals who were worshiped in the countries where they died. This was the opinion of Clement, Eusebius, Cyril, Tertullian, Athenagoras, Epiphanius, Lactantius, Arnobius, Julius Firmicus, and many others <note>These are "Church Fathers," early Christian theologians and writers who shaped Christian doctrine.</note>. What is more to the point, it was the opinion of the heathens themselves—the very people by whom these gods were honored. Yet, it is still a mistake. 

Regarding the Church Fathers, their entire argument relies on the "concessions of the Gentiles" <term>meaning: the admissions or points granted by the non-Christian pagans</term>. These early writers of the church were not conducting a strict chronological or historical inquiry; instead, they were working to convert the pagans. Therefore, they argued with them based on the pagans' own principles and refuted them using their own testimony. 

The Romans had their *Immortal Gods* <note>original Latin: Dii Immortales</note> and the Greeks their *Immortal Gods* <note>original Greek: Θεοι Αθανατοι</note>, yet both acknowledged that these beings had once been men, and that they had died and been buried. Cicero admits that "the deaths and burials of the gods are demonstrated by Euhemerus" <note>original Latin: ab Euhemero et mortes, et sepulturæ demonstrantur deorum. Euhemerus was a Greek mythographer who argued that gods were originally great kings or heroes.</note>. It does not matter whether this notion was actually true; the Church Fathers very fairly made use of it. They took advantage of these admissions to prove the absurdity of pagan worship and the inconsistency of their beliefs. Even Maximus Tyrius, the Platonic philosopher, could not help but smile at being shown a temple and a tomb for the same deity in the same place ¹⁴—"a temple of a God and a tomb of a God" <note>original Greek: ἱερον Θεου, και ταφον Θεου</note>. These supposed places of burial <term>original: sepulture</term> were so numerous that Clement of Alexandria tells us they were beyond counting.

He points out the logical contradiction of "immortal gods" having well-known tombs and burial sites.</summary>

"But if I were to go through all the tombs you worship, even all of time would not be enough for me." <note>original Greek: Αλλα γαρ επιόντι μοι τους προσκυνουμενους ὑμιν ταφους, εμοι μεν ουδ’ ὁ πας αν αρκεση χρονος.</note> But after all, these *Taphoi* <note>original: Ταφοι; tombs</note> were not tombs, but conical mounds of earth <note>original Greek: λοφοι μασοειδεις (lophoi masoeideis)</note> upon which, in the earliest ages, offerings were made by fire. For this reason, the word *tupho* <note>original Greek: τυφω</note> signified making a smoke, such as arose from incense upon these *Tupha*, or high places. 

Furthermore, if these were deified men who were buried under these hills, how can we explain the problem of the same person being buried in different places and at different times? To this, it is answered that it was a *different* Bacchus or a *different* Jupiter. Yet this only adds to the difficulty, for it is hard to believe that anyone in any country who happened to have the name "Jupiter" would be made a god. 

Additionally, Homer and Hesiod, as well as the authors of the Orphic poetry, knew of no such duplicates. There is no hint of this kind among the ancient writers of their nation. It was a refinement of later ages, introduced to resolve the difficulties that arose from the absurdities in the pagan system. Arnobius <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 300 AD) known for his work *Against the Heathens*.</note> rightly ridicules the useless excuses made to make a shameful theology seem plausible. Gods of the same name and character were multiplied to make their myths consistent, so that there might always be one ready at hand for any chronological emergency. Consequently, no difficulty could arise concerning a deity without one being produced that was adapted to every climate and every age.

Because of this, it is absolutely necessary for those who believe these figures were real men (and who draw conclusions from their life stories) to state explicitly which one they mean and to give good reasons for their choice.

If he were a different person, the circumstances of his life should be different. But the person of whom he treats is in all respects similar to the Jupiter of Greece and Rome. He has a father, Saturn, and his mother was Rhea. He was nursed in Crete and had wars with the Titans. He dethrones his father, who flees to Italy, where he introduces a Golden Age <note>original: "Age of Gold"</note>. We find the mythology concerning him to be uniform in all respects. It is, therefore, to little purpose to substitute another person of the same name as a way of reconciling these matters, unless we can suppose that every person so named had the same relations and connections, and that the same occurrences in life were repeated—which is impossible. 

It is therefore, I think, plain that the Grecian deities were not the persons they were supposed to be, and that their assigned names <note>original: "imputed names"</note> were titles. A history similar to that of Opheltes is given of Archemorus, who was said to have been left in a garden by his nurse, Hypsipyle, and killed by a serpent while she was away. In many of these places, there was an ancient tradition of some person having been injured by a serpent in the beginning of life, which they have represented as the state of childhood. The mythology on this occasion varies: sometimes the figures described are killed by the serpent; at other times they kill it; and there are instances where both stories are told about the same person. But whatever the outcome, the history is generally made to refer to a state of childhood. ## SERPENT WORSHIP <note>original: "OPHIOLATRIA"</note>

> Among all those you consider gods, the serpent is recorded as a great symbol and mystery. <note>original Greek: Παρὰ παντὶ τῶν νομιζομένων παρ’ ὑμῖν Θεῶν Ὄφις σύμβολον μέγα καὶ μυστήριον ἀναγράφεται. Justin Martyr, *First Apology*, Book 1, page 60.</note>

It may seem extraordinary that the worship of the serpent should have ever been introduced into the world; and it must appear still more remarkable that it should have prevailed almost universally. Since mankind is said to have been ruined through the influence of this Being, we could hardly expect that it would, above all other objects, have been adopted as the most sacred and beneficial <note>original: "salutary"</note> symbol, and rendered the primary object of ¹ adoration. Yet, we find that this was indeed the case. In most of the ancient rites, there is some al-

¹ "Serpents—are worshipped intensely." <note>original Greek: Ὄφεις—τιμᾶσθαι ἰσχυρῶς. Philarchus as quoted in Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals*, Book 17, Chapter 5.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the historical study of "Ophiolatria" (serpent worship), noting the paradox that the serpent—traditionally blamed for humanity's downfall—was universally revered as a sacred symbol in ancient religions.</summary>

They were often crowned with ³ serpents and continued to make the same frantic exclamation. One part of the mystery rites of Jupiter Sabazius <note>A Phrygian horseman and sky god who was later equated with Dionysus or Zeus</note> involved letting a snake slip down the chest <note>original: "bosom"</note> of the person being initiated, which was then removed from below ⁴. These ceremonies and this symbolic worship began among the Magi, who were the sons of Cush <note>original: "Chus"</note>: and through them, these practices were spread to various regions.

Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century church father known for his works against heresy</note> believes that the invocation "Eva, Eva" referred to the great ⁵ mother of mankind, who was deceived by the serpent; and Clement of Alexandria is of the same opinion. He supposes that by this term was meant ⁶ "that Eve, through whom the deception followed" <note>original Greek: Ευαν εκεινην, δι' ην η πλανη παρηκολούθησε</note>. But I would suggest that "Eva" was the same as *Eph*, *Epha*, or *Opha*, which the Greeks rendered as *Ophis* <note>original Greek: Οφις</note>, and by it denoted a serpent. Clement acknowledges that the term *Eva*, when properly aspirated <note>pronounced with an 'h' sound at the beginning</note>, had such a meaning. ⁷ "The name 'Evia,' when aspirated, is interpreted as..."

**Serpent.** <note>original Greek: Οφις (Ophis)</note> Olympias, the mother of ^8 Alexander, was very fond of these sacred rites <note>original: "Orgies," referring here to the secret religious ceremonies of Dionysus</note>, in which the serpent was introduced. Sacred mounds, or *Tapha* <note>original: *Tapha*; these refer to ancient burial mounds or shrines</note>, were named this way after the serpent Deity to whom they were dedicated.

Sanchoniathon <note>A semi-legendary Phoenician author</note> mentions a history that he once wrote about the worship of the serpent. The title of this work, according to Eusebius, was *Ethothion* or *Ethothia*. Another treatise on the same subject was written by Pherecydes of Syros, which was probably a copy of the former; for he is said to have composed it <note>original: *παρὰ Φοινίκων λαβὼν τὰς ἀφορμάς*</note> *taking his starting points from the Phoenicians*. The title of his book was the *Theology of Ophion*, who was called Ophioneus; and of his worshipers, called Ophionidae. Thoth and Athoth were certainly titles of the Deity in the pagan <note>original: "Gentile"</note> world, and the book of Sanchoniathon might very possibly have been named *Athothion* for this reason. But from the subject it covers, as well as from the treatise of Pherecydes, I would suggest that *Athothion* or *Ethothion* was a mistake for *Ath-ophion*, a title more directly related to the worship the writer was discussing.

*Ath* was a sacred title, as I have shown. I imagine that this dissertation did not merely relate to the serpentine Deity, but also contained accounts of his followers, the Ophites <note>serpent-worshipers</note>, the most important of whom were the sons of Cush <note>original: Chus</note>. The worship of the serpent began among them, and they were consequently named Ethiopians and Aithiopians, which the Greeks rendered *Aithiopes* <note>original: Αἰθίοπες</note>. Their complexions were probably of a darker hue <note>original: "deeper die"</note>, but they were called this after Ath-Ope and Ath-Opis, the God they worshiped. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the migration of the Cuthite people, specifically focusing on the Hivites or Ophites (serpent-worshippers) and how their presence influenced the names and legends of various Greek islands and regions.</meta>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 481

They were Hivites or Ophites <note>The Hivites were a biblical people, here identified by Bryant with the "Ophites" or serpent-worshippers, from the Greek "ophis" meaning serpent</note>, and as a result, the island was named Ophiusa in ancient times. There was also a tradition that it had once swarmed with ³⁴ serpents. A similar notion prevailed almost everywhere they settled. They arrived under more general titles such as the Leleges and Pelasgi <note>Ancient groups of people who inhabited the Aegean region before the Greeks</note>, but more specifically as Elopians, Europians, Oropians, Asopians, Inopians, Ophionians, and Ethiopians. This is evident from the names they left behind; in most places where they resided, traditions were handed down that alluded to their original title of Ophites. In Phrygia and on the Hellespont <note>The narrow strait in northwestern Turkey</note>, where they sent out colonies very early, there was a people called *Ophiogeneis*, or "the serpent-breed," who were said to retain a kinship and connection with ³⁵ serpents. A belief also prevailed that some hero who had led them was transformed from a serpent into a man. In Colchis <note>An ancient kingdom on the Black Sea coast</note>, there was a river named Ophis; there was another of the same name in Arcadia. It was named after a group of people who settled on its banks and were said to have been led by a serpent: ³⁶ *the leader became a serpent* <note>original: Τον ηγεμονα γενεσθαι δρακοντα</note>. # THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 482

Strabo <note>original: L. 3. c. 96 (likely Thucydides) and L. 10. p. 692</note> mentions a people of Aetolia called ³⁸ **Ophionians**; and the temple of Apollo at Patara in Lycia seems to have had its first establishment by a priestess of the same ³⁹ name. The island of Cyprus was called *Ophiusa* and *Ophiodes* because of the serpents with which it was supposed to have ⁴⁰ abounded. The specific species of these serpents is nowhere mentioned, except that near Paphos, there was said to have been a ⁴¹ kind of serpent with two legs. By this, the author means the **Ophite race**, who came from Egypt and Syria and gained a foothold on this ⁴² island. 

They also settled in Crete, where their numbers increased greatly. Because of this, the King Minos was said, through a crude allegory, ⁴³ **to have vomited serpents** <note>original: οφεις εμησαι (opheis emesai)</note>. The island of Seriphus was one vast rock, called by the Romans the ⁴⁴ *Seriphian stone*; it was used as a large-scale prison for banished people. It is described as having once been full of serpents, and it is styled by Virgil as *serpentifer* (serpent-bearing), a passage which was accurately corrected by the scholar Scaliger:

They had been from two different communities. Eustathius likewise tries to solve the problem using nearly the same principles, and with similar success. Some had mentioned of Cecrops that he underwent a metamorphosis <sup>54</sup> <note>original: απο οφεως εις ανθρωπον ελθειν</note>, meaning *he was changed from a serpent to a man.* According to Eustathius, this signified that Cecrops, by coming into Greece <note>original: Hellas</note>, divested himself of all the rudeness and barbarity of <sup>55</sup> his native country and became more civilized and humane. This is too high a compliment to pay to Greece in its infant state, and it greatly detracts from the character of the Egyptians. The learned Marsham, therefore, observes <note>original: animadverts</note> with great justice: <sup>56</sup> *It is more likely that he brought more civilized customs from Egypt into Greece* <note>original: Est verisimilius illum ex Ægypto mores magis civiles in Græciam induxisse</note>. It is more probable that he introduced the urbanity of his own country into Greece than that he was indebted to Greece for anything from there. 

Regarding the mixed character of this personage <note>Cecrops was traditionally depicted as having the upper body of a man and the tail of a serpent.</note>, I think we may easily account for it. Cecrops was certainly a title of the deity who was worshiped under this <sup>57</sup> emblem. Something of a similar nature was mentioned regarding Triptolemus and <sup>58</sup> Erichthonius, and the same has been said above concerning Hercules. The natives of Thebes in Boeotia, like the Athenians mentioned above, considered themselves to be of the serpent race. The Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> likewise traced their origins back to the same source.

They were certainly Hivites <note>an ancient people often associated by early scholars with the Hebrew word for serpent, "hiwwa"</note> from Egypt, and the same story is told of that country. Egypt is represented as having been overrun with serpents in ancient times and almost depopulated because of their numbers. Diodorus Siculus seems to understand this $^{62}$ literally; however, a region that was annually flooded—and for such a long season—could not easily be liable to such a calamity. They were "serpents" of another nature with which the land was infested: the history actually relates to the Cuthites, the original Ophites <note>original: Ophitæ; from the Greek "ophis," meaning serpent. # THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 486

The migration continued from Egypt to Syria and reached the Euphrates. Accounts mention a specific breed of serpents found along that river which were harmless to the locals but deadly to everyone else $^{63}$. This, I believe, cannot be taken literally. The "wisdom of the serpent" may be great, but it is not enough to make such fine distinctions between people. These serpents were of the same nature as the $^{64}$ birds of Diomedes <note>Legendary birds said to be friendly to Greeks but hostile to foreigners</note> or the dogs in the temple of Vulcan. These histories actually refer to Ophite <note>original: Ophite; from the Greek "ophis," meaning serpent</note> priests, who were known to spare their own people but sacrifice strangers—a custom that prevailed at one time in most parts of the world. I have previously mentioned that the Cuthite <note>The "Cuthites" are identified by the author as the descendants of Cush, whom he believes were the architects of ancient civilization and religion</note> priests were highly learned. Since they were Ophites, anyone who had the benefit of their knowledge was said to have been "instructed by serpents." This is the origin of the tradition that Melampus <note>A legendary healer and prophet</note> gained his prophetic powers through communication with these $^{65}$ animals. A similar story is told about the prophet Tiresias.

As serpent worship was so widespread in antiquity, many places and peoples were named after it. Those who settled in Campania <note>a region in southern Italy</note> were called Opici, which some writers would change to *Ophici* because they were named after serpents. $^{66}$ "And they say that they were called Ophici, because of the serpents" <note>original: ῾Οι δε (φασι) ὁτι Οφικοι, απο των οφιων</note>. In reality, both names have the same meaning and reveal the origin of the people. We find many places with similar names, such as Opis, Ophis, Ophitea, Ophionia, Ophioessa, Ophiodes, and Ophiusa. This last name was an ancient title by which—according to...

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 487

According to Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary</note>, the islands of Rhodes, Cythnus, Besbicus, Tenos, and the entire continent of Africa were distinguished [by names related to serpents]. There were also cities named in this way. In addition to these, there were places named Oboth, Obona, and—in reverse—Onoba; these names were derived from *Ob*, which had the same meaning <note>original: "of the same purport"; referring to a serpent</note>. Clement of Alexandria says that the term *Eva* signified a serpent. <gloss>67</gloss> Epiphanius says the same, and we find that there were several places with this name. There was a city called Eva in <gloss>68</gloss> Arcadia, and another in <gloss>69</gloss> Macedonia. There was also a mountain named Eva or Evan mentioned by <gloss>70</gloss> Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note>, located between Ithome and the city of Messene. He also mentions an Eva in Argolis, describing it as a large <gloss>71</gloss> town. 

Another name for a serpent, which I have not yet mentioned, was *Patan* or *Pitan*. Many places in various regions were named using this term. These included a city in <gloss>72</gloss> Laconia and another in <gloss>73</gloss> Mysia, which Stephanus identifies as a city of Aeolia. These places were undoubtedly named after the worship of the serpent *Pitan*. They likely contained *Dracontia* <note>Ancient monuments or temples dedicated to serpent worship, often featuring large stones</note>, which featured figures and symbols related to the prevailing religion. Ovid mentions this latter city and alludes to its ancient history when he describes Medea flying through the air from Attica to Colchis.

The Greeks have so confused the Cyclopian Deity with his followers that it is difficult to speak precisely of either. They sometimes mention him as a single person, the same as Nilus of Egypt, who was esteemed the father of the Gods. The Cyclopian Deity was $^{18}$ Ouranus <note>Heaven personified</note>, and the Cyclopes were his priests and followers, some of whom had divine honors paid to them and were esteemed as Gods. People of this family settled upon the southern coast of Sicily at Camarina; which some have supposed to have been the Hypereia <note>original: Hupereia</note> of Homer, where the Phaeacians <note>original: Pheacians</note> once resided.

> <note>original Greek: Οι πριν μεν ποτ' εναιον εν ευρυχορω Ὑπερεια, Αγχυ Κυκλωπων ανδρων ὑπερηνορεοντων. Odyssey, Book 6, line 5.</note>

But there is no reason to think that the city of Hypereia was in Sicily, or that the Phaeacians came from that country. The notion arose from a common mistake. All the Greek and Roman poets—and even Strabo with other respectable writers—have taken it for granted that the Cyclopes of Homer were near Mount Etna in Sicily. Others object to their being near Etna and insist that they were in the vicinity of Eryx <note>A mountain and city in western Sicily</note> upon the opposite part of the island. But Homer does not once mention the island during his whole account of the Cyclopes; nor does Ulysses arrive in Sicily until after many subsequent adventures. That there were Cyclopes near Etna is certain; but those mentioned by Homer were of another country and are represented as natives of the continent, though his account is very indeterminate and obscure. There were probably people of this family in many parts of Sicily, especially about the city of Camarina. They seem to have been of the Anakim <note>A biblical race of giants often associated with the early inhabitants of Canaan</note> race and worshipers of the Sun. Camarina, which was named after a city of the same name in $^{21}$ Chaldea—the "Ur" mentioned in the Scriptures. Polyphemus is described as a musician and a shepherd, but one with a savage and brutal nature. This characterization arose from the cruel rituals practiced by the Cyclopians. According to $^{22}$ Bacchylides, it was said that Galatus, Illyrius, and Celtus were the sons of Polyphemus. By this, the author certainly meant that the Galatians, Illyrians, and Celts were of Cyclopian origin and belonged to the Anakim <note>a biblical race of giants</note> race; they were all equally Amonians <note>descendants of Ham or Ammon</note>. Lycophron mentions the cave of this personage, by which he meant an ancient temple, and he calls it $^{23}$ "the house of the one-eyed Charon" <note>original Greek: μονογληνα ςεγας Χαρωνος</note>. But here, as I have often observed, the place is mistaken for a person—the temple for the deity. Charon was actually the place itself: the ancient temple of the Sun. It was therefore called *Char-On* after the God who was worshiped there, and according to Egyptian custom, an eye was engraved over its entrance. These temples were sometimes called Charis <note>original Greek: Χαρις</note>, which is a compound of *Char-Is* and signifies a *prytaneum* <note>a public building housing a sacred communal hearth</note>, or a place sacred to Hephaestus <note>the Greek god of fire</note>. Since fire rituals were once practiced almost everywhere, there were many places with this name,

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the etymology and geographical distribution of the name "Charis," arguing that the mythological "one-eyed" monsters like the Cyclopes and Arimaspians were actually misinterpretations of architectural features (towers with fire-beacons).</meta>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 499

Especially in $^{25}$ Parthia, Babylonia, and Phrygia. The Greeks translated *Char-Is* as *Charis* <note>original Greek: Χαρις</note>, a term in their own language that signified grace and elegance. Nothing demonstrates their attachment to ancient terms more than their constant use of them, even though they were unaware of their true meaning. The Arimaspians were Hyperborean <note>from the far north</note> Cyclopes; they had temples named Charis or Charisia, at the top of which a perpetual fire was maintained. They belonged to the same family as the Cyclopes of $^{26}$ Sicily and shared the same rituals, particularly the worship of the Ophite <note>serpent-worshiping</note> deity under the name of $^{27}$ Opis. Aristeas of Proconnesus wrote their history and, among other things, mentioned that they had only one eye, which was positioned in their "graceful forehead."

> $^{28}$ "Each has a single eye in his graceful forehead." <note>original Greek: Οφθαλμον δ' ἐν' ἕκατος ἔχει χαρίεντι μετώπῳ</note>

How could the forehead of a Cyclops—one of the most hideous monsters ever created by poetic imagination—be described as graceful? The entire account is based on a misunderstanding of terms. What this writer misapplied actually referred to *Charis*, which was a tower; the "eye" was simply a window or opening in the top of the building where a light and fire were kept burning. This mistake was further confirmed by the—

<meta>This page continues the argument that mythological beings often originated from misunderstood names of ancient towers or temples. Specifically, it transitions from discussing the Cyclopes to explaining the origins of the Graces as being rooted in solar worship and architecture.</meta>

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 501

The Graces were said to be related to the Sun, who was in reality the same as Vulcan <note>the Roman god of fire</note>. Among the people of the East, the Sun was called *Hares*, or with a guttural sound, *Chares*. His temple was styled *Tor-Chares* <note>Tower of the Sun</note>. Just as the name *Tor-Pator* <note>Tower of the Father</note> was changed to *Tripator* <note>Three Fathers</note>, so *Tor-Chares* was transformed into *Trichares*. The Greeks expressed this as *Tricharis* <note>original: Τριχαρις</note>, and from that name they developed the idea of there being three Graces. 

Cicero says that the Graces were the daughters of Night and Erebus <note>the personification of darkness</note>. However, Antimachus—in a way more consistent with this etymology—maintained that they were the offspring of the Sun and Light: "Daughters of Aegle and Helios" <note>original: Αιγλης και Ηλιου θυγατερας</note>.$^{33}$ These seeming contradictions are not difficult to reconcile.

The Amonians <note>descendants of Ham, often associated by Bryant with ancient Egyptian and solar-worshipping peoples</note>, wherever they settled, were celebrated for their superiority in science and particularly for their skill in building. Trophonius and his brother Agamedes belonged to this group and were represented as masters of their profession. According to Pausanias,$^{34}$ they were truly wonderful for the temples they erected to the gods and for the stately buildings they constructed for men. They were the architects who designed the temple of Apollo at Delphi and the treasury built for Hyrieus <note>original: "Urius"</note>. They were, I have no doubt,

***

$^{33}$ Pausanias, Book 9, p. 781. Similarly, Coronis is said to have been the daughter of Phlegyas (Pausanias, Book 2, p. 170) and Cronus the son of Apollo (Book 2, p. 123). Chiron was the son of Saturn; Charon the son of Erebus and Night. The hero Charisius was the son of Lycaon—and this Lycaon was none other than Apollo, the god of light. These were all originally names of places, but they were later described as people and made the "children" of the deity to whom those places were sacred.

$^{34}$ "They were skilled at building both temples for the gods and palaces for men; for they built the temple at Delphi for Apollo, and the treasury for Hyrieus." <note>original Greek: Δεινοι Θεοις τε ἱερα κατασκευασασθαι, και βασιλεια ανθρωποις· και γαρ τῳ Απολλωνι τον ναον ῳκοδομησαντο τον εν Δελφοις, και Ὑριει τον θησαυρον.</note> Pausanias, Book 9, p. 785.
"Towers, as Aristotle says, were invented by the Cyclopes." <note>original Latin: Turres, ut Aristoteles, Cyclopes (invenerunt).</note> Pliny, Book 7, chapter 56.

When the Sibyl <note>a priestess and prophetess in ancient Greece and Rome</note> in Virgil's poetry shows Aeneas the place of torment in the underworld and leads him through many somber passages, we find that the entire area was separated from the regions of bliss by a wall built by the Cyclopians. Accordingly, at their exit, the Sibyl tells him:

-><sup>35</sup> *I see the walls forged in the furnaces of the Cyclopes.*<-
-><note>original: "Cyclopum educta caminis Mænia conspicio."</note><-

From this, we find that they were the reputed builders of the dwellings in the underworld. This idea arose from the actual buildings they constructed. For all the ancient concepts of the underworld and the torments of hell were derived from the temples in each country, and from the religious rites and inquisitions <note>meaning formal examinations or trials</note> practiced within them.

But the Cyclopians were not merely imaginary laborers. They founded several cities in Greece and constructed many temples to the gods that were highly esteemed in ancient times. They were so highly respected for their skill that, as the commentator <term>Scholiast</term> on the poet Statius observes, everything great and noble was regarded as "Cyclopian": <sup>36</sup> *Whatever is noble because of its great size is said to have been manufactured by the hand of the Cyclopes.* <note>original: "quicquid magnitudine suâ nobile est, Cyclopum manu dicitur fabricatum."</note> This was not a fiction, as one might suspect, for they were, for the most part, actual architects. And if, instead of those monstrous beings known as the Cyclopes <note>original: Κυκλωπες</note>, we substitute a colony of people called Cyclopians, we will find that all the accounts are true, which [is]...

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 503

They were undoubtedly a part of the people called Academians who lived in Attica <note>the region surrounding Athens</note>. There, they founded the Academia and the Ceramicus <note>a district of Athens famous for its pottery and cemetery</note> and introduced human sacrifices. Because of this, we are informed that during a plague, the Athenians sacrificed the three virgin daughters of Hyacinthus at the tomb of Geræstus the Cyclops. 

However, Geræstus was not a person, but a place. *Γεραισος* <note>original: Geraisos</note> is a slight variation of *Ker-Astus* and signifies the temple of Astus, the god of fire. This was certainly the ancient name of the place where these sacrifices were performed, and the *taphos* <term>original Greek: tomb or burial mound</term> was actually a Cyclopean altar upon which the rites were carried out. The Cyclopes are also said to have built the ancient city of Mycenae, which the hero Hercules, in a play by Seneca, threatens to destroy:

> Why do I delay? A greater war remains for me at Mycenae, so that the Cyclopean walls, overturned by my own hands, may fall.
> <note>original Latin: "quid moror? majus mihi Bellum Mycenis restat, ut Cyclopea Eversa manibus mænia nostris concidant." — Seneca, *Hercules Furens*, Act 4, v. 996.</note>

Nonnus also describes the city in the same way:

> Mycenae, encircled by a crown of walls built according to the rules of the Cyclopes.

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 510

[This symbol was] common to the temples of ⁶⁰ Osiris and was intended to signify the superintendency of Providence, from whom nothing was hidden. Among others, the serpent was esteemed a most salutary emblem, and they made use of it to signify superior skill and knowledge. A beautiful female countenance surrounded with an assemblage of serpents was made to denote divine wisdom, which they styled Meed and Meet—the *Metis* <note>original Greek: Μητις</note> of the Greeks. Under this characteristic, they represented a heavenly personage and joined her with Eros, or divine Love; and by these two, they supposed that the present mundane system was produced. Orpheus speaks of this deity in the masculine gender:

> ⁶¹ "And Metis, the first progenitor, and Eros, the much-delighting." <note>original Greek: Και Μητις, πρωτος γενετωρ, και Ερως πολυτερπης.</note>

On this account, many ancient temples were ornamented with this curious hieroglyphic, and among others, the temple of Caphisus ⁶² in Argolis. Caphisus is a compound of *Caph-Isis*, which signifies *Petra Isidis* <note>Latin: "The Rock of Isis"</note>, and relates to the same deity as Metis. For we must not regard sexes, nor differences of appellations, when we treat of ancient deities.

# THE ANALYSIS OF ANCIENT MYTHOLOGY. 511

I have noted that the Cyclopians of Thrace were called *Charopes*; they must have received this name from their religious rites and their place of worship. *Char-Opis* signifies the temple of the Python, or serpent: and we find that it was located near a poisonous pool. It was sacred to the Sun; and there were many temples of this name in <margin>⁶⁵</margin> Egypt and other countries. The Sun was called *Arez*; and the lion, which was a symbol of the Sun, had the same name. There is reason to think that the emblem upon *Charopian* temples was sometimes a lion. Homer undoubtedly had seen the fierce figure of this animal upon some sacred gateway in Egypt; he often refers to this when he speaks of a *Charopian* lion.

> <margin>⁶⁶</margin> "Bears, and wild boars, and fierce [Charopian] lions." <note>original Greek: Αρκτοι τ’, αργοτεροι τε Συες, χαροποι τε Λεοντες.</note>

The symbols upon temples were often regarded as talismans, and supposed to have a hidden and beneficial influence. These names—Aithousa, Alphiousa, Ampelousa, Anthemousa, Pithecousa, Scotousa, Arginousa, Lampadousa, Amathousa, Ophiousa, Asterousa, Acherousa, and Pelousa—signify the temple of Metis, or Divine Wisdom. *After-Ous* was a temple on Mount Caucasus; *Amath-Ous*, the same in Cyprus; *Ampel-Ous*, a temple in Mauritania; *Alphi-Ous*, in Elis; and *Achor-Ous*, in Egypt: all were dedicated to the Deity under different titles.

<margin>⁶⁵</margin> "The Egyptians decorate the doorways of their temples with lion's gaping mouths." <note>original Greek: Χασμασι λεοντειοις τα των ἱερων θυρωματα κοσμεσιν (οἱ Αἰγυπτιοι).</note> — Plutarch, *Isis and Osiris*, p. 366.
<margin>⁶⁶</margin> Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 11, line 610. It is a term that seems to have confused the commentators. "Charopian: striking, or fearful." <note>original Greek: Χαροποι, επιπληκτικοι, φοβεροι.</note> — Scholiast, ibid. It was certainly an Amonian term <note>Bryant uses "Amonian" to describe his theory of a global religion originating from the descendants of Ham, centered on sun worship</note>; and the Poet was referring to a Charonian temple.
"She [the Chimaera] had three heads: one of a fierce [Charopian] lion." <note>original Greek: Της δ’ ην τρεις κεφαλαι, μια μεν χαροποio λεοντος.</note> — Hesiod, *Theogony*, line 321.
Homer in another place mentions, "The howling of wolves, and of fierce [Charopian] lions." <note>original Greek: Λυκων κλαγγην, χαροπων τε Λεοντων.</note> — *Hymn to the Mother of the Gods*, line 4.

Just as a lion was called *Charops* for this reason, it was also named *Charon* after another temple. "Charon, the lion," <note>original Greek: Χαρων ὁ λεων.</note> according to Hesychius. Achilles is called a "spear-bearing Charon," <note>original Greek: Αιχμητης Χαρων</note> by Lycophron, line 260—meaning a martial Charonian Lion.

by which the building was preserved. In the temple of Minerva at Tegea, there was a sculpture of Medusa which the Goddess was said to have given, so that <margin>⁶⁷</margin> "the city might be unconquerable for all time" <note>original Greek: αναλωτον ες τον παντα χρονον ειναι (την πολιν)</note>. The idea of the Cyclopes forging thunder and lightning for Jupiter arose chiefly from the Cyclopeans engraving hieroglyphics of this kind upon the temples of the Deity. Because of this, they were later described as actual people.

> <margin>⁶⁹</margin> "They who gave thunder to Zeus, and forged the lightning bolt." <note>original Greek: ‘Οι Ζηνι βροντην τ’ εδοσαν, τευξαν τε κεραυνον.</note>

The poets viewed them merely as blacksmiths and condemned them to work at the anvil. This misunderstanding arose because the chief Cyclopean Deity was called *Acmon* and *Pyracmon* <note>The name Acmon is related to the Greek word for "anvil," which led to the association with blacksmithing.</note>. He was worshiped under the former title in Phrygia, where there was a city and district called Acmonia, mentioned by Alexander <margin>⁷⁰</margin> Polyhistor. The Amazons paid similar reverence to him, and there was a sacred grove called Acmonium.

Along the $^{71}$ Thermodon river, there was a place held in great repute. Acmon was viewed by some as the offspring of Heaven; by others, he was worshiped as Uranus and Cœlus <note>Latin: Cœlus, meaning "Heaven"</note>, the heaven itself. Acmonides was supposed to have been his $^{72}$ son, whom some mythologists identified as the ruling spirit of the earth. Because of this, Simmias of Rhodes introduces Divine Love displaying his influence and saying that he produced Acmonides—that mighty monarch of the earth—and at the same time founded the sea.

> "Behold me, the lord of the broad-breasted earth, Acmonides, who also established the sea." <note>original: Λευσσε με τον Γας τε βαρυςερνε Ανακτ’ Ακμονιδαν, ταν αλα θ’ εδρασαντα.</note> $^{73}$

Acmon seems to have been worshiped in ancient times at Tiryns, that ancient city of Greece whose towers were said to have been built by the Cyclopeans. For Acmon was the Cyclopean Deity; he is represented by Callimachus as the protecting <note>original: tutelary</note> God of the place, though the passage has been interpreted in other ways.

The term has commonly been looked upon as an adjective, and the passage has been translated as "Such a Tirynthian, unwearied" <note>original: Talis Tirynthius indefessus</note>, which makes little sense.
